item.title: App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings

Our Google Ads app campaign assets came out of the pipeline that already took our store screenshots, with one recording step, one JSON spec per language, and a width check for Korean headlines.

A Google Ads app campaign doesn't take a finished ad. You hand it headlines, descriptions, images and videos, and Google assembles the ads itself, so you need the same scenes in several aspect ratios and every language you run. For our puzzle game Arrow Knots we didn't edit any of that by hand. We bolted screen recording onto the automation that already took our Play Store screenshots, and it produced 24 images and 6 videos.

Ad assets are never one-and-done. Every new hook or headline means another round, and here the second round needed no new recording, only an edited spec file.

Screen recording on top of the store-capture code

On the evening of October 8, 2026, the operator asked whether it was time to add campaigns or assets in Google Ads. The agent (Claude Code) advised against spending money yet and suggested preparing the assets first, since that part is free. The reply was to go ahead and prepare everything properly.

The agent borrowed our Galaxy S21 for 30 minutes and started with Block Turn, the other game in the same repository. By that evening the ad text, images, videos and a campaign runbook (the step-by-step document the operator follows) were in one commit. Arrow Knots then took the same scripts and changed only the colours and font.

It went that fast because the code for opening boards and making moves already existed. Both games have a capture build, a release-code build with ads and analytics off, that a script drives over adb (Android's command-line tool for controlling a device over USB) to take store screenshots. The new record_play.py makes exactly the same moves and simply turns on the phone's screen recorder (adb shell screenrecord) around them. The ad images weren't shot again at all: they are the store captures with a caption and background added.

Four scenes, three ratios and two languages give 24 images. The videos come in portrait, landscape and square for each language. A portrait phone recording has to sit differently in each frame: the caption goes left in the wide image, right in the square one and on top in the tall one. One function in the compose script, layout, decides that for every format.

One JSON spec, and only real gameplay

The structure of each video lives in videos.json, not in code. Each scene names a raw recording, the start and end seconds to cut, and the title and subtitle to lay over it. The first Korean cut ran level 95 solved from the first move, then the Neon Rush bonus game that appears every 25 levels, then the big level 705 board, then an end card with the app name. Here is the first English scene:

{"src": "play", "start": 2.5, "end": 16.2, "title": "Tap. Slide. Untangle.", "sub": "Find the order\nthat frees them all"}

The compose script reads that line, trims the raw recording play.mp4, draws the caption with Pillow (the Python imaging library) and lets ffmpeg overlay it on the footage.

The recorder's docstring says "Real play only". Google Ads' Misrepresentation policy bans designs that mimic system notifications and non-functional elements that look like buttons, and it flags ads that don't match the app. The repository goes a step further: no staged failures and no mocked screens, only moves the recording script actually made. Images follow the same rule, so they start from store captures.

We had done this the other way before. Our Korean spell-checker app's store-image commit from October 1 (2598823) carried a separate compose script for each screen, plus more for tablet and feature graphics. Every new screen meant a new script. The game pipeline split the work into a spec file and one script.

Keep your ad-asset scripts in the same repository as your store-capture scripts, on the same recordings. If they live apart, the ads keep showing the old screens after the store listing moves on.

Korean headlines count each character as two

App campaign headlines are capped at 30 characters and descriptions at 90. Google Ads help says each double-width character, as in Korean, Japanese or Chinese, counts as two toward the limit.

So a headline in Korean only fits about 15 characters. The v2 headline 남은 화살표가 우르르 ("the rest of the arrows tumble out") is 11 characters but 20 wide. Measure it with len() and a line can pass that Google Ads counts as over the limit.

The repository's check_text.py does the measuring, and the core is one function. It reads each character's East Asian width from Python's standard unicodedata module and counts wide (W) and fullwidth (F) characters as two:

import json, unicodedata
LIMITS = {"headlines": 30, "descriptions": 90}
def width(s):
    return sum(2 if unicodedata.east_asian_width(c) in "WF" else 1 for c in s)

If any line is over, the script exits with code 1. Here is part of the output when we reran it on November 12, 2026:

OK  ko head  16/30 톡 누르면 스르륵
OK  ko head  22/30 25레벨마다 보너스 게임
...
OK  en head  28/30 A bonus game every 25 levels
...
OK  en head  26/30 1,000 brain-teasing levels

All 20 lines passed. The longest English headline used 28 of 30, the longest Korean one 23. Mixed digits, commas and Hangul are hard to count by eye, so the check runs every time the copy changes.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We uploaded videos through Google Ads, not the YouTube API

The agent set out to post the six Block Turn videos to YouTube as unlisted, so their links could go into the campaign, and turned on the YouTube API in a Google Cloud project and wrote an upload script. The login carrying upload permission was refused twice, first with a 400 error and then with a "This app is blocked" page; that story is in gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate. Building our own OAuth client (a sign-in app registered under our name) and consent screen (the page that asks a user for permission) wasn't worth it for six videos, so the runbook was rewritten in commit e13d4d4: upload the files in Google Ads while adding assets, and they go to the linked YouTube channel. The upload script stays in the repo for when we have our own OAuth client.

The agent had repeatedly said to create a new Google Ads account. There already was one, running ads for the spell-checker app, and the runbook switched to it. The same night the operator set a rule: anything that costs money or looks odd gets asked first (the agent wrote it down as "costs money or is hard to undo"). How that rule shapes daily budget work is in A daily Google Ads budget check that only suggests.

v2 changed the spec, not the recording

The October 11 marketing plan called for new Korean assets with a board emptying within the first two seconds. v1 solved level 95 from the first move, so that moment came around 7 s in.

The v2 script imports the v1 compose script and only writes a new scene spec. It cuts the same recording from 6.5 s to 12.8 s, where the board empties, puts that first, and swaps the order of the big board and Neon Rush. New Korean headlines went through the width check, and after the operator approved, some of them and the new video went into the campaign that night. All three v2 formats run 22.7 seconds.

Whether the faster hook works is still open. Our harness, an automated setup where AI agents run marketing and operations jobs on a daily schedule, on November 6 logged the asset ratings Google Ads gives each asset for the week before. The v1 portrait video was rated "Best" and the v2 portrait video "Low". With 50 and 57 impressions, that says nothing either way. Spend and cost per install are in Google Ads for a puzzle game: CPI 30x break-even.

The day after v2, its first 11.8 seconds became a TikTok and Instagram Reels clip (the Reel went up on October 20), and on November 6 two Shorts made by the harness were added as video assets to both games' Korean campaigns. Planning those clips is covered in TikTok, Reels and Shorts plans with Claude Code.

Seven steps from capture build to re-cut

This assumes your app has a build that a script can drive.

  1. Turn off ads and analytics in the capture build. Our capture and test builds send no analytics events, so device recordings never reach the GA4 reports.

  2. Import the move-making code from your store-capture script and write one recording function per scene. Start with adb shell screenrecord; stop it with SIGINT (the same interrupt Ctrl+C sends), or the mp4 may not be finished properly.

  3. Put a scene spec per language in JSON: raw clip name, start and end, title, subtitle, end-card text.

  4. Decide the per-ratio layout in one function. Draw captions with Pillow and overlay and concatenate with ffmpeg. Build images from store captures in 1.91:1, 1:1 and 4:5 frames.

  5. Run headlines and descriptions through a width checker that counts wide characters as two and fails when a line is over.

  6. Upload videos as files in Google Ads when you add assets. The YouTube API route needs your own OAuth client.

  7. For a new cut, keep the recordings and change only the cut points and order in the spec.

Silent videos and a button-shaped end card

These videos have no sound; the compose script adds a silent audio track. On November 1 the operator rejected our harness's short-form videos partly for silent gameplay, and the ads still have the same gap.

The end card's "Play free now" is text inside a rounded rectangle in the button colour. The script's comment says it is not a fake store badge or install button, but it sits close to the policy's "non-functional elements that resemble buttons".

Raw recordings are not committed to git. v2 came from originals still in a cache folder; without them, it's back to the phone. A test phone also tends to be shared between sessions. On October 8, eight to ten minutes after the recording finished and the S21 was handed back, another session taking store captures on the same phone had a Block Turn screen pop up and lost one shot. We never found out which session opened it.

The next thing to check is the Shorts assets added on November 6: on November 13 their installs are due to be compared with the seven days before.

As of November 12, 2026. sugar-game git history (18ad250, 8fef5d5, e13d4d4, cc43582) and asset files; the v2 build script and posting log (Oct 17 to 20, 2026); the Oct 8 work-session log; the Oct 11 marketing plan; check_text.py rerun and ffprobe/ffmpeg measurements (Nov 12, 2026); spell-checker app commit 2598823; Google Ads help on text length limits and the Misrepresentation policy (checked Nov 12, 2026).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

item.title: gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate

gcloud's built-in login app could not get the analytics scope (nor YouTube or Sheets), so impersonate a service account and let it hold the analytics token.

If you add the analytics scope to gcloud auth application-default login so a script can read Google Analytics 4 (GA4), the browser shows Google's "This app is blocked" page (the operator's Korean screen read 차단된 앱). Changing the scope list changed nothing. SugarMount saw that page three times between October 8 and 15, 2026, asking for YouTube and analytics scopes, and each time the login command came from an AI coding agent.

On the 15th we switched to service account impersonation: your own account fetches a short-lived token on behalf of a service account. Less than five minutes after the block, the agent was listing GA4 properties, and no key file was ever created.

Three runs into the same page

On the night of October 8 the agent wanted to upload ad videos to YouTube and proposed a login asking for drive.file and youtube.upload together. Google answered with a 400 saying those scopes cannot be requested together. Dropping drive.file and asking for the YouTube scopes on their own, from a separate gcloud config folder, produced "This app is blocked", and the agent gave up on the API upload and moved the videos to the Google Ads upload screen (App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings). On the 11th the same page appeared while wiring GA4 into a personal dashboard server, and on the 15th while looking at uninstall counts for two games.

The block is on gcloud's own login app

On the 15th the starting point was a 403 with ACCESS_TOKEN_SCOPE_INSUFFICIENT. The diagnosis was right: the token from ADC (Application Default Credentials, the default credentials scripts borrow) had no analytics scope. The fix was wrong. gcloud auth application-default login opens the consent screen with the OAuth client built into gcloud. Changing the scope list did not help, and neither did a separate config folder. On the 11th, a desktop OAuth client we created ourselves asked for the same analytics.readonly and went through.

What memory held of October 8 was one parenthetical inside a game release status note: the gcloud client is blocked for YouTube scopes. On the 15th the session read that note and, 39 seconds later, proposed the same shape of login command with the analytics scope swapped in. When an agent hands you a gcloud login command and says one more scope will fix it, don't run it.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Getting an impersonated token without a key

  1. In the Cloud project linked to GA4, enable the IAM Credentials API (the API that issues service account tokens) and the Analytics Data API, and create a service account. Do not create a key.

  2. Give your own Google account the Service Account Token Creator role (roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator) on that service account.

  3. In GA4 Admin, under account access management, add the service account's address as a Viewer. Adding it at the account level covers every property.

  4. Mint a token and send it in the Authorization header as a Bearer token to the GA4 Data API.

    gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account=<service account address> --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly

Your login only uses the cloud-platform scope (general Google Cloud access) it already had, to call the IAM Credentials API; the analytics scope sits on the service account's token. gcloud's impersonation flag needs a gcloud user login, so on a Windows PC with only ADC we changed the tool to call the IAM Credentials API directly (October 22). On the 15th, Claude Code's auto-mode permission classifier (an automatic check that hands risky commands to a person) refused steps 1–2 (the role grant included), so the operator ran them by hand, and also did step 3 in the GA4 screen.

On October 11, after the operator asked why that account's credentials were going into the report service, the dashboard server moved from the full gcloud credential copied to it to a token from our own desktop OAuth client, limited to AdMob read, GA4 read and Gmail send (commit 4254b7f). That route means keeping a client secret file, and on the 15th the command that searched for such a file was refused by the classifier, so the agent chose impersonation, which leaves no secret to leak.

One reference note in memory

That evening the agent wrote a separate reference note in the game folder's memory, just for GA4 access. Its first line is the working command, followed by Why and How to apply fields (why the rule exists, when to use it): putting analytics.readonly into ADC gives "This app is blocked", and the tool to use instead.

Claude Code memory lives per project folder, so the note only works there. Two days later, in a session for another app (a Korean document viewer), a subagent hit a GA4 Data API 403 and again left an ADC login command in its report; that session's misreading is in An AI agent reported "GA4: zero in 28 days"; the table report had 43 users. On October 25 another project tried a spreadsheets scope the same way and hit "This app is blocked" a fourth time. The October 8 runbook change (commit e13d4d4) had already moved the video upload to the Google Ads screen. We have not tried Gmail send, AdMob read or YouTube upload through impersonation.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does Google say "This request contains scopes that cannot be requested together"?

Some scope pairs are refused in a single login request. On October 8 the pair was drive.file and youtube.upload. Dropping drive.file and asking for the YouTube scopes alone made the 400 go away, but the YouTube scopes then hit "This app is blocked" through gcloud's default login.

Do I need a service account key file to read the GA4 Data API?

No. Give your account the Token Creator role on the service account, add the service account as a Viewer in GA4 account access management (the agent said doing this through the API would need a scope gcloud's login is blocked from, so the operator did it in the GA4 screen), and mint short-lived tokens with --impersonate-service-account. The service account in this note has read GA4 since October 15 with no key file.

Checked 2026-11-12. Claude Code session transcripts (Oct 8, 11, 15, 17 and 25; UTC converted to KST), the game folder's memory (reference note, Oct 15), personal dashboard server commit 4254b7f (Oct 11), game repository commits e13d4d4 (Oct 8) and 7a61407 (Oct 22).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Where an Android theme colour leaks into dialogs – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

No XML file said white, yet the dialog buttons vanished: three places a theme colour leaked

Our dialog and bottom-sheet buttons inherited the app bar colour. We now override the theme for those windows only and measure contrast on the shown view.

In SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling app, the Cancel and OK buttons on a delete confirmation were drawn almost white on a white dialog. The contrast ratio was 1.02:1, far below the 4.5:1 that body text needs. When we fixed it on September 16, 2026, no layout XML set that text to white: the theme colour picked to keep the app bar light had flowed into the button labels.

Eleven days later the same colour came back in two new bottom sheets, and this time it only showed up on a Galaxy S21 running the release build. The first fix had covered dialogs only; the correction sheet's test only checked that the text colour matched the intended one, and the mini window's test did not check colour at all. If your app uses its app bar colour as the theme's primary colour, any new dialog or sheet can leak the same way.

The app bar colour reached button text in three places

At 13:25 KST on September 16 the operator reported that the buttons on the activity-history delete popup were white and unreadable in light mode. The agent (Claude) followed the style definitions in Material Components 1.14.0, Google's Android UI library, and found that the button text colour ends in a single theme attribute:

AlertDialog button
  → buttonBarButtonStyle
  → Widget.MaterialComponents.Button.TextButton
  → mtrl_text_btn_text_color_selector (enabled colour)
  → ?attr/colorPrimary

colorPrimary is the theme's main colour slot, and our app theme (AppTheme) put the app bar colour there: #fafdff in light, black in dark. Black on the white dialog is 21:1, which is why only light mode broke.

Changing the global colorPrimary would have recoloured the app bar, so that was out. Our accent blue only reaches 3.80:1 on white, short of the bar. The first fix (c3f4f87) added a theme overlay that applies to dialog windows only, alertDialogTheme, in both light and dark, and inside it overrode just colorPrimary with a darker blue. The overlay keeps the original dialog theme as its parent.

The two screens added on September 27 picked up the same colour another way. The correction sheet that opens when you tap a coloured word and the mini window behind the text-selection menu are both BottomSheetDialogs, panels that slide up from the bottom, and both inflated their content (built view objects from layout XML) with the activity context. Views inflated that way never pass through the sheet's theme overlay, so they read colorPrimary straight from the activity's AppTheme. The fill of the "Why is this wrong?" button and the text of OK, Copy correction and Open in app all came out #fafdff, 1.00 to 1.02:1 on the white sheet.

Dark mode had one more cause. This app's dark AppTheme also inherits from a light theme (Theme.MaterialComponents.Light), so the correction sheet stayed white in dark mode, and the correction text colours made brighter for dark mode sat on it at 3.2:1. The mini window was the reverse: a dark #212121 surface, but its result text took the theme's default black (1.30:1 by our calculation).

The fix was to inflate the sheet content with the sheet's own context (dialog.context) and add a sheet-only overlay (bottomSheetDialogTheme) to AppTheme that sets the sheet surface and a dedicated button colour. On September 28 the correction sheet was fixed first, together with the overlay (4c27ac7); twenty-one minutes later the mini window, already under that overlay, only needed its context and button colour changed.

The first test read XML; the rewrite reads the shown button

The test in the first commit (c3f4f87, 13:54) read resource XML as text: it checked that the overlay line existed and that the button colour value cleared 4.5:1 on white. The white text only exists after the theme resolves its attributes at runtime, so a check on XML values can't see this bug.

At 14:10 the operator asked whether everything had really changed and told the agent to cross-check before release. Only then did the agent write a Robolectric test (99e6bf4; Robolectric runs Android code on the JVM without a device), on the grounds that what the XML says and what the widget draws are different things. The test builds a dialog on a context themed with AppTheme, calls show() and reads the colour each button actually draws (currentTextColor). With the one overlay line deleted from the light theme, the original symptom came back as numbers:

OK     #fafdff on #ffffff = 1.02:1   FAIL
Cancel #fafdff on #ffffff = 1.02:1   FAIL
buttons readable in dark mode        pass

The September 27 correction sheet did ship with a Robolectric test, but it only compared the corrected word's currentTextColor with the intended red highlight colour. If the colour matches, the test passes whether that word sits on a white sheet or a dark one. After the September 28 check on the S21, the rewritten test first reads the sheet's real surface colour (the first check argument is a Korean label meaning "correction, type colour"):

// sheet surface view
val sheet = dialog.findViewById<View>(com.google.android.material.R.id.design_bottom_sheet)
// fill colour of the sheet's background shape
val bg = (sheet.background as MaterialShapeDrawable).fillColor!!.defaultColor
check("교정(유형 색)", dialog.findViewById<TextView>(R.id.correction_corrected).currentTextColor, bg, 4.5)

It measures the sheet's text and buttons this way, in light and dark. Filled buttons get two checks: text on fill at 4.5:1 and fill on sheet at 3:1. Measure theme colour bugs from the shown view's currentTextColor and the surface actually behind it, not from XML values.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The highlight colours kept their hue; only lightness moved

A separate problem, one the agent had flagged four minutes before the dialog report, was in the spelling highlights, where colour tells the user the error type: red for spelling, teal for spacing, blue for statistics-based corrections, orange for possible non-standard words, and violet for a type that Naver (Korea's largest portal, whose checker the app calls) marks separately. The dark-mode colour folder (values-night) defined none of the five, so dark mode used the light values, and violet on the #212121 background was 2.70:1.

At 13:21, answering the operator's question about whether anything else needed testing, the agent flagged that violet and said a single lighter violet for dark mode would fix it. That clears the bar easily, but in HSL the hue turns by nearly 5 degrees and saturation goes to 100%, a different violet. When the operator asked for a proper fix, the agent added all five dark values but changed only orange in light mode, leaving red, teal and blue as they were and keeping red and teal as the app's familiar colours.

At 13:40 its own 4.5:1 test failed all three, and the agent reported that the test had refuted its judgement. In the output, temp1 is blue, temp2 teal and temp4 red:

light/temp1 #3982ff on #fafdff = 3.54:1
light/temp2 #009a9a on #fafdff = 3.38:1
light/temp4 #ee4b4b on #fafdff = 3.58:1

Only light violet and dark orange stayed as they were; the other eight values (the seven under 4.5:1, plus dark teal at a thin 4.67:1) kept their hue and moved lightness only: darker for light mode, lighter for dark. Recomputed, the largest hue shift is 0.2 degrees (blue). The agent first computed values that landed just over 4.5:1, then retargeted dark mode at 5.0:1 for some margin.

The c3f4f87 message records the decision as "red stays red, green stays green" (its green is the teal above). Don't rotate the hue of a colour that means something. Move lightness, and define the value in both values and values-night. On the web side we search for dark text colours the same way, one lightness percent at a time, as described in Measuring 4.5:1 colour contrast in the site build.

Measuring contrast on the shown view, step by step

  1. Follow the widget style of the unreadable text until it ends. If it ends in a theme attribute such as ?attr/colorPrimary, check whether that attribute holds a colour chosen for something else (here, the app bar).
  2. Leave the global theme colour alone and override it for that window only (alertDialogTheme, bottomSheetDialogTheme). Inflate the content with dialog.context. The dialog side looked like this: 
    <!-- inside AppTheme (both values and values-night) -->
<item name="alertDialogTheme">@style/AlertDialogTheme</item>
<style name="AlertDialogTheme" parent="ThemeOverlay.MaterialComponents.Dialog.Alert">
    <item name="colorPrimary">@color/dialog_button_text</item> <!-- #0063c6 -->
</style>
  3. Check that every theme the manifest names gets the overlays, and that no parent="Theme.…" cuts it off from the theme before the dot.
  4. For colours that carry meaning, lock the HSL hue and move lightness, finding light and dark values separately.
  5. In Robolectric, show() the screen and measure currentTextColor against the real surface (for a sheet, the fillColor of its MaterialShapeDrawable) in light and dark.
  6. Revert one line of the fix and confirm the test fails with the original number, 1.02:1 in our case. On September 16, six such reverts were all caught.
  7. Install the release APK on a real device and open each new screen once in light and dark.

Each screen needs its own measuring test, so a new screen without one surfaces on a device first, as the sheets did on September 28. That day's S21 check is in Agent code review: fix what survives refutation. Robolectric does not reproduce device rendering, and this app is built from XML views; we have not measured Jetpack Compose screens.

Two places the overlay doesn't reach: NoActionBar and the framework AlertDialog

At 14:19 on September 16, while matching every dialog call to its manifest theme, the agent flagged one more thing. AppTheme.NoActionBar reads like a child of AppTheme, but it is declared with parent="Theme.AppCompat.NoActionBar". In Android styles, an explicit parent attribute replaces the inheritance implied by the dotted name. This theme therefore carries neither of the two overlays.

One screen uses it: the launch screen. Its version and permission popups are a custom-layout window that never touches colorPrimary, so nothing has leaked there yet. The changelog for app version 1.6.018 warns that adding an AlertDialog to that screen would bypass the fix, and on November 10 the parent was unchanged.

The September 16 audit counted three places that build a dialog (activity-history delete, greeting cards, the subscription screen) as covered because all ran under AppTheme. Only the activity-history one, the dialog in the report, was an androidx dialog; the other two used the framework's built-in android.app.AlertDialog. The greeting-card call has since been removed, but on the remote develop branch as of November 10 one call on the subscription screen (shown only when a user holds more than one subscription) is still the framework class. The September 16 measuring test shows the androidx dialog, so that one call's button colour has not been measured on a shown dialog yet.

As of November 11, 2026. Based on the SugarSpeller repository history, the 1.6.018 changelog and the September 16 session log; contrast ratios were recomputed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula. The current state is as of the remote develop branch on November 10.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

item.title: Release gates that checked the wrong input – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

Our release gates were checking something other than the release: a plaintext AAB and one missing dart-define

A plaintext-signaling AAB passed one of our release gates, and another gate's ad SDK check compared a dependency list (classpath) the intended release never used. Both gates read inputs built next to the release, not the release.

An Android app bundle (AAB) built from a development config, one our own deployment doc called "not for submission", got a PASS from a release gate. That was September 13, 2026, in our Flutter peer-to-peer chat app. The server address was localhost, and the signaling that sets up connections ran unencrypted. A month later, in AXFamily, a family schedule app, the gate's ad SDK check turned out to be comparing a dependency list from a different build than the one we meant to ship.

We built both gates with an AI coding agent, and both judged an input produced next to the release instead of the release itself. If you read a green gate as proof the release was checked, the first question is what that PASS actually read.

A plaintext-signaling AAB passed

Before building, the chat app's release workflow checked its dart-define file (the key=value settings Flutter compiles into the app) with one line:

grep -Eq 'example\.invalid|CHANGE_ME' "$f"   # fail if found

The production config still had a placeholder host, so it was blocked. The development config points at localhost with TLS off, but contains neither string, so it passed. On September 13, CI built a 43 MB test AAB from exactly that config, signed with the upload key, and the bundle verification script said PASS.

The deployment doc written that day called the AAB "a pipeline test build, not for submission", and still summarized that there were no blockers left on the code side. Per the repository's own release rules, nothing outside the app config stops plaintext ws:// signaling, so the same workflow could have shipped a signed, submittable AAB with plaintext signaling.

The cross-check two days later opens with its reason: judging whether to ship from documents its own author wrote would be self-confirmation, not a cross-check. So it didn't rely on the deployment doc's claims, re-measured the repository, and concluded "not ready to ship yet" (held back by three operational decisions, with three defects found along the way).

That night, commit 184e5ee put the same rule into both the workflow and the verification script: TLS must be on, and an empty host, localhost, or a private, loopback or link-local IP fails. A pipeline rehearsal has to turn on allow_insecure_signaling, a flag that defaults to false, and then passes with a warning. Six fixtures (inputs made on purpose to test the rule) were run by hand and the results written into the doc; a re-run of the same check appears further down.

The same commit fixed the signature check. The certificate tool keytool writes its errors to standard output, so the 'could not read signature' branch never ran and the script quit without a reason, skipping the checks after it. No bad build got through. The script now looks for the certificate owner line (Owner:). The crypto tests CI skipped that night are covered in Silently skipped tests keep CI green.

AXFamily's gate judged another ad SDK

AXFamily shows ads through the google_mobile_ads 9.1.0 plugin, which picks the Android ad SDK from the build's dart-defines. Its build.gradle decodes the Gradle property dart-defines (base64-encoded KEY=VALUE pairs joined by commas) and decides like this:

def useNextGenSdk = dartEnvironmentVariables.USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK ? dartEnvironmentVariables.USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK : false

With a value you get the Next-Gen SDK (ads-mobile-sdk); without one, the Legacy SDK (play-services-ads). flutter build hands dart-defines to Gradle through that property. Call Gradle on its own and the property isn't there, so you always get Legacy.

Commit 5427191 added the gate on October 9 in four steps: wipe the build folder, build a fresh AAB, have Gradle list the release dependencies, then judge. Step three passed no dart-defines. Whatever values built the AAB, the gate judged the Legacy list, and the committed reference list (the snapshot) it compared against came from the same command, so the comparison could only ever match.

The dart-define check was off the other way. The gate only accepted keys on its allow list, and USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK wasn't on it.

The build that survived 2,000 random-input events on a Galaxy S21 that day was Next-Gen. The only build this gate could pass was Legacy, which that test never touched, and the verified config would have been blocked for carrying an unknown key.

On October 10, commit c38703b made step three pass the same values as the AAB build, as -Pdart-defines in the format flutter build uses, without printing the values. The dart-define check now accepts USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK only when it is exactly 'true'. The plugin's ternary follows the truthiness rules of Groovy, the language build.gradle is written in, where any non-empty string is true, so 'false' also gives you Next-Gen.

Regenerating the snapshot with the fixed command changed it as below, and the tests gained three cases that must fail: 'false', an empty string, and a missing key.

Snapshot lines that changedBeforeAfter
Lines211214 (5 removed, 8 added)
Ad SDKplay-services-ads, play-services-ads-apiads-mobile-sdk
Companions3 measurement and ad-services modules6 Cronet (Chrome's network stack) modules, kotlinx-coroutines-guava

One command made the snapshot too

On the AXFamily side the cause had three layers. The gate listed dependencies with a different command from the one that built the release, and since the plugin picks dependencies from dart-defines, that changed the result. The commit that added the gate shows no check that the two commands got the same inputs. The last layer is that the reference, the snapshot and the test fixture, came out of that same command. There's no record of a full gate run before the fix.

In the chat app, the development config already in the repository did go through the gate, but until the fix nobody treated it as an input that had to fail.

About six and a half hours before c38703b, commit 1fcc1e1 gave the AXFamily gate a step that opens the AAB's dex files (the compiled app code) and libapp.so (where Flutter's compiled Dart code lives) directly to make sure no end-to-end test mode leaked in. The gate already had a way to read the release, and the SDK list was still judged from a Gradle report.

The missing check was in the decision record

AXFamily's October 5 decision record already had the condition: Next-Gen is opt-in, so CI pins USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK=true and checks that the release APK contains ads-mobile-sdk. The item's status is "recommendation, presumed accepted": one the operator did not object to. The backlog's acceptance criteria asked for the same dart-define. The October 9 gate had neither, and committed a Legacy list as its snapshot instead.

Both gates, both fixes, and the wrong deployment summary all came from commits co-authored by Claude. The cross-check doc, not a person, corrected the summary; on the record the human part ends at not objecting to the decision record's recommendation.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Required values, not banned strings

Had we only added localhost to the placeholder list, 192.168.0.10 and 172.20.1.5 from the fixtures would still pass with TLS on. Instead of listing addresses to block, the fix requires what a release must have (TLS on, a public host), and because the pipeline still needs rehearsals, the exception opens only through the default-false flag.

For AXFamily, the gate could have accepted any non-empty USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK. That matches the plugin, but a config reading 'false' would produce a Next-Gen build and the gate would say nothing. Only an exact 'true' passes.

Checks that read a side file skip locally

The chat app's new TLS check and the older dart-define record check don't open the AAB. They read dart_defines.txt, a record the workflow writes from the config and leaves next to the AAB. Run the script locally without that file and both checks print SKIP; if everything else passes, the result is PASS. Nor does the script confirm the AAB and the record belong together.

Below is the new TLS check alone, re-run on November 11 against seven fixtures. The first six match the September 15 results; the seventh has no record file. signal.example.com is a reserved placeholder domain.

The AXFamily gate builds its own AAB, which made passing it the same inputs easy. The chat app workflow's host check only judges IP literals, so a name that looks public but resolves to a private IP is not caught.

The fixed gate inputs have no tests

The chat app's fixtures were run by hand, and only the results went into the doc. 184e5ee touched just the workflow and the verification script, and no commit has changed either file since. In AXFamily, no test looks at whether the gate passes -Pdart-defines to Gradle.

Drop that argument and the SDK step now fails against the Next-Gen snapshot. But the usage comment of the snapshot script that the error points to also omits it, so regenerating the snapshot as that comment says would put the gate back where it started. The gate also still lacks the check the decision record asked for: ads-mobile-sdk inside the release (the record says APK).

One must-fail fixture per gate

So this is the order we now use to check the gate itself. The three-stage pre-upload check we use for a separate set of Android apps is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

  1. For each gate step, write down what it reads: the release itself (the AAB's manifest, dex, signature), the inputs that built the release, or an input built separately.
  2. If it's built separately, confirm it uses the same arguments as the command that built the release. In Flutter, pass the same values to Gradle with -Pdart-defines. The AXFamily gate does it like this from the android folder (locking and output capture left out), where $DEFINES is the JSON file given to --dart-define-from-file: 
    DD="$(node -e 'const d=JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1],"utf8"));process.stdout.write(Object.entries(d).map(([k,v])=>Buffer.from(k+"="+v).toString("base64")).join(","))' "$DEFINES")"
./gradlew --no-daemon -q :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath "-Pdart-defines=$DD"
  3. For a step that compares against a snapshot, check that the snapshot came from a command with the same arguments. At least once, confirm the SDK from the release side. The October 9 device test confirmed Next-Gen by finding the Next-Gen package on 111 lines of mapping.txt, the name map R8 leaves behind. 
    grep -c 'com.google.android.libraries.ads.mobile.sdk' build/app/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt
    Don't use com.google.android.gms.ads to detect Legacy: Next-Gen ships compatibility classes under that name (37 lines in the same record). The line above restates that check; there's no record of it being run exactly as written.
  4. Require the values a release must have (TLS on, a switch exactly 'true') instead of listing banned strings. Open exceptions only through a flag that defaults to false and warns when on.
  5. Give every gate one fixture that must fail: the development config already in the repository, a dart-define file missing a switch, an unsigned AAB. Check that it fails and that the reason gets printed.
  6. Commit that fixture as a test. When you fix a gate, put the input it should have blocked into the same commit.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can flutter build --dart-define change Android dependencies?

It can, depending on the plugin. google_mobile_ads 9.1.0 reads USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK from the Gradle property dart-defines and attaches either the Next-Gen or the Legacy ad SDK, so a separate Gradle call needs the same values through -Pdart-defines to resolve the same dependencies.

Does USE_NEXT_GEN_SDK=false give you the Legacy SDK?

Not in 9.1.0. The plugin treats any non-empty string as true, so 'false' still means Next-Gen; to get Legacy you have to leave the key out.

As of 2026-11-11, rechecked against the git history of both app repositories, the cross-check doc, the ad SDK device-test notes, the decision record and the plugin source. Server addresses, signing key details and the app's package name are left out.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • A malicious file set for a document viewer: ZIP bombs, CFB loops and XSS, generated and wired into tests
  • Silently skipped tests keep CI green: three crypto cross-checks and an integration test that went stale for six days
  • The 95.2% realism score never came out of the runner, and the 3D view was a fixed drawing
  • Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in

item.title: Claude Code login and a first unattended question – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Claude Code login and a first unattended question

You are done when you have two sign-ins, one for everyday chat and one for scheduled jobs, and claude -p answers a question and finishes with exit code 0.

Windows harness series, part 4 of 11 · Previous Install Git and Claude Code · Next Install Docker Desktop

Claude Code, installed in part 3, does nothing until you sign in. In this part you sign in through your web browser, then try claude -p, which answers one question and exits without opening a chat screen. Finally you create a second sign-in, kept in its own folder, for the jobs you will schedule later.

Every command goes into the Windows PowerShell window from part 2. If claude --version printed a version number at the end of part 3, you are ready.

What you will have

  • Result: an everyday sign-in and a separate sign-in for scheduled jobs, and claude -p answering a question
  • You need: a PC that finished part 3, a paid Claude plan, a web browser
  • Cost: on Claude's pricing page, Pro is $20 a month ($17 a month billed annually), Max $100 and Ultra $200 (as of Nov 11, 2026)

Step 1: Make a work folder and sign in

Everything in this series lives in a harness folder inside your user folder. The first time Claude Code runs, it asks you to sign in through the browser.

  1. Open a new Windows PowerShell window, paste the line below and press Enter. This creates the harness folder.

    mkdir $HOME\harness

  2. Move into it. If you are unsure where you are, type (Get-Location).Path from part 2 and check that the path ends in harness.

    cd $HOME\harness

  3. Start Claude Code.

    claude

  4. On the first-run screens, follow the text on screen. If one asks how you want to sign in, choose the option that signs in with your subscription (your Claude account).

  5. A browser window opens; sign in with your Claude account. If no browser opens, press c in the PowerShell window to copy the sign-in address, then paste it into the browser's address bar.

  6. If the browser shows a code after you sign in instead of returning, paste that code into PowerShell where it says Paste code here if prompted. For anything else, follow the text on screen.

It worked if

PowerShell prints Login successful and asks you to press Enter. Your credentials are saved, so Claude Code will not ask again next time.

Step 2: Have one ordinary chat

Press Enter and follow any other text on screen. You then reach Claude Code's chat screen, where you type a question and read the answer.

  1. Type a question and press Enter, for example Explain the game-ad metric CPI in one sentence.

  2. Read the answer, then close the PowerShell window.

Step 3: Ask a first question with claude -p

With -p, Claude Code skips the chat screen: it answers one question and exits. The jobs you schedule in part 7 run this way.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 passes text to other programs using the encoding stored in $OutputEncoding, and the default is ASCII, which holds English letters only. The example below asks in Korean, so we switch to UTF-8 first. Do the same whenever a question contains non-English characters.

  1. Open a new PowerShell window and go to the harness folder.

    cd $HOME\harness

  2. Set the encoding. Nothing is printed when it works. Enter this line again in every new window.

    $OutputEncoding = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8

  3. Send the question. echo prints the text, the vertical bar | (a pipe) hands that text to claude -p as its input, and --model haiku picks the Haiku model. This is the exact command we ran; the Korean text asks the same CPI question as step 2.

    echo '게임 앱 광고 지표 CPI를 한 문장으로 설명해 줘.' | claude -p --model haiku

  4. Check the exit code, the number a program leaves behind when it finishes. Claude Code exits with 0 on success and another number on failure. Failures such as a missing sign-in are also printed where the answer would be, so trust the number, not the text.

    $LASTEXITCODE

It worked if

An answer appears under the question and $LASTEXITCODE prints 0.

An unattended run can only use tools you allowed in advance. That list goes in the allowedTools field of the part 6 job card (a job definition file in the jobs folder).

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Give scheduled jobs their own sign-in

Claude Code keeps its settings, chat history and sign-in in one folder, .claude in your user folder by default. If you set the environment variable CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR (a named value programs read when they start) to another folder, Claude Code keeps a separate sign-in and settings there. Sharing one folder means that switching accounts in a chat also switches the account your scheduled jobs use. So scheduled jobs get a dedicated settings folder of their own, .claude-harness.

  1. Open a new PowerShell window.

  2. Point Claude Code at the dedicated settings folder. The name .claude-harness matches what the kit's job cards in part 6 expect.

    $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude-harness"

  3. Run Claude Code. The folder has no sign-in yet, so the browser sign-in from step 1 appears again. If it does not, type /login.

    claude

  4. When you see Login successful, press Enter and close the window.

  5. Open a new window and check that the credentials file exists.

    Test-Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude-harness\.credentials.json"

It worked if

It prints True. Per the Claude Code docs, on Windows the sign-in is stored in .credentials.json inside the settings folder.

Scheduled jobs follow the CLAUDE.md instructions file (rules Claude always applies) in the dedicated settings folder. Copy your chat instructions in unchanged and their answer format follows into job reports, so write job-specific instructions only when you need them.

Step 5: Find out when your sign-in ends

Sign-ins expire. This step has two halves: check the date now, and sign in again later, before that date.

Check now

  1. In a new PowerShell window, enter the $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR line from step 4 again. This window now uses the dedicated settings folder.

  2. Send a short question.

    echo hi | claude -p --model haiku

  3. If the answer starts with a line beginning Warning: this sign-in ends, write the dates from that line in your calendar.

On Nov 12, 2026, a claude -p run with this PC's dedicated settings folder began its answer with this line:

Warning: this sign-in ends between 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-21 (in 7 days at the earliest). Renewing it does not move those dates. Run claude auth login before then, or use claude setup-token for unattended jobs.

It means this sign-in ends between Nov 18 and Nov 21 (in 7 days at the earliest), and renewing it does not move those dates. Those are this PC's dates; write down the ones in your own window.

Sign in again before that date

You don't need to do this now. Before the date you wrote down, do this:

  1. In a new PowerShell window, enter the $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR line from step 4 again.

  2. Run claude, type /login and sign in through the browser again.

  3. When you see Login successful, press Enter and close the window.

The warning also mentions claude setup-token. It creates a one-year token (a secret string that stands in for a sign-in) but does not store it anywhere, so you would have to keep that secret safe yourself. This series recommends signing in again instead. The kit you download in part 6 spots this warning. Its log gets a Korean line, 주의: Claude 로그인 만료 예고가 나왔습니다. 전용 설정 폴더에서 다시 로그인하세요 (an expiry notice telling you to sign in again in the dedicated folder), and the 끝: (done) line it prints at the end adds 로그인 만료 예고 있음 (expiry notice present). In part 7, the status table (the table status.ps1 shows) says 다시 로그인 필요 (sign in again).

If you get stuck

If you see thisWhyDo this
You signed in, but Claude Code says you cannot use itThe free Claude plan does not include Claude CodeMove to Pro or higher, then sign in again with /login
A Korean or accented question does not get through properly$OutputEncoding was not set in this windowEnter that line first, then send the question again
A failure message instead of an answer, and $LASTEXITCODE is not 0Often a folder with no sign-inRead the message; if it is about signing in, redo step 4
claude : The term 'claude' is not recognizedThe PATH fix from part 3 has not reached this windowFinish part 3, step 5, and open a new window

In the real harness

SugarMount's harness got a dedicated settings folder after Sept 10, 2026. It still ran inside a Linux environment on Windows then, and switching accounts with /login in a chat window overwrote the scheduled jobs' sign-in; the jobs could not authenticate again and stopped.

A check on Nov 11, 2026 found the chat instructions copied into the real harness's dedicated settings folder, including a rule to end every answer with a summary of what was done, the result and what is left. The game app's social-media job on Nov 10 ended its answer with that summary.

A prompt passed as a command argument was once read as part of the --allowedTools list, so the harness sends prompts on standard input, as in step 3.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Install Docker Desktop

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can scheduled jobs use a different Claude account?

They use whichever account you sign in with in step 4; the Claude Code docs suggest CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR for running several accounts side by side.

Does claude -p use my subscription?

It uses the account you signed in with. But if the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable is set on your PC, a -p run always uses that API key, and usage is billed to the API.

As of Nov 12, 2026. Claude Code documentation (setup, quickstart, authentication, headless mode, environment variables; checked Nov 11), claude.com/pricing (Nov 11), Microsoft's PowerShell 5.1 documentation, output from commands run on this PC (Nov 11 and 12), harness operating records.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate
  • Run a first Claude Code harness job with the kit
  • Open PowerShell and paste your first command
  • Capping Vertex AI test costs: a 2,500 KRW stop line missed a 2,956 KRW bill, so we changed the defaults
  • App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings
  • No XML file said white, yet the dialog buttons vanished: three places a theme colour leaked

item.title: Run a first Claude Code harness job with the kit – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Run a first Claude Code harness job with the kit

Unzip the kit into your harness folder and run hello once with run-job.ps1. You get a log, a report and a state file, and you see each one before anything is scheduled.

Windows harness series, part 6 of 11 · Previous Install Docker Desktop · Next Schedule it to run every day

In this part you download a small practice kit from SugarMount and run one job by hand. The kit is a zip file with four PowerShell scripts (text files of commands ending in .ps1), job cards (job definition files in the jobs folder), prompts and practice data. Part 7 schedules the job; first you see what one run leaves behind.

You keep using the harness folder and the dedicated settings folder for scheduled jobs (.claude-harness) from part 4. If you skipped Docker in part 5, that is fine.

When you finish this part

  • Result: the hello job runs once and leaves records in the logs, reports and state folders.
  • You need: a PC that has finished part 4 (Claude Code installed, signed in to the dedicated settings folder).
  • Cost: the kit is free. Runs use the Claude plan you signed in with in part 4.

Step 1: Download the kit

The kit is one zip file, harness-kit.zip. Pick one of the two methods below.

Method 1: from the browser

Click download harness-kit.zip. If it was saved somewhere other than your Downloads folder, move it there.

Method 2: from PowerShell

Paste this line and press Enter.

Invoke-WebRequest https://sugarmount21.com/assets/ax/harness-kit.zip -OutFile "$HOME\Downloads\harness-kit.zip"

Check the file

Whichever method you used, check that the file is there.

dir $HOME\Downloads\harness-kit.zip

You are done when

One line appears with harness-kit.zip in the Name column.

Step 2: Unzip the kit

Unzip with a PowerShell command, not File Explorer. We checked that this command gives all 24 files and keeps the Korean text inside the scripts intact.

  1. Paste this line. It unzips into the $HOME\harness folder you made in part 4.

    Expand-Archive -Path "$HOME\Downloads\harness-kit.zip" -DestinationPath "$HOME\harness" -Force

  2. Go into that folder and list it, one line at a time.

    cd $HOME\harness
dir

  3. To see the same folder in a File Explorer window, enter this line. Parts 8 and 9 use the same trick when you drop data files in.

    explorer $HOME\harness

You are done when

You see three folders (data, jobs, prompts) and six files (README.txt, four .ps1 scripts and status.cmd).

NameWhat it does
run-job.ps1Runs one job. We call it the runner (this part).
register-job.ps1, remove-job.ps1Schedule a job daily at a fixed time, and remove it (part 7).
status.ps1, status.cmdShow each job's last result and next scheduled run in a status table (part 7).
jobs, promptsFour job cards (hello, ga4-daily, ads-check, shorts-plan) and their prompts. English prompts are in prompts\en.
dataMade-up practice data: GA4 and ads CSV files, a game description

The kit is written for Korean readers. The runner's closing line, the log lines it adds and the status table headings are in Korean; this page translates each one where it appears. The default prompts are Korean too, so Claude answers in Korean unless you switch to the English prompts (step 3).

Step 3: Read a job card

A job card says what to ask, which model to use and how many seconds to allow. Open the hello card in Notepad with notepad .\jobs\hello.json:

{
  "description": "동작 확인용 작업",
  "prompt": "prompts/hello.md",
  "model": "haiku",
  "allowedTools": [],
  "configDir": "~/.claude-harness",
  "timeoutSeconds": 300
}
FieldMeaning
descriptionA note for people ("a job to check that things work"). The runner ignores it.
promptThe prompt file. For hello it says: use no tools, name in one line the three numbers a game marketer should check first each morning, and end with a verdict line.
modelA Claude model alias. The other three jobs use sonnet.
allowedToolsThe tools the job may use. An unattended run can only use tools on this list (part 4). hello needs none, so the list is empty.
configDirThe folder whose sign-in the job uses. ~ means your user folder; this points at the dedicated settings folder you signed in to in part 4, step 4.
timeoutSecondsA time limit in seconds. After 300 seconds (5 minutes) the runner stops the job.

To get English answers, change the prompt line to "prompt": "prompts/en/hello.md", and save. The same works for the other three jobs (prompts/en/ga4-daily.md and so on). We ran all four English prompts on Nov 12, 2026; each finished ok and wrote an English report.

The runner reads the card and works in this order. The comment lines in run-job.ps1 (lines starting with #) carry the same numbers.

  1. If the same job is still running, end without running it.
  2. Tell Claude to use the sign-in in the configDir folder.
  3. Start claude -p --model haiku and feed it the prompt file as input.
  4. If the time limit passes, stop claude and every program it started, and record a timeout.
  5. Write the answer to the log, and only when the result is ok, write a report too: a dated file plus a copy called latest-hello.md.
  6. Save the last result in a state file.
  7. Print one closing line on screen that starts with 끝: ("done").

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Allow scripts in this window only

Windows PowerShell blocks .ps1 scripts according to a rule called the execution policy. Microsoft's documentation says the default on Windows client PCs is Restricted, which blocks scripts. When we tried different settings on our PC, we saw two different errors, both in English:

  • A message containing running scripts is disabled on this system means scripts are switched off (the Restricted setting).
  • A message containing is not digitally signed means the file came from the internet and was blocked (RemoteSigned). When we unzipped with File Explorer, every file got that internet mark.

  1. In the window where you will run the kit, paste this line and press Enter. If the next prompt appears with no message, it worked.

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force

What this line changes

-Scope Process means "this window only". Microsoft's documentation puts it the same way: it affects only the current PowerShell session and is lost when the session is closed. Paste it again in each new window. In a window with this line, the kit scripts ran without being blocked, so only run scripts you know, like the kit, in that window.

Step 5: Run hello and read the result

Stay in the same window. A few seconds after you start the job, one line beginning with 끝: appears.

  1. Run the hello job.

    .\run-job.ps1 -Name hello

  2. Open the log.

    Get-Content .\logs\hello.log

  3. See what landed in the reports folder.

    dir .\reports -Name

  4. Open the report in Notepad. latest-hello.md is a copy of the newest report, so you can open it without knowing the date.

    notepad .\reports\latest-hello.md

The 끝: line gives the job name, the result (status), the exit code (exit) and where the report is. The exit code is the number a program leaves when it ends; 0 means it finished without an error (part 4). If the line ends with / 로그인 만료 예고 있음, a sign-in expiry warning was seen. Read the log from the top:

  • 시작 model=haiku timeout=300s: the runner's start line.
  • Warning: this sign-in ends between ...: Claude Code's notice that the sign-in will expire. It is the same warning as in part 4, step 5: sign in again in the dedicated settings folder before the first date shown. It stays in the log and is left out of the report.
  • The answer and 판정: 완료 (verdict: done): Claude's reply to the prompt. The prompt asks for the verdict on the last line, but in this run one more paragraph followed it. The wording and shape of the answer change on every run.
  • 주의: Claude 로그인 만료 예고가 나왔습니다. 전용 설정 폴더에서 다시 로그인하세요: the runner found the warning and adds "sign-in expiry warning seen; sign in again in the dedicated settings folder". With no warning, this line does not appear.
  • 종료 status=ok exit=0 (4s): the result, exit code and time taken (4 seconds).

The state file state\hello.json keeps only the last result; the status table in part 7 (the table status.ps1 shows) reads it. This is what a hello run at 02:18 the same day left:

{
    "status":  "ok",
    "loginWarning":  true,
    "finishedAt":  "2026-11-12T02:18:45",
    "exitCode":  0,
    "job":  "hello"
}

Step 6: Try the time limit (optional)

Shorten the limit on purpose to see that it really works.

  1. Open the card with notepad .\jobs\hello.json, change 300 to 3 and save. Leave everything else as it is.

  2. Run hello again and look at only the last three lines of the log.

    .\run-job.ps1 -Name hello
Get-Content .\logs\hello.log -Tail 3

  3. When you are done, change 3 back to 300 and save.

It worked if

The 끝: line shows status=timeout exit=1 in red, and the last log line is 종료 status=timeout exit=1 (3s). Because the result is not ok, no report is written, and the report from step 5 stays as it was.

If you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
running scripts is disabled on this system or is not digitally signedScripts are blocked in this window.Paste the step 4 line in the same window and run again.
The prompt returns with no 끝: lineThe same job was still running, so this run was skipped. The log gets a Korean line saying so.Run again after the earlier run ends.
The 끝: line has status=errorClaude ended with an error. Failures inside the run, such as a missing sign-in, are printed in the log where the answer would be.Read the log; for a sign-in problem, redo part 4, step 4.
The 끝: line ends in 로그인 만료 예고 있음The sign-in in the dedicated settings folder ends soon.Sign in again before the date in the log's Warning line, as in part 4, step 5.

  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Schedule it to run every day

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do I have to paste the execution policy line in every new window?

A setting made with -Scope Process disappears when you close that window, so paste it once in each window where you run kit scripts by hand.

Do scheduled runs need that line too?

Scheduled runs work without it: the command that register-job.ps1 registers in part 7 already includes -ExecutionPolicy Bypass.

item.title: GA4 CSV export to a daily morning report – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

GA4 CSV export to a daily morning report

Put a CSV you downloaded from GA4 into the data\ga4 folder, and every morning at 09:30 the ga4-daily job reads that one file and writes a short report for you to check.

Windows harness series, part 8 of 11 · Previous Schedule it to run every day · Next Ad budget checks and approvals

This part turns a GA4 (Google Analytics 4) report into a morning briefing. You download the report as a CSV file, and the kit's ga4-daily job reads it on a schedule. The job never signs in to GA4. It only reads the file you hand it, so the harness holds no GA4 login and no secret.

You keep using the $HOME\harness folder from part 6 and the scheduling command from part 7.

What you will have

  • Result: a GA4 morning report appears in the reports folder every day at 09:30.
  • You need: a PC that finished part 7, and a GA4 role that can export reports (step 1).
  • Cost: nothing new. The job runs on the Claude plan you signed in with in part 4.

Step 1: Download a GA4 report as CSV

The menu names below are quoted from Google's English help page.

  1. Open https://analytics.google.com in your browser and sign in.

  2. Click Reports in the left menu and open the report you want.

  3. Click Share this report at the top right of the report.

  4. Click Download File.

  5. Choose Download CSV. The same list offers Download PDF and Export to Google Sheets, but the kit reads only CSV files.

To export a report you need the Viewer role on the property (the GA4 container for one app's data).

Which report you download is up to you and your game. A report with a date (Date) on every row lets the job compare trends. If the columns differ from what the job expects, it says so first: the top of the report lists the "columns read" and any "missing columns", so the first run tells you whether your file works.

Step 2: Put the file in data\ga4

The job sorts the CSV names in data\ga4 alphabetically and reads only the last one. Put today's date at the front of the name and your file comes last.

  1. Open the data\ga4 folder in File Explorer. From a PowerShell window, this line opens it:

    explorer $HOME\harness\data\ga4

  2. Move the downloaded CSV into this folder.

  3. Add today's date to the front of its name, for example 2026-11-12-events.csv.

It worked if

data\ga4 holds your dated CSV. Leave 0000-practice-sample.csv (the fictional practice file) where it is: its name starts with 0000, so it sorts before any dated file and is read only when no dated file exists.

No GA4 file yet? Skip this step and try step 4 on the practice file first.

Step 3: Switch to the English prompt and read it

The kit was written for Korean readers, so each job card (the job definition file in the jobs folder) points to a Korean prompt by default. English prompts sit in prompts\en. Open the job card in Notepad.

cd $HOME\harness
notepad .\jobs\ga4-daily.json

Change the line "prompt": "prompts/ga4-daily.md", to "prompt": "prompts/en/ga4-daily.md", and save. Then open the English prompt.

notepad .\prompts\en\ga4-daily.md
RuleWhat it means
One file onlyRead the last CSV by name. If there is none, write No GA4 file: put a CSV in data/ga4 and Verdict: partial failure (no file).
Columns firstList the column names from the file's header row as "Columns read". If a needed column is missing, write "Missing columns: ..." and do only what the other columns allow.
Is it today's file?On the practice file, start with "This report was run on the practice file" and give the verdict on the content, with no date rule. On any other file whose date is not today's, the verdict is partial failure (no file for today).
Only numbers in the fileNever invent a number, and mark any guessed cause with "(guess)".
Small samples as fractionsFor a rate under 20 users, write the fraction too, like 75% = 6/8. A gap of one or two users counts as "about the same".

"Level pass rate" is level_up users (cleared a level) divided by level_start users (started one). If the file is not split by level, the report says "all levels combined". If your game sends different event names, edit that line of the prompt.

The last line is always Verdict: done or Verdict: partial failure (reason). A state of ok only means the job ended without an error, so this line is where you see whether it did the work.

The job card allows two tools, Read and Glob (find files). The job cannot change any file.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Run it and read the report

  1. In a PowerShell window, enter these three lines one at a time. The second is the run-scripts line from part 6.

    cd $HOME\harness
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force
.\run-job.ps1 -Name ga4-daily

  2. When it ends, the window prints one line starting with 끝: (Korean for "end") that shows status=ok exit=0 and reports\latest-ga4-daily.md. Open that latest copy. The same report is also saved under a dated name in reports.

    notepad .\reports\latest-ga4-daily.md

  3. Read it from the top.

Every number in the screenshot is fictional practice data. For the last day (Nov 8) the report picked 352 active users (-14.7% against the prior seven-day average), 71 new users (-25.2%) and a level pass rate of 59.4% (41/69) against 71.0% (449/632) for the seven days before. It named the drop in level-up users, from an average of 64.1 to 41 (-36.1%), as the biggest change, and it said the pass rate covers all levels combined. Its two checks for you, whether Nov 8 was a full day and whether a release or campaign change was behind the drop, both carried the "(guess)" tag. On the practice file there is no date rule, so the verdict was Verdict: done. We recomputed every number from the same CSV and all of them were correct. Still, check the arithmetic yourself for the first few runs.

We also tried a file with different columns, using the Korean prompt. It had only Event name, Event count, Total users and no date column, and we gave it today's date in its name. The report listed "missing columns: date column" and marked the trend comparison "cannot judge". It still worked out the level pass rate from the columns it had (61/88, about 69%), told the person to export again with a Date column, and ended with "partial failure (no date column)".

When the end line in the window adds a Korean note that a sign-in expiry notice appeared, open logs\ga4-daily.log. That notice (part 4) is not written into reports.

Step 5: Schedule it every day

The order part 11 recommends is to get a week of ga4-daily reports first, then switch on the other jobs one at a time. That is why this schedule comes first.

  1. In the same window, schedule the job for 09:30 every day.

    .\register-job.ps1 -Name ga4-daily -At 09:30

  2. Check it in the status table. Double-clicking status.cmd in File Explorer shows the same table (part 7).

    .\status.ps1

It worked if

The ga4-daily row in the status table shows 09:30 as the next run.

From now on, drop a fresh CSV in before 09:30 each day. On Nov 12 we left only a file dated Nov 10 in the folder: the job read it and marked the verdict as partial failure because there was no file for today. The English prompt gave the same result on that file: Verdict: partial failure (no file for today). With a file dated Nov 12, the Korean prompt's verdict was done; we did not run that case with the English prompt.

Limits of this kit

You download the CSV by hand every day. We have not tested the kit on a file downloaded from a real GA4 screen. Instead, after the first run, the "columns read" and "missing columns" lines at the top of the report tell you right away whether your file works (we tested a file with different column names, step 4).

When you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
No GA4 file: put a CSV in data/ga4 and Verdict: partial failure (no file)No CSV in the folder.Redo step 2 and check the name ends in .csv.
"This report was run on the practice file" at the topNo CSV whose name starts with a date.Check that your file's name starts with the date.
partial failure (no file for today)The last file's date is not today.Add today's CSV and rerun the third line of step 4.
"Missing columns" naming a date column, and a partial failure verdictYour report has no Date column.Download a report with a date on every row.
The report is in KoreanThe job card still points to the Korean prompt.Redo the job card change in step 3.
Level pass rate says "column missing"Your file has no level_start or level_up user columns.Edit that prompt line to match your column names.

In the real harness

Our own harness does not download CSVs by hand. A data collector server, running in Docker, gathers the previous day's numbers into a snapshot file at 09:00 every day, and the game's daily job reads that snapshot. On Oct 11, its first day, the scheduled runs failed because no Google credentials had been set up; after credentials went in, every scheduled run from Oct 12 succeeded.

Once the label was wrong rather than the number. In an approval request the harness called a ratio the "first-level solve rate". It actually came from a per-version event query with no level ID: users who finished three tutorial levels, out of users who launched the game for the first time. The report body stated both numbers correctly, but the label was wrong, and the harness read the existing record in the repository without comparing the two. Just as the kit's report adds "all levels combined" to its pass rate, every number needs to say what it counted.

Real reports also tag each number with its source, such as [GA4] or [AdMob API], the same way as the kit's [GA4 CSV]. The filter we use to drop test devices is written up in GA4 installs: 11 of 19 were test devices.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Ad budget checks and approvals

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can the job pull GA4 numbers automatically?

Not in this kit. It reads only a CSV you downloaded, so the harness never gets GA4 access. Our real harness uses a data collector server at 09:00 every day, but building that server is outside this series.

What are the menu names in another GA4 display language?

We did not check. Reports, Share this report, Download File and Download CSV are the names in Google's English help page. In another language, follow the same order: report, share, file, CSV.

As of Nov 12, 2026. Google Analytics Help: share and export reports (checked Nov 11, 2026), output of the kit run on our PC (fictional practice data, date-rule tests and a file with different column names), harness run logs and data collector run logs.
