item.title: A daily Google Ads budget check that only suggests – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

A daily Google Ads budget check that only suggests

The ads-check job never touches your ad account. It reads a campaign CSV, suggests raise, cut or keep for each campaign by fixed rules, and lists the decisions that are yours to make.

Windows harness series, part 9 of 11 · Previous A morning GA4 report job · Next Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts

A budget change spends money, so in this kit the AI does not make it. The ads-check job reads a Google Ads campaign table you exported as CSV, applies fixed rules, and writes suggestions. You decide, and you change the budget in Google Ads yourself.

It works like part 8: you drop a file in a folder, the job reads it, and a report appears.

What you will have

  • Result: every day at 09:40, a report with a suggestion per campaign and a numbered list of decisions lands in reports.
  • You need: a PC that finished part 7, and a Google Ads account where you can see the campaign table.
  • Cost: the job adds nothing. Following a raise suggestion increases your ad spend (step 4).

Step 1: Export the campaign table as CSV

The job never signs in to Google Ads; it reads only the file you give it. The labels below are from Google's English help page.

  1. Open https://ads.google.com in your browser and go to the page with the Campaigns table.

  2. Set the table's date range to the last 7 days. The rules work on 7-day numbers.

  3. Click the download icon at the top right of the table.

  4. Click Download and choose Excel CSV. There is no option called plain "CSV".

  5. Open the data\ads folder. From a PowerShell window, this line opens it:

    explorer $HOME\harness\data\ads

  6. Move the downloaded file into this folder and put today's date at the front of its name, for example 2026-11-12-campaigns.csv.

Leave 0000-practice-sample.csv (the fictional practice file) in the folder. The job sorts names alphabetically and reads the last one, so any file whose name starts with a date wins over it.

The practice file has these seven columns. A real export may use different column names.

Practice columnMeaning
campaignCampaign name
daily_budget_krwDaily budget (KRW, Korean won)
cost_7d_krwCost over the last 7 days
installs_7dInstalls over the last 7 days
conv_value_7d_krwConversion value over the last 7 days
days_runningDays the campaign has run
end_dateEnd date (blank if none)

Step 2: Switch to the English prompt and read the rules

As in part 8, the job card points to a Korean prompt by default. Open it in Notepad.

cd $HOME\harness
notepad .\jobs\ads-check.json

Change "prompt": "prompts/ads-check.md", to "prompt": "prompts/en/ads-check.md", and save. Then open the English prompt.

notepad .\prompts\en\ads-check.md

The rules hang on ROAS (return on ad spend). The prompt computes it as 7-day conversion value / 7-day cost x 100. Conversion value is the amount assigned to the installs or purchases the ads brought in.

ConditionSuggestion
ROAS 100% or more and 20 or more installs in 7 daysRaise the daily budget by KRW 500 to 1,000
ROAS under 30% and running 7 days or moreCut by KRW 500 to 1,000, never below KRW 1,000
Already at KRW 1,000 and still meets the cut rule"consider pausing (person decides)"
A raise would push one campaign over KRW 5,000 or the total over KRW 12,000"held back by the cap"
End date before todayWritten first: "end date passed: ads are stopped (person to check)"
Anything else"keep"
Change one campaign at most once every three days, by at most KRW 1,000A rule you keep yourself. The job does not know your past decisions, so you keep it with the log in step 4.

The file rules match part 8. With no CSV it writes No ads file: put a CSV in data/ads and Verdict: partial failure (no file). On the practice file it starts with "This report was run on the practice file" and judges the content with no date rule. On any other file whose date is not today's, the verdict is partial failure (no file for today). The report also starts with the "columns read", and if a column the rules need is missing, it lists "Missing columns: ..." and marks the rules that need it "cannot judge".

These amounts come from the budget rules the operator handed to our real harness. The real harness counts the KRW 5,000 cap per app, not per campaign, and keeps the three-day gap so that a campaign's learning is not reset.

Google's help page says a campaign past its end date shows as Ended and its ads stop running, and that you can change the end date at any time.

Fit the rules to your budget

The KRW 1,000 floor, the KRW 5,000 per-campaign cap and the KRW 12,000 total cap in the prompt are our real harness's amounts. If your ad budget is different, open the prompt, change those three amounts to yours, and save with Ctrl+S. The 1,000 KRW floor appears in two places. Ranges such as "+500 to 1,000 KRW" are step sizes.

notepad .\prompts\en\ads-check.md

Step 3: Run it and read the report

  1. In PowerShell, enter one line at a time.

    cd $HOME\harness
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force
.\run-job.ps1 -Name ads-check

  2. When it ends, the window prints one line starting with 끝: (Korean for "end") that shows status=ok exit=0 and reports\latest-ads-check.md. Open that latest copy.

    notepad .\reports\latest-ads-check.md

  3. Read the columns read, the table (the ROAS calculations are in it), the totals, and the decisions.

All three campaigns and every number in the screenshot are fictional practice data. The campaign names read "puzzle game KR installs", "JP" and "TW".

  • Puzzle game KR: 23,100 / 20,400 x 100 = 113.2% with 46 installs, so the report suggests raising KRW 3,000 to 4,000.
  • Puzzle game JP: 2,900 / 13,800 x 100 = 21.0% after 14 days, so it suggests cutting KRW 2,000 to the KRW 1,000 floor.
  • Puzzle game TW: its end date, Nov 10, 2026, has passed, so "ads are stopped (person to check)" comes first. By the numbers alone it would be kept.

The daily total is KRW 6,500 before and after, inside the KRW 12,000 cap. The decision list adds that a +500 step for KR, or a -500 step for JP, is also within the rule. When we ran the same file with the Korean prompt, it chose exactly those smaller steps (KRW 3,500 and 1,500). Both answers are inside the rule, so how much to change is your call. We recomputed everything from the same CSV and it was all correct.

The Korean run also ended with a short summary block. That came from an instruction file in the separate settings folder our PC used for scheduled jobs; the settings folder you made (.claude-harness) has no such file, so you will not see it.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Decide, and write it down

You change budgets in the Google Ads interface yourself. This series does not cover that screen.

Note

Google's help says a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, and no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget over a month. Raise a daily budget to KRW 4,000 and some days may cost up to KRW 8,000.

After each decision, write one line with the date, the campaign and the change, in Notepad or a spreadsheet.

2026-11-12 | Puzzle game KR | 3,000 -> 4,000 KRW | report decision 1

The job reads only that day's CSV and has no idea what you changed yesterday. To keep the once-every-three-days rule, you need this log.

Step 5: Schedule it every day

The order part 11 recommends is to get a week of ga4-daily reports first, then switch on the other jobs one at a time. Once part 8's schedule has run for a week, switch this one on.

  1. In the same window, schedule it for 09:40, ten minutes after part 8's ga4-daily.

    .\register-job.ps1 -Name ads-check -At 09:40

  2. Find the ads-check row in the status table (.\status.ps1, or double-click status.cmd in File Explorer).

It worked if

The ads-check row in the status table shows 09:40 as the next run.

From then on, drop in a fresh CSV before 09:40 each day.

Limits of this kit

We have not tested the kit on a file downloaded from a real Google Ads screen. Instead, after the first run, the "columns read" and "missing columns" lines at the top of the report tell you right away whether your file works. We tested a file with different column names on part 8's ga4-daily, and the ads-check prompt uses the same rule. Automation that changes your ad account is outside this series.

When you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
No ads file: put a CSV in data/ads and Verdict: partial failure (no file)No CSV in the folder.Redo step 1, item 6.
"This report was run on the practice file" at the topNo CSV whose name starts with a date.Check that your file's name starts with the date.
partial failure (no file for today)The last file's date is not today.Add today's CSV and run it again.
"Missing columns: ..." and "cannot judge"Your file lacks a column the rules need (cost, conversion value, days running, end date and so on).Export a table that has those columns.
The report is in KoreanThe job card still points to the Korean prompt.Redo the job card change in step 2.
A raise suggested for the same campaign several days in a rowThe job does not know your past decisions.Check your log and keep the three-day gap yourself.

In the real harness

Our harness finished shadow running (reports only, no changes) and switched on real changes on Oct 27. Adjusting daily ad budgets inside rules was a separate step: the operator handed that over on Oct 30, and the rules in step 2 are the ones set then. The harness reads budgets from the screen before and after each change, and new campaigns, pausing and bid changes go to an approval queue (a Notion table); only what the operator approves is carried out.

The two campaigns belong to our games: Arrow, an arrow-untangling puzzle, and Block, a block puzzle.

  • Campaigns stopped by an end date: Block KR had already stopped at its Nov 1 end date, and Arrow KR's end date was Nov 2, the day its budget was cut, so its ads stopped quietly from the next day. The harness found both and sent them to the approval queue, and each came back on after the operator approved. That is why the kit's report checks the end date first.
  • Spending twice the daily budget: on Oct 28 and 29, Arrow KR spent a little over twice its KRW 2,000 daily budget, two days in a row. That is past the daily maximum Google's help describes, so the harness flagged it for a check.
  • Holding a raise on a day with an outlier: on Nov 8, Arrow's ROAS jumped, but an interstitial ad click-through rate of 45% or more came with it. The harness noted the ROAS might be inflated and did not raise the budget.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Should I let an AI change my Google Ads budgets?

This kit does not. Our real harness adjusts daily budgets only inside fixed caps with read-back checks, and anything else goes through approval. Start with suggestions only and watch whether they hold up; part 11 covers the order we recommend.

A day cost more than my daily budget. Is that a bug?

Google's help says a day can cost up to twice the average daily budget, and a month no more than 30.4 times it. If days over twice the budget keep coming, it is worth a check.

As of Nov 12, 2026. Google Ads Help (download a report, average daily budget, campaign status, checked Nov 11, 2026), output of the kit run on our PC (fictional practice data), and the game repository's dated marketing logs.

item.title: Open PowerShell and paste your first command – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Open PowerShell and paste your first command

Open Windows PowerShell from the Start menu and look at the start of the line. When it begins with PS, you are in the right window for every command in this series.

Windows harness series, part 2 of 11 · Previous What a harness is · Next Install Git and Claude Code

Everything in this series, from installing tools to running jobs, happens by typing commands into a PowerShell window. PowerShell is a command window that ships with Windows: you type a line of text and a program does the work. This part teaches only four moves: open the window, paste a command, run it, and read what comes back.

Part 1 explained what a harness is. From here on you use the keyboard, and the moves below repeat in every later part.

When you finish this part

  • Result: you can open PowerShell, paste a command into it, and tell which folder you are in.
  • You need: one Windows PC
  • Cost: none

Step 1: Check your Windows edition and version

Each tool in this series asks for a different Windows edition or version, so check yours before you install anything.

  1. Hold the Win key and press R. A small box for typing opens.

  2. Type the word below and press Enter.

    winver

  3. In the window that opens, find the edition name (Home, Pro and so on), the version and the build number, and compare them with the table.

ToolWhat the official docs requireIn this series
Claude CodeWindows 10 1809 or later (or Windows Server 2019 or later), an x64 or ARM64 processor, 4 GB of RAM or moreRequired
Docker DesktopWindows 11 Pro, Enterprise or Education 23H2 (build 22631) or later, or Windows 10 Pro, Enterprise or Education 22H2 (build 19045)Part 5, optional

The Claude Code requirement names a version only, not an edition. The Docker list does not name Home at all. If you run Home, skip part 5 (Docker); Docker is optional, so the rest of the series still works.

You are fine if

You run Windows 11, which is newer than the Claude Code minimum (Windows 10 1809), or you run Windows 10 version 1809 or later.

Step 2: Open Windows PowerShell

Windows also has CMD (Command Prompt), which looks similar but accepts different commands. The commands in this series fail in CMD, so pick the right window.

  1. Click the Start button at the bottom of the screen and type PowerShell.

  2. In the results, click Windows PowerShell. Skip any entry ending in (x86): that is the 32-bit version, and Claude Code will not install from it. Skip Windows PowerShell ISE too, the entry with ISE in its name.

  3. A new window opens with Windows PowerShell in its title.

  4. Look at the first line inside the window. This line is called the prompt; it means the window is waiting for a command.

You are in the right window if

The prompt starts with PS. Claude Code's own setup page uses the same test: PowerShell shows PS before the path, while CMD shows the drive letter with no PS.

Step 3: Copy and paste a command

Copy commands from this page instead of typing them; one wrong character is enough to break a line. Practise with a command that prints your PowerShell version.

  1. Select the text in the grey box below with your mouse and press Ctrl+C.

    $PSVersionTable.PSVersion

  2. Click once inside the PowerShell window.

  3. Press Ctrl+V. The text appears after the prompt.

  4. Press Enter to run it.

It worked if

You see four columns, Major, Minor, Build and Revision, and the first two numbers are 5 and 1 (the top half of the picture in step 4). That is Windows PowerShell 5.1, the version built into Windows and the one this series is written for.

When a block holds several lines, paste and run them one line at a time. You see the result of each line, so if something breaks you know exactly where.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Find your user folder and read a path

A path is a folder's address: folder names joined by \. For example, $HOME\harness means "the harness folder inside my user folder". $HOME is a name PowerShell fills with your own user folder, so the same command works for everyone even though the real folder names differ.

  1. Paste this and press Enter. cd moves you into another folder.

    cd $HOME

  2. Print the folder you are in now.

    (Get-Location).Path

  3. After the commands from steps 3 and 4, the window looks like this.

It worked if

One line under the last command shows your user folder's path. The path after PS in the prompt points to the same folder.

Every file this series creates lives in $HOME\harness. You create that folder with a command in part 4.

Step 5: Know when you need an admin window

An admin window is a PowerShell window allowed to change settings for the whole PC. A mistake there reaches further, so open one only when a step asks for it. Installing Claude Code does not need one; the official docs say you do not need to run as Administrator.

Admin rights

The only place in this series where you open an admin window is the WSL install in part 5. There you right-click PowerShell in the Start menu and choose Run as administrator. Every other command goes into a normal window.

If you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
No PS at the start of the lineYou opened CMD (Command Prompt)Close it and open Windows PowerShell as in step 2
Claude Code does not support 32-bit WindowsYou opened the (x86) entryOpen Windows PowerShell without (x86)
Red text under your commandThe command ended in an error, often because only part of it was copiedCopy the whole line again and paste one line at a time

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Install Git and Claude Code

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can I follow this series in CMD instead?

The series is written for PowerShell. Claude Code has a separate CMD install command, but the kit in this series is a set of PowerShell scripts, so you need a PowerShell window.

Do I always have to open PowerShell as administrator?

Installing Claude Code and every job in this series run in a normal window. The only place in this series where you open an admin window is the WSL install in part 5.

As of 2026-11-12. Claude Code setup docs, Docker Desktop for Windows install docs and Microsoft's WSL install docs (checked 2026-11-11), plus PowerShell output run on the PC this series was written on.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: TikTok, Reels and Shorts plans with Claude Code – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

TikTok, Reels and Shorts plans with Claude Code

The AI only writes the plan. A person films the video, posts it to each channel and writes down the next day's view count, and that log shapes the next plan.

Windows harness series, part 10 of 11 · Previous Ad budget checks and approvals · Next Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Short-form videos are the vertical clips people watch on a phone: TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts. In this part the kit's shorts-plan job writes one plan each morning for the video you will film that day. The goal is to stop deciding from scratch every day and to let your past view counts pick the next video.

You keep using the harness folder from part 6 and the scheduling steps from part 7.

What you get

  • Result: a plan for one video lands in the reports folder, and a fresh one is written every morning.
  • You need: the kit from part 6 (harness-kit.zip), the separate settings folder for scheduled jobs (.claude-harness) you signed in to in part 4, TikTok, Instagram and YouTube accounts, and a way to record gameplay.
  • Cost: nothing extra for the kit. You need a paid Claude plan (part 1).

Step 1: Split the work between the AI and you

One short video involves four jobs: planning, filming, posting and logging. The kit takes only the first.

JobWhoWhat it produces
Write the planshorts-plan job (AI)a plan file in reports
Film and edityoua vertical video file
Postyouposts on three channels
Log the viewsyoua new line in data\game\posted.csv

The job card (the job definition file in the jobs folder) explains why the kit can't post. In jobs\shorts-plan.json, allowedTools (the tools the AI may use) lists only Read (read a file) and Glob (find files). With no tool for writing files or driving a browser, the job can only read and write a plan. The prompt's first line says the same: plan only, a person films and posts.

Step 2: Switch to English and describe your game

The kit's prompts write Korean plans by default. English versions of all four prompts sit in prompts\en, and the job card decides which one runs.

  1. In PowerShell, enter these two lines one at a time. The second one opens the job card in Notepad.

    cd $HOME\harness
    notepad .\jobs\shorts-plan.json

  2. Find the line "prompt": "prompts/shorts-plan.md", and change it to the line below. Save with Ctrl+S and close Notepad.

    "prompt": "prompts/en/shorts-plan.md",

  3. Open the game description. The AI plans from what this file says and nothing else.

    notepad .\data\game\game.md

  4. The file is in Korean. Its first line is a heading that says "game description (practice sample: replace with your own game)". Delete the part in brackets.

  5. Below it are five lines: name, genre, length of one round, the moment to show off, and audience. Replace the text after each colon with your game's details.

  6. Be most specific in "the moment to show off". In our Nov 12 test the English plan built its climax on that line: the block that fits the last gap, then four lines clearing at once.

  7. Press Ctrl+S to save, then close Notepad.

data\game\posted.csv is your posting log. It ships with four made-up rows, and its first line says they are not real view counts. Leave them in for the first run.

Step 3: Get a plan and read it

  1. In the same window, allow scripts for this window only. It's the same line as in part 6.

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force

  2. Run the job.

    .\run-job.ps1 -Name shorts-plan

  3. Open the latest copy of the plan. The same plan is also saved under a dated name in reports.

    notepad .\reports\latest-shorts-plan.md

It worked if

the window ends with one line such as 끝: shorts-plan status=ok exit=0 보고서 reports\latest-shorts-plan.md. The runner's messages are Korean: 끝 means finished and 보고서 means report. If your sign-in is close to expiring, / 로그인 만료 예고 있음 (sign-in expiry warning) is added at the end. The plan itself has shots by the second and a Verdict: done line.

The evidence section copied the log row with the most views, 2026-11-08,youtube,한 번에 네 줄,530, word for word, and added that TikTok got 42 for the same title. It also wrote that the log is practice data and that one sample on one channel is thin evidence.

The prompt keeps every plan vertical and 60 seconds or shorter. It also has four quality rules: recorded gameplay footage, game sound or music, large text near the centre of the screen, and the game made clear within the first two seconds. Three of these came from a real incident, described under "In the real harness" below.

The prompt allows only facts found in game.md and posted.csv, and asks the AI to mark guesses with "(guess)". Settle those marked parts yourself before you film. Our test plan marked two: the 20-second length and the posting times, which it aimed at commuting hours. The Korean run of the same job titled its plan "five lines" even though no file mentions five, and the plan itself said to change the number to however many lines the real play clears. Check details like that before filming too.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Film and post to three channels

Record gameplay in the order of the shot list and export a vertical video. YouTube counts a video as a Short when it is vertical or square and three minutes or shorter (for uploads from Oct 15, 2024). The prompt's 60-second cap keeps plans inside that limit.

TikTok (desktop browser)

  1. In a desktop browser, open https://www.tiktok.com/tiktokstudio (TikTok Studio) and log in.

  2. Click Upload.

  3. Click Select video and choose your file.

  4. Paste the plan's TikTok caption and follow the on-screen steps to post.

A browser upload sends the whole video; to trim it, upload from the TikTok app. Scheduling from the desktop is open only to Business accounts or accounts with 10,000 or more followers. If yours qualifies, turn on the schedule toggle and pick a date and time, from 15 minutes to 10 days ahead, in your computer's time zone. If not, post by hand at the planned time.

Note

A scheduled TikTok post can't be edited, only deleted. Check the caption and video before you schedule.

YouTube Shorts

Upload from the YouTube app or YouTube Studio (YouTube's channel dashboard). Both take Shorts up to three minutes. Use the plan's YouTube Shorts caption as the description.

Instagram Reels

Follow the Instagram app's upload steps. We could not confirm Reels length limits or scheduling in official documentation, so we don't state them here.

The plan spreads the three channels over different times, because the prompt says not to post all three at once and to keep TikTok posts at least two hours apart.

Step 5: Log the next day's views and schedule the job

Tomorrow's plan can only learn from what you write down. A CSV file is a table saved as text, with commas between the columns.

  1. On the day you first post for real, remove the practice rows. Open the file:

    notepad .\data\game\posted.csv

  2. Delete the first line (it starts with # and marks the rows as practice data) and the four rows that start with 2026-11-08 or 2026-11-09. Keep only date,channel,title,views_next_day.

  3. The next day, look up each video's view count and add one line per channel: date, channel, title, views. Write the channel as tiktok, instagram or youtube, and replace the last field with the number.

    2026-11-12,youtube,Clear 4 lines in ONE move,(views)

  4. Leave commas out of titles, because a comma starts a new column. Save with Ctrl+S.

  5. The order part 11 recommends is to get a week of ga4-daily reports first, then switch on the other jobs one at a time. When this job's turn comes, schedule it as in part 7. 10:00 is the example time from part 7.

    .\register-job.ps1 -Name shorts-plan -At 10:00

It worked if

the next day's evidence section quotes your line with the most views. With an empty log, the prompt tells the AI to write "no history" (we did not test that case).

If you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
Red text containing running scripts is disabledscripts are blocked in this windowenter the Set-ExecutionPolicy line from step 3 first (part 6)
The evidence section mentions practice datathe practice rows are still in posted.csvdelete them as in step 5
A Verdict: partial failure (…) linepart of the plan could not be writtenread the reason, fix game.md or posted.csv, run again
No schedule toggle on TikToknot a Business account and under 10,000 followers, or a phone browserpost by hand at the planned time
YouTube doesn't treat it as a Shortlonger than three minutes, or landscapere-export at three minutes or less, vertical or square
On-screen text doesn't match your gamethe AI filled a gap in game.md with a guessadd detail to game.md and fix the text before filming

In the real harness

The SugarMount harness has made game videos every day since Oct 31, and unlike the kit it posts them itself. Three things it ran into ended up in the kit.

On Nov 1 the operator judged the videos too low in quality. The game video had no sound, all three apps' videos were slideshows of still frames, and small text near the edges was hidden by TikTok's on-screen buttons. Since then a video goes out only after a machine check and a review by a separate AI, and three of the kit's four quality rules (real gameplay, sound, large centred text) come from that verdict.

In October, TikTok videos posted two to four minutes apart got zero views. TikTok posts have been at least two hours apart since, and the kit's prompt keeps the same gap.

Results also split sharply by channel for the same video. In the chart, video A got 1,279 views on YouTube Shorts and 1 on TikTok, and video B got 1,213 on YouTube and 97 on TikTok. That is why posted.csv has a channel column and you log each channel separately.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

As of Nov 12, 2026. Official help pages: YouTube Help on Shorts length, TikTok Help on making a post and scheduling (checked Nov 11, 2026), and TikTok's newsroom post on TikTok Studio (May 24, 2024); output from running the kit on our own PC (Nov 12, 2026); harness run logs and game marketing records (Oct 31 to Nov 11, 2026).

item.title: Game difficulty tests: two speed fixes that failed – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Incident

We slowed a mini game down twice before checking why it was hard: players couldn't recall the answers

Beginners in Spell Rain were stuck on remembering the correct spelling, not on the falling speed. We changed the speed twice before a player model showed us that.

When we replayed the October 15, 2026 build (vc99, words falling in 24 seconds instead of 12) through a player model, the beginner profile lost a heart within the first minute in 100% of 300 runs. That build existed because the operator had said the on-screen keyboard covered half the sky and they "couldn't type anything." On the morning of October 17 the operator came back with "even 62 points is hard" and "I can't think of the answers." The rebuilt version (vc100) kept the model's beginner alive for 3.4 minutes and to level 3, but finished games in the first two weeks after release averaged level 2.0.

Sources: git history of the SugarSpeller repository (4867e24, 73d8ce8, 1948777, 78d7283), the October 14 to 17 working-session log, the release note, and the monitoring log (GA4, October 17 to 31). Constants were rechecked on the remote default branch on November 9, 2026.

Two speed changes in two days; after the first one, still too hard

Spell Rain is a mini game inside SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling checker. Misspelled words fall from the top, for example 되요 (the common misspelling of 돼요, "it works"), and the player types the correct form to clear them. A word that reaches the ground costs one of five hearts; every 10 correct words raise the level. The first build on October 14 (4867e24) dropped a word every 3.2 seconds with a 12-second fall, and a code comment reasoned that typing "안 돼요" on a phone takes 2 to 4 seconds, so a first-timer would clear the first ten comfortably.

At 21:39 KST on October 15 the operator, playing on a real phone, said the keyboard halved the visible sky and the words came too fast, and asked for 50% slower. The agent answered "I'll halve the fall speed" and committed 73d8ce8 48 minutes later: 24-second fall, 9-second floor, a new word every 4 seconds. Slower words bunched up and overlapped on a Galaxy S20, so the same commit also forced consecutive words at least two lanes apart.

At 07:56 on October 17 the operator wrote that every word on screen is wrong, 62 points is hard, and the answers just don't come to mind. This time the agent named the cause: the screen only shows the wrong form, so a player who doesn't know where a word like 희안하다 is wrong can't type it no matter how much time there is. Then at 08:05 the operator also asked for slower words and fewer at once, and at 08:06 the agent changed the constants first: 30-second fall, 6-second spawn, three words on screen. A moment later the operator wrote again, roughly: you're supposed to be the level-design expert, do I have to keep asking like this, do it properly.

An unknown word reaches the ground even with a 24-second fall

SpellRainBalanceTest, written at 08:08, runs the real game engine 300 times each with a beginner, an average and a skilled player model. The model looks at the lowest word first. If it knows the answer, it spends a recall time, a per-syllable typing time and a submit time; the beginner uses 2.5 s, 0.9 s per syllable and 0.8 s. Whether it knows a word is decided once per word: the beginner knows easy words with probability 0.80, medium 0.50 and hard 0.25. Words it doesn't know are left alone until a hint appears.

vc99 had no hints and no tiers, so every word could fall from level 1, and the screen showed only the wrong form: a player who doesn't already know the right one has nothing to work from. Over the 124 bundled words the model uses (hand-rated that day as 47 easy, 40 medium, 37 hard), the beginner knows about 54%. The other 46% reach the ground untyped whether the fall takes 12 seconds or 24, and each costs a heart. Slowing down only moves the moment the heart is lost, which is why this build's beginner lost a heart within the first minute in 100% of runs.

The October 15 complaint about speed was real (the keyboard did hide half the sky), but the recall problem sat underneath it the whole time.

vc100 added help with recall. Levels 1 and 2 use only easy words, levels 3 and 4 add medium ones, and level 5 opens everything. The differing letters of each wrong word are drawn red and underlined; the code comment says this tells the player where to fix the word but leaves how to them. Once a word passes the halfway line, the correct form appears faintly under it, and typing it then earns half points. Each level-up returns one heart, up to five.

The speed relief the operator asked for went in too. On October 15 the spawn interval had stopped at 4 seconds because doubling it seemed boring; this time it went to 6 seconds, and the on-screen cap went from 8 to 3 at level 1. Below are the options on record, plus the comparisons nobody ran:

OptionBeginner model resultDecision and reason
Speed only, halved (vc99, Oct 15)1.1 min, level 1, 100% first-minute heart lossDropped: the operator played it and still found it hard
vc100 minus the level 1–2 easy-only rule and the level-up heart3.2 min (08:14, 0.2 min below full vc100)Both kept (two engine tests failed; the balance test still passed)
Full vc1003.4 min, level 3, 0%Adopted (Oct 17)
Remove only the hint, or only restore vc99 speedModel not runNever split, even inside the model

The first test modeled a typist who knows every answer

The first build's test (4867e24), 처음_하는_사람도_첫_10개는_하트를_안_잃는다 ("a first-timer loses no heart in the first ten") assumes a player who looks at the lowest word and always types the correct answer 3.5 seconds later.

if (typingUntil < 0) typingUntil = e.elapsedMs + 3_500
if (e.elapsedMs >= typingUntil) {
    assertEquals(Result.HIT, e.submit(e.lowest()!!.word.right))

In that model the player knows everything, so the only difficulty knobs are fall time and spawn interval. When the operator said "too fast," those were the only numbers the agent had to turn. The October 17 model put the chance of not knowing into the same spot:

// lowest first: a word it knows, or one already showing the hint
val pick = e.drops.sortedByDescending { it.y }.firstOrNull { d ->
    knows.getOrPut(d.id) { rnd.nextDouble() < p.know(d.word.tier) } || d.hinted
} ?: continue

When players say a game is too hard, don't start by changing the speed. Write down the steps a player takes for one item (see, recall, type, submit) and put the probability of not knowing into the model first. The rule saved to the agent's project memory that day says the same: split difficulty feedback into speed, density, cognitive load and learning aids before touching numbers, and ship the change with a simulation table.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The record says "reproduced, then tuned"; the session shows the reverse order

The 1948777 commit message says the curve was tuned to targets after reproducing vc99 (beginner 86 points), and the changelog says the numbers were not changed by feel. The session log has a different order.

Oct 17, KSTActionResult
08:06Constants changed (30 s, 6 s, three on screen)No model yet
08:08Balance test written, target assertions includedBefore the first run
08:09First runBeginner 3.4 min, level 3, 675 points, 0% first-minute heart loss
08:10Same model on the vc99 engineBeginner 1.1 min, level 1, 86 points, 100%
08:14Run with the level 1–2 easy-only rule and level-up heart removedTwo engine tests fail; beginner 3.2 min
08:27Commit 1948777, internal test uploadUnit tests 531/531

The constants were set before the model existed and never changed after the first run passed. The simulator checked a hand-picked curve; it did not find one. Because the targets were written before the first run, the check still means something, but anyone reading only the commit would assume the model produced the numbers.

The release note says the replay "matches the user's 62 points." In the vc99 replay the beginner's median score was 86, 24 points above what the operator scored by hand. The average and skilled profiles scored 216 and 1,066, so the beginner was simply the closest of the three; the model still played better than the person.

The operator's "I can't think of the answers" at 07:56 named the bottleneck first. Right after the 08:06 constant change the operator asked whether they had to keep asking like this, and instead of shipping another build for the operator to try, the agent wrote the balance test at 08:08.

Real players averaged level 2.0, below the model's 3

Version 1.6.030 began a staged production rollout on October 17, and the November 1 review (78d7283) recorded GA4 numbers for October 17 to 31. 133 users opened the game (267 times), 87 started it (207 games), and 35 users finished 93 games, 45% of the games started. Finished games averaged level 189/93 = 2.0 and 127 seconds (2.1 minutes). The review marked the design target (beginner median of at least 3 minutes and level 3) as missed.

The two numbers are not directly comparable. The model value is a median over 300 beginner runs; the field value is a mean over all players, beginners and experts mixed. level was registered in GA4 only as a metric, so no median was available, and rain_over counts only finished games.

The knowledge probabilities (0.80, 0.50, 0.25 for the beginner) and the word tiers were set by hand, and the only real score used to calibrate them was one person's 62 points. The model also has no screen: it knows nothing about the keyboard covering half the sky, which is where the October 15 complaint started.

We copied the 73d8ce8 engine to replay the 62-point build

  1. Write down the steps for one item and give each a time and a probability of not knowing. This game used recall, per-syllable typing, submit and hint-reading times, plus a knowledge probability per tier.
  2. Take the engine from the build the person actually played and run the same model on it. Here the 73d8ce8 engine file was copied into the test folder under a new class name. If the result is far from their score, fix the model before the constants.
  3. Write the targets as test assertions before the first run: here, at most 10% of beginner runs losing a heart in the first minute, a median of 3 minutes and level 3, average players at level 5 to 8, skilled players finishing within 25 minutes.
  4. Pick constants after running the model. If you picked them first, as happened here, say so in the commit message.
  5. Remove each device in turn and confirm the balance test fails, not just an engine test.
  6. After release, log the same measures as events and register them so a median is available.

The method of choosing difficulty numbers with a player model, with a full table of candidate values, is in Puzzle game time limits: 3-star par by simulation.

Still open: a 36-second easy stretch and a refit model

The November 1 review set the next task: widen the easy stretch, for example by lengthening the level 1 and 2 fall from 30 to 36 seconds, and recalibrate SpellRainBalanceTest. On November 9 the remote default branch still has 30 seconds, 6 seconds and three words. The review's rule says that if the real median level is below 2, the simulator model gets refit to field data before the easy stretch grows, but that median can't be read yet because of how level was registered. The events also don't record hint use or missed words by tier, so a refit still couldn't correct the knowledge probabilities from field data.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can game difficulty balance be checked with test code?

If the engine is plain logic with no Android dependency, a JUnit test can play hundreds of games through a player model. This game runs 300 games each for beginner, average and skilled profiles and asserts on median survival time and level.

If players say a typing game is too hard, should I slow it down?

Not if some items are ones players don't know: those reach the ground at any speed. Our earlier build lost a heart in the first minute in 100% of beginner-model runs even with a 24-second fall; the rebuild combined slower pacing with highlighted wrong letters, a halfway hint and easy words first.

What do you calibrate a player model against?

The build the complaining player actually played, and their score on it. We ran the same model on the vc99 engine the operator had scored 62 on, and it scored 86.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Vertex AI test costs: hard caps in code – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Capping Vertex AI test costs: a 2,500 KRW stop line missed a 2,956 KRW bill, so we changed the defaults

On every path where a coding agent can spend money, make a missing value mean zero, make deploys dry-run by default, and count usage by what gets billed.

Our model evaluation runner had a code cap that stopped it at 2,500 KRW (about $1.80 at 1,400 KRW per dollar). On October 11, 2026, the budget alert showed 2,956 KRW actually billed. Almost all of it went on the Vertex AI model evaluation an AI coding agent ran on October 8 and 9 (about 330 call attempts in the main run, plus follow-up runs) while choosing a model for AXFamily, a family schedule app that hadn't launched yet. The runner's ledger counted the responses it received, and it badly underestimated the output of 62 attempts that ended with no response, 61 of them on 3.8 Flash. After that, we went through each path where the agent could spend money and changed what happens when a value is missing.

Sources: the AXFamily app repository's internal-test release plan (written Oct 9, corrected Oct 11), model evaluation notes, cost and security status doc, decision record, and commits cc54a82, 5c9e018 and 04a5cf3. Billed amounts come from the budget alert's costAmount; token counts come from Cloud Monitoring, priced at 1,400 KRW per dollar. Rechecked against the repository on 2026-11-10. Times are KST. Project and billing account identifiers are left out.

A 2,500 KRW stop line in code, 2,956 KRW on the bill

For each call, the runner added the cost from the response's usageMetadata to a ledger and refused to make the next call once the total passed 2,500 KRW. Attempts that ended without a response were counted at an estimated 1,500 output tokens each. When the evaluation finished, the ledger held 918.1 KRW from responses plus 666 KRW for 62 such attempts (61 of them on 3.8 Flash), 1,584.2 KRW in total. It never reached the stop line.

On October 11 the agent read the budget alert during an operations audit: 2,956 KRW for October. Pricing Cloud Monitoring's token counts for October 6 to 11 gives about 3,490 KRW, and about 72% of that, roughly 2,520 KRW, is 3.8 Flash output. The ledger had 595.6 KRW for 3.8 Flash, and that figure already included thinking tokens. So no further 3.8 Flash tests were run.

The three numbers cover slightly different ground. The 1,584.2 KRW ledger covers the main evaluation only; the 2,956 KRW bill and the token counts also include follow-up runs on October 9 (229.7 KRW by the ledger plus about 2.7 KRW for the quota test, about 232 KRW in all). We haven't confirmed why the token-count estimate of about 3,490 KRW is higher than the 2,956 KRW billed. The cost status doc only notes that billing may not have caught up yet and that the real total could rise to around 3,500 KRW.

In one run, 17% of 3.8 Flash attempts (10 of 59) went past the 60-second timeout, and a request the client abandons returns no response and so no usage. The agent had even written in the evaluation notes that it could not confirm from public docs whether the server keeps processing and billing a request the client dropped at 60 seconds. The cap still priced each of those attempts at only 1,500 output tokens.

The app's Cloud Function had a hole of the same kind. It counted output tokens from candidatesTokenCount alone, but 3.8 Flash produced thinking tokens even with thinkingBudget set to 0: 50 to 166 per call on average, up to 526. Thinking tokens are billed at the output rate. Commit 5c9e018 (Oct 11, 14:17) made output tokens the sum of response and thinking tokens. If the response token count is missing, the new code doesn't build a number from thinking tokens alone; it returns null, and that call is charged against the full unit cap. That rule was already in place, because returning 0 would leave the token budget open. The evaluation notes gained a line saying the ledger is a lower bound and is never used to judge cost, and the remaining ten or fewer real calls were limited to 3.5 Flash-Lite at 2 to 3 KRW each.

The plan's 1,700 KRW estimate came from the ledger

The agent wrote the internal-test release plan (04a5cf3) at 18:35 on October 9. Its second conclusion read: keep costs near zero with hard caps in code; budget alerts arrive hours late, so treat them as a backup. Its fifth conclusion put expected test spend at about 1,700 KRW, worst case 8,000 KRW plus whatever the alert delay lets through, and the cost table's first row put the evaluation already spent at the ledger value, 504 KRW, in a column labelled "confirmed". The total came to about 1,726 KRW.

By billing, 2,956 KRW had been spent before the plan was written; the running total had been flat since the morning of October 9. Had the test-period budget been created at 8,000 KRW as planned, the 50% line at 4,000 KRW would switch off AI, photo upload, notifications and media viewing, with only 1,044 KRW of room left.

On October 9 the operator lowered the monthly budget from 20,000 to 10,000 KRW, with two lines: switch features off at 50%, unlink billing at 100%. The agent applied the operator's October 11 instruction (features off at 5,000 KRW, billing unlinked at 10,000 KRW) to the test period's total in the plan as well. The status doc written that day explains why a monthly budget can't do it alone: it restarts from zero on November 1, so it can't cap a test that runs into November. The agent changed the planned custom-period budget to 10,000 KRW (October 8 to December 31, credits excluded) and added a correction under the plan's cost table.

A quota lowered to 1,000 let all 4 requests through

On October 8 the per-model input token quotas for Vertex AI were lowered to 2,000,000 a day and 200,000 a minute, which put the worst day at roughly 3,000 to 4,000 KRW per model. On October 9 we tested whether the quota actually bites. With 3.5 Flash-Lite's per-minute input token quota set to 1,000, the granted value showed 1,000 within two seconds. Two requests with 1,581 input tokens went out, then two more two minutes later. All four returned 200, with no 429. The quota went straight back to 200,000; the test cost about 2.7 KRW.

We couldn't tell whether enforcement was delayed or whether this quota doesn't apply to calls on the global endpoint. Since then the quota doesn't count as a cost block, and the app function's daily limit is the first line.

A default for each path that spends money

The evaluation runner, the deploy script, the production switches and CI are all paths the agent runs. For each one we decided what happens when a value is missing or wrong.

PathWhen the value is missing or wrongSource
Production deploy scriptDry-run (read only). A real deploy needs --execute; --force is an errorcc54a82
Deploy preflightAny failed check stops the deploy. Model and location are confirmed with one free countTokens callcc54a82
Daily AI service cap0 (no AI). Test values: 10 units and 15 Vertex calls a dayPlan, function config
Production switchesPreflight fails if the AI or photo switches are on at deploy timecc54a82
Model usageNo token count means the full unit cap. Output = response + thinking tokens5c9e018
Test-period budgetPreflight error if the custom-period budget doesn't exist5c9e018
CIOnly the demo emulator project. Deploy or login commands, or cloud credentials, fail the buildf43326e, e42f657

Run with no arguments, the deploy script from cc54a82 (Oct 10, 15:20) collects facts, runs the preflight, prints the deploy commands and stops with "DRY-RUN: checks passed. Use --execute to deploy." (translated from Korean). The commit added 987 lines across 11 files, and its message lists 44 fixture tests for the checks. The preflight includes a countTokens call that sends the single word "ping" and isn't billed. A check of that kind the same day found that both models returned 404 in the locations this commit allowed (Seoul and Tokyo), and the operator picked global. What that did to the privacy policy is in our note on the AI processing location in the privacy policy.

Commands that change production settings were blocked by the agent's auto mode, so the operator ran them, and the result is checked with another dry-run preflight. Which clicks a person makes is covered in the AI agent permission table note.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

budget-guard logged four 429s after its redeploy

This project's budget alerts also go to Pub/Sub, where a budget-guard function switches off four features (AI, upload, notifications, media) at 50% of the budget and unlinks billing from the project at 100%. We still don't make it the first line. Alerts can arrive hours late, and the function itself can lag: after its October 10 redeploy it logged four "no available instance" 429s alongside 122 successful runs. Alerts are redelivered, so the block isn't lost.

The circuit breaker defaults the other way

Zero-when-missing and dry-run-by-default fit only the side that spends money. The budget-guard function runs in test mode only when the DRY_RUN environment variable is exactly true; with it unset, it really switches features off and unlinks billing. A breaker that defaulted to test mode would block nothing the day someone forgot a setting.

None of this reaches services outside the Google Cloud budget. Photo storage on Cloudflare R2 and Workers is designed to be held by free-plan limits and a daily automatic pause (the Worker isn't deployed yet), watched by a $0.5 billing alert. Billing data shows up the next day, so while an evaluation runs the ledger is the only number you have. Keep its stop line well below the budget and estimate cut-off attempts generously. Once real users arrive, a test-period budget isn't enough and you need a per-day call cap; we did that for our spelling app in the note on LLM explanation costs and limits.

Seven defaults that spend nothing when a value is missing

  1. Make any script that calls a paid command dry-run when run with no arguments, and act only on an explicit flag such as --execute. Don't accept --force.
  2. Stop on any failed preflight check. Confirm model and location with a call that isn't billed, such as countTokens.
  3. Set the server's daily AI cap to 0 in code, and close it when the config document is missing the value or holds a string. Refuse to deploy while the AI switch is on.
  4. Count output as response plus thinking tokens, and count a call with no token count as the full unit cap, never 0.
  5. Let the evaluation runner judge its stop line from the ledger, then compare against billing the next day and treat the ledger as a lower bound.
  6. Set two budgets, monthly and a custom test period, and wire 50% to switching features off and 100% to unlinking billing. Make the deploy preflight fail if the custom-period budget is missing.
  7. Keep CI on emulator projects only, and fail the build when deploy or login commands show up in the repository's scripts or workflows.

Still open: the 10,000 KRW custom budget is pending

The repository's cost status doc (updated October 11) still lists the 10,000 KRW custom-period budget as pending. The deploy preflight errors without it, so it has to exist before any production deploy. The 100% path that unlinks billing has been checked only by 13 unit tests and a permissions review; we haven't actually cut billing. Whether the cut-off 3.8 Flash requests were billed is still unconfirmed at the SKU level, because billing export isn't turned on.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does a Firebase budget alert stop Vertex AI charges at the limit?

An alert alone doesn't stop billing. We have a function that switches features off at 50% and unlinks billing at 100%, but because alerts arrive late, the app function's daily limit comes first.

Does lowering a Vertex AI quota cap spending?

Not in our test. Right after we cut the per-minute input token quota to 1,000, four requests of 1,581 tokens all succeeded.

Is the Vertex AI countTokens call billed?

No; it isn't a generation call. Our pre-deploy check sends the single word "ping" just to see whether the model answers in that location.

Does thinkingBudget 0 mean no thinking-token cost?

Not with 3.8 Flash. With 0 it still produced 50 to 166 thinking tokens per call on average, up to 526, billed at the output rate.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Install Git and Claude Code on Windows – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Install Git and Claude Code on Windows

Install Git from its official download page, then install Claude Code by pasting one line into PowerShell. The Claude Code install does not need an administrator window.

Windows harness series, part 3 of 11 · Previous Before you start: PowerShell · Next Log in and ask a first unattended question

This part installs two programs. Claude Code is the AI program that does the work in this series. Git for Windows brings along a tool Claude Code uses to run commands. When both are in, a fresh PowerShell window prints their version numbers.

Use the Windows PowerShell window from part 2, and copy and paste commands the same way.

When you finish this part

  • Result: in a new PowerShell window, git --version and claude --version print versions, and claude doctor reports No installation issues found.
  • You need: part 2 (opening PowerShell), Windows 10 1809 or later, an internet connection, 4 GB of RAM or more
  • Cost: nothing to pay in this part. To use Claude Code you sign in with a paid plan in part 4; the free plan does not include Claude Code.

Step 1: Download Git for Windows

Git for Windows installs Git Bash, a command shell. When Git Bash is present, Claude Code runs commands through its Bash tool; without it, Claude Code falls back to its PowerShell tool. The official docs call Git recommended, not required. This series installs it so that every reader follows the same path.

  1. Open the official Git for Windows download page in your browser: https://git-scm.com/install/windows

  2. Under the Windows tab, click Click here to download in the first line, where the red box is in the picture below.

  3. If your PC has an ARM64 processor, click Git for Windows/ARM64 Setup. instead.

It worked if

Your browser downloads an installer. On 2026-11-11 the link pointed to Git-2.56.1-64-bit.exe; the number follows whatever the latest release is on the day you download.

Step 2: Install Git and check it

The installer offers several choices, and none of them needs changing for this series. The download page does not walk through those screens, so this guide does not describe them one by one either.

  1. Run the installer you downloaded. You'll find it in your browser's downloads list or in your Downloads folder.

  2. If a Windows confirmation box (User Account Control) appears, click Yes.

  3. Leave the settings as they are and click Next through the screens, then Install. When it finishes, click Finish.

  4. Close any PowerShell window you already had open and open Windows PowerShell again, as in part 2. A window opened before the install may not find the new program.

  5. Run this command.

    git --version

It worked if

You get a line that starts with git version. On the PC this series was written on it read git version 2.45.2.windows.1; a fresh download shows a higher number.

Step 3: Run the Claude Code install command

Installing Claude Code takes one line in PowerShell. The command comes from the official setup page: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup

  1. Open a Windows PowerShell window. It does not have to be an admin window; the official docs say you do not need to run as Administrator.

  2. Copy the command below, paste it, and press Enter. It is the same command as in the box under Windows PowerShell: on the official page; scroll down the page a little to see that box.

    irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

  3. Wait. The official docs say the command shows no progress while it downloads Claude Code. Leave the window open even if it looks stuck.

The first half, irm, fetches the install script from the internet, and the second half, iex, runs what was fetched. That is why you paste the whole line, including iex.

It worked if

The command finishes and a new prompt line starting with PS appears. If the output mentions Setup notes:, do step 4 and then step 5 as well.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Check the install in a new window

The window you installed from may not find the claude command yet. The official docs also tell you to open a new terminal window before checking.

  1. Close PowerShell and open Windows PowerShell again.

  2. Check the version.

    claude --version

  3. Run the diagnostics. claude doctor does not start a session; it only reads and reports the state of the install and your settings.

    claude doctor

It worked if

claude --version prints a number followed by (Claude Code), like 2.1.322 (Claude Code), and the claude doctor output includes No installation issues found.

Three lines in claude doctor are worth reading. Running: native means Claude Code was installed the officially recommended way. Path: shows where claude.exe lives: the .local\bin folder inside your user folder. Auto-updates: enabled means updates are on. A native install downloads updates in the background, and the new version takes effect the next time you start Claude Code.

A line starting Managed settings (remote): not fetched is normal on a personal plan. The line right below it, Organization policy: not applicable to individual subscription plans, says why: company-managed settings do not apply to individual plans, so nothing was fetched.

Step 5: Fix PATH if you saw Setup notes

Do this step only if the step 3 output showed Setup notes: with a sentence ending in .local\bin is not in your PATH. Otherwise skip it.

PATH is the list of folders Windows searches when you type a program's name. It is stored as a per-user setting called an environment variable. The installer does not edit that list itself; it only prints the warning and the fix.

  1. Paste these two lines one at a time, pressing Enter after each. The first reads your current list; the second adds the Claude Code folder to the end and saves it.

    $currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", 'User')

  2. Close PowerShell and open a new window. The change only applies to windows opened afterwards.

  3. Run claude --version again.

It worked if

As in step 4, the version number is followed by (Claude Code).

If you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
'irm' is not recognized as an internal or external commandYou pasted into CMDPaste it into a Windows PowerShell window
The token '&&' is not a valid statement separatorYou pasted the CMD command into PowerShellUse the irm command from step 3
A message containing The term 'claude' is not recognizedThe window predates the install, or the folder is missing from PATHTry a new window; if it persists, do step 5
Claude Code does not support 32-bit WindowsYou opened the (x86) PowerShellOpen Windows PowerShell without (x86)
A message ending in because it is being used by another processAnother process is holding the install filesRun Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude\downloads", then repeat step 3
Script text scrolls past and nothing installsThe | iex part at the end of the line was missingPaste the whole line again: irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Log in and ask a first unattended question

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can I install Claude Code without Git?

Without Git for Windows, Claude Code still installs and runs commands through its PowerShell tool instead of the Bash tool. This series installs Git so that everyone follows the same steps.

Can I install it with winget instead?

The official docs list winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode too, but a winget install does not update itself; you have to run winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode now and then. This series uses the step 3 method, which updates automatically.

Do I need to open PowerShell as administrator?

The Claude Code docs say you run the install command from PowerShell or CMD and do not need to run as Administrator.

As of 2026-11-12. The official Git for Windows download page, Claude Code setup and install troubleshooting docs (checked 2026-11-11), and output run on the PC this series was written on.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Install Docker Desktop on Windows with WSL 2 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Install Docker Desktop on Windows with WSL 2

You can skip this part. Docker is only needed if you plan to run a data-collection server or an MCP server in containers; the kit from part 6 runs without it.

Windows harness series, part 5 of 11 · Previous Log in and ask a first unattended question · Next Download the kit and run a first job

You can skip this part. The kit you use from part 6 on runs on Claude Code and PowerShell alone and never touches Docker.

Docker Desktop is a Windows app that runs programs in containers: self-contained bundles that run apart from the rest of your PC. You need it only to run something like a server that collects ad numbers every day, or an MCP server, which connects Claude Code to outside services such as GitHub, in a container.

What you will have

  • Result: docker run --rm hello-world prints Hello from Docker!
  • You need: a PC that meets the table in step 1 (Windows Pro, Enterprise or Education) and an account that can use administrator rights
  • Cost: free for personal use and small businesses (under 250 employees and under $10 million in annual revenue); larger companies need a paid subscription for professional use (Docker docs, checked Nov 11, 2026)

Step 1: Check that your PC qualifies

These are the conditions Docker's documentation sets for an install on WSL 2. If your PC misses any of them, skip this part.

  1. Press Win+R, type winver and press Enter.

  2. Compare the edition (Pro, Home and so on) and build number in that window with the table below.

ItemDocker's requirement
Windows 1164-bit Pro, Enterprise or Education, 23H2 (build 22631) or later
Windows 1064-bit Pro, Enterprise or Education, 22H2 (build 19045)
Memory8 GB RAM
VirtualizationHardware virtualization turned on in BIOS/UEFI (your PC's firmware settings)
WSL2.1.5 or later (checked in step 2)

Windows Home is not in this list (see the FAQ). The full requirements are in the System requirements section of Docker's install page.

Step 2: Install WSL from an administrator PowerShell

WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) runs Linux inside Windows. By default Docker Desktop runs its containers on WSL 2.

  1. Click Start and type PowerShell.

  2. Right-click Windows PowerShell in the results and choose "Run as administrator".

  3. Enter the line below in the administrator window. It turns on the features WSL needs and installs Ubuntu, a Linux distribution.

    wsl --install

  4. When it finishes, restart the PC.

  5. When the Ubuntu window first opens after the restart, wait while it unpacks its files, then create a user name and password for Linux. The Linux password stays invisible while you type it.

  6. Open an ordinary (non-administrator) PowerShell window and check the WSL version.

    wsl --version

It worked if

The WSL version on the first line is 2.1.5 or later. On this PC, set to Korean, it read WSL 버전: 2.1.5.0 ("WSL version").

If wsl --install only prints help text, WSL is already installed. Run wsl --update in the same administrator window and check wsl --version again.

Note

This step uses administrator rights to install Windows features and restarts the PC. Save any open documents first.

Step 3: Download the Docker Desktop installer

  1. Open Docker Desktop's Windows install page in your browser.

  2. Click the blue "Docker Desktop for Windows - x86_64" button, the one for ordinary Intel and AMD PCs. On a PC with an Arm processor, click the third button, "Docker Desktop for Windows - Arm (Early Access)".

  3. Your browser downloads Docker Desktop Installer.exe.

Step 4: Install with WSL 2 and launch it

  1. Double-click the downloaded Docker Desktop Installer.exe.

  2. Leave the installation mode on per-user, which is selected by default. It installs and updates without administrator rights.

  3. On the Configuration page, choose WSL 2 as the backend (what actually runs the containers). Version 4.97 and later list WSL 2 and Docker VMM (Beta) as options; older installers show a "Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V" checkbox instead.

  4. When the installation finishes, click Close.

  5. Docker Desktop does not start on its own after installing. Click Start, type Docker and open Docker Desktop from the results.

  6. Click Accept on the Docker Subscription Service Agreement. Docker Desktop will not run until you do.

  7. You do not need to sign in to a Docker account (see the FAQ).

Note

Do not pick the all-users install; it asks for administrator rights. Turning on WSL 2 for the first time on a PC needs administrator rights once (Docker docs).

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 5: Check it with hello-world

With Docker Desktop open, start a new ordinary PowerShell window.

  1. Check the version. You want both a Client section (the side that sends commands) and a Server section (the Docker engine).

    docker version

  2. Run a test container. --rm deletes the container when it finishes; the first run downloads the hello-world image (the template a container starts from) from the internet.

    docker run --rm hello-world

It worked if

You see Hello from Docker! and This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.

The hello-world check comes from Docker Engine's Linux install docs; Docker Desktop's own getting-started guide uses a different example, welcome-to-docker.

Step 6: Cap the memory (optional)

Docker Desktop runs on WSL 2, so a memory cap on WSL also caps Docker. Do this only if Docker has to share memory with other heavy work. The values below are the ones this PC has used since Oct 22, 2026.

  1. In an ordinary PowerShell window, check whether a .wslconfig settings file already exists. False means go on; True means a file is already there, so stop here rather than overwrite it.

    Test-Path "$HOME\.wslconfig"

  2. Create the file. This is a single line.

    Set-Content -Path "$HOME\.wslconfig" -Value '[wsl2]','memory=3GB','processors=2','swap=1GB','[experimental]','autoMemoryReclaim=dropCache'

  3. Check the contents. You should see six lines.

    Get-Content "$HOME\.wslconfig"

  4. Restart the PC. The settings apply the next time WSL starts.

According to the notes in this PC's settings file, memory is WSL's memory cap, processors the number of logical processors, swap a small spare space that keeps WSL from being killed when memory runs short, and autoMemoryReclaim=dropCache hands Linux's cache back to Windows while WSL is idle.

Do not run wsl --shutdown to stop WSL. It shuts down all of WSL, and the Docker engine and any running containers go down with it.

If you get stuck

If you see thisWhyDo this
wsl --version shows a WSL version below 2.1.5WSL is out of dateRun wsl --update in an administrator window
No "Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V" checkbox on the Configuration pageSince 4.97 the backends are a list of optionsPick WSL 2 from the list
No Hyper-V option on the Configuration pageHyper-V is only offered in an all-users installPick WSL 2

In the real harness

SugarMount's harness uses Docker for two things. The first is a data-collection server. Every day at 09:00 Korea time it gathers the previous day's AdMob, GA4 and Google Ads numbers, and the game app's daily job reads them.

The second is GitHub's MCP server. Each Claude session starts its own container, and on the morning of Nov 11, 2026 seven were running, so count them when you check memory use.

The step 6 values fit this PC, which shares its memory with Android app builds. The harness guard, a check that blocks risky commands just before Claude runs them, blocks wsl --shutdown and wsl --unregister.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Download the kit and run a first job

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does Docker Desktop work on Windows 11 Home?

We have not tested it. Docker's requirements list only Pro, Enterprise and Education; Home appears only in the Windows containers note, which says Home can run Linux containers only. With nothing that settles it either way, this series does not recommend installing on Home. On Home, skip this part.

Do I need a Docker account?

By default you can use Docker Desktop without signing in. Signing in matters only for some features, such as pushing images to Docker Hub, Docker's image library.

As of Nov 12, 2026. Docker Desktop's Windows install and license documentation, Docker Engine's install documentation, Microsoft's WSL install documentation (all checked Nov 11), output from commands run on this PC (Nov 11 and 12), this PC's WSL settings file, harness operating records.
