item.title: 17 days of a Claude Code harness: how to start – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

17 days of a Claude Code harness: how to start

Take reports only for the first week, log failures by date, read the verdict line instead of trusting "ok", put the sign-in expiry date on your calendar, then add jobs one at a time.

Windows harness series, part 11 of 11 · Previous Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts

In Parts 6 to 10 you built four jobs with the kit. This part takes SugarMount's own harness log from October 25 to November 10, 2026 (17 days) and turns it into a start-up order and a morning check routine for your kit.

When you finish this part

  • Result: each morning you check the harness with the status table and the verdict line, and you know which job to switch on next.
  • You need: hello scheduled (Parts 6-7) and the ga4-daily job (Part 8).
  • Cost: nothing extra.

Step 1: Take reports only for the first week

Shadow running means the AI analyzes and reports but changes nothing. The kit's three report jobs tell Claude "do not edit or create files" and allow only reading tools (Read, Glob), so using the kit as shipped is already shadow running.

  1. Open PowerShell and go to the kit folder.

    cd $HOME\harness

  2. Allow scripts in this window only (Part 6). Do this first every time you open a new window.

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force

  3. Schedule ga4-daily for 09:30 every day. Skip this if you already registered it in Part 8.

    .\register-job.ps1 -Name ga4-daily -At 09:30

  4. From the next day, for a week, put that morning's GA4 CSV into the data\ga4 folder before the scheduled time, with a name that starts with today's date, such as 2026-11-12-events.csv (Part 8).

  5. After the scheduled time, open the latest report.

    notepad .\reports\latest-ga4-daily.md

  6. Pick three numbers tagged [GA4 CSV] in the report and find the same numbers in the original CSV in the data\ga4 folder.

It worked if

For a whole week, every number you picked matches the CSV. If even one doesn't, don't move on to the next job yet.

From SugarMount's log

SugarMount's harness ran in shadow mode for three days, October 25 to 27, and the reports went wrong at least twice in that time. Once a failure-rate calculation used the wrong denominator, and a correction line was added. Another time a report said the old chat-session schedule "appears not to have run"; in fact the AI had searched the records with a date-only query that missed that day, and the next day's report corrected it.

Step 2: Look at failures by date

Writing results down by date shows whether a failure repeats, and whether several jobs failed on the same day.

  1. Each morning, double-click status.cmd in the harness folder in File Explorer to open the status table (Part 7). From PowerShell, this line opens the folder:

    explorer $HOME\harness

  2. For any job whose 마지막결과 (last result) column isn't ok, open its log in a PowerShell window (after the cd line from Step 1).

    Get-Content .\logs\ga4-daily.log

  3. Write the date, the job and the last result on one line in Notepad.

In a PowerShell window, the two lines from Step 1 followed by .\status.ps1 show the same status table.

It worked if

The table shows ok under 마지막결과 (last result), today's date under 끝난시각 (finished at), and tomorrow's time under 다음예약 (next run). The kit prints these column names in Korean.

The number after exit in the chart below is an exit code: the number a program leaves behind when it ends. 0 means it finished without an error. The Nov 6 cells are green because that morning's failed runs were rerun the same day and succeeded.

From SugarMount's log

7 of the 51 cells failed. On October 30 all three jobs hit the plan's weekly usage limit (You've hit your weekly limit). On November 4 only the Korean app stopped, because the previous day's run had left changed files behind. Right after that, for about 38 hours, uncommitted edits to the harness code stopped every scheduled job at the preparation step (Part 7).

Step 3: Don't read "ok" as success

ok in the status table only means the run ended without an error. Whether the work got done is in the verdict line that all four kit jobs write at the end of each report. With the default Korean prompts it reads 판정: 완료 (done) or 판정: 일부 실패(reason) (partly failed). If you switched a job to the English prompts in prompts/en (Part 8), it reads Verdict: done or Verdict: partial failure (reason).

  1. Open that day's report.

    notepad .\reports\latest-ga4-daily.md

  2. Near the bottom, find the line that starts with 판정: or Verdict:.

  3. If it says partly failed, read the reason in brackets. "No file" (파일 없음) means there is no CSV in the data\ga4 folder; "no file for today" (오늘 넣은 파일 없음) means no file name starts with today's date.

It worked if

You see 판정: 완료 or Verdict: done.

From SugarMount's log

On November 10, 2026, the utility app's social job found its video queue empty and posted nothing, yet the runner recorded ok, and that night's daily status board showed "0 failed or missed". From November 11 every job ends with a verdict line, and all four kit prompts carry the same line.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Put the sign-in expiry on your calendar

A Claude Code sign-in has an end date, and without a sign-in a run fails. Before it ends, sign in again in the separate settings folder for scheduled jobs (.claude-harness).

  1. If the 로그인경고 (sign-in warning) column shows 다시 로그인 필요 (sign in again), open that job's log. It has a Korean line from the runner, 주의: Claude 로그인 만료 예고가 나왔습니다. 전용 설정 폴더에서 다시 로그인하세요 (sign-in expiry notice: sign in again in the jobs' settings folder), and a line that starts with Warning: this sign-in ends between. Read the two dates in the second one; it appears only in the log, not in the report.

    Get-Content .\logs\hello.log

  2. Pick a day before the first date and write "Claude sign-in" on your calendar.

  3. On that day, open a new PowerShell window and point it at the jobs' settings folder (Part 4).

    $env:CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR = "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude-harness"

  4. In the same window, start Claude Code, type /login, and follow the browser steps.

    claude

It worked if

The terminal shows Login successful. Press Enter to continue.

From SugarMount's log

On November 12, 2026, every run that used the real harness's settings folder printed this line at the top of its answer:

Warning: this sign-in ends between 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-21 (in 7 days at the earliest). Renewing it does not move those dates. Run claude auth login before then, or use claude setup-token for unattended jobs.

The claude setup-token it suggests creates a one-year token but does not save it anywhere (official docs), so you would have to store the token yourself. This series recommends signing in again instead.

Step 5: Add jobs one at a time

After the shadow week, switch on one job at a time and move to the next row only when the condition is met. Space out the start times so runs don't overlap.

OrderSwitch onMove on when
1hello, scheduled (Parts 6-7)The status table shows ok and a next run time
2ga4-daily at 09:30 (Part 8)For a week the report's numbers match the CSV
3ads-check at 09:40 (Part 9)A person reads each suggestion and writes down what they changed
4shorts-plan at 10:00 (Part 10)A person posts the video and logs views in posted.csv
5Approval inbox (beyond this series)Only requests a person approved get carried out
6Automatic changes within limits (beyond this series)Set caps first. The real harness caps daily ad budgets at 5,000 Korean won per app and 12,000 won in total

Common problems once it's running

If you see thisWhyWhat to do
Several jobs end within seconds and the log says You've hit your weekly limitYour Claude plan's weekly usage limit was reachedOnce the limit resets, run the job by hand, for example .\run-job.ps1 -Name ga4-daily
Last result is ok but the report says 판정: 일부 실패 or Verdict: partial failureThe run ended without an error but didn't finish the workRead the reason in brackets and check the data folder
No report file for todayThe runner writes a report only for runs that end okOpen the log and check the status in its last 종료 (end) line
The sign-in warning column says 다시 로그인 필요The settings folder's sign-in is about to expireSign in again as in Step 4

In the real harness

SugarMount's harness sorts work into three permission levels:

  • Do it now: free marketing, store listing text, documents, and releases that passed their checks.
  • Ask first (approval inbox): money, new or paused campaigns, ad settings, permissions, app names, prices, and big changes.
  • Never (blocked by the guard hook): force-overwriting code history, printing secrets, installing packages, and 100% rollouts.

How that split was decided is written up in A permission table for a scheduled AI agent.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

This is the last part.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

How long should shadow running last?

SugarMount ran it for three days (October 25 to 27) and switched on live changes on October 27; adjusting daily ad budgets was handed over separately, on October 30 (Part 9). The reports went wrong at least twice even in those three days, so this series suggests a full week when you start.

Can a job show "ok" when the work didn't happen?

Yes. On November 10, 2026, one of SugarMount's posting jobs had no video to post and posted nothing, yet its status was ok. Read the report's verdict line as well.

As of Nov 12, 2026. SugarMount harness dispatcher state files and runner logs (Oct 25 to Nov 10, 2026), the shadow-run comparison reports (Oct 26 and 27, 2026), kit output run on Nov 12, 2026, and the Claude Code official docs (code.claude.com).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • TikTok, Reels and Shorts plans with Claude Code

item.title: What a Claude Code harness is, for game marketing – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

What a Claude Code harness is, for game marketing

A harness runs Claude Code at set times with nobody watching, saves every result to a file, and hands anything risky to a person. This part shows what you will build and whether it fits you.

Windows harness series, part 1 of 11 · Next Before you start: PowerShell

This series shows how to hand daily game-app marketing chores to an AI on one Windows PC, in 11 short parts. Part 1 installs nothing: you see what you will end up with and decide whether your PC and accounts are ready.

When you finish this part

  • Result: you know what a harness is, what this series builds, and whether it suits you.
  • You need: nothing yet.
  • Cost: none. From Part 4 (signing in) on you need a paid Claude plan (Step 4).

Step 1: See one day of a harness

A harness is the whole setup around an AI that runs it at fixed times without a person, records results and failures, and blocks risky actions. In this series the AI is Claude Code, a program that lets you use Anthropic's Claude from a command window.

The chart below shows when SugarMount's own harness actually ran on November 10, 2026.

How to read it:

  • From 09:11 the three apps' morning jobs ("dailies") run one after another, never at the same time.
  • The game daily started at 10:07 and took 13.8 minutes. It checks GA4 numbers, ads, and promo video material.
  • The game's social job ran at 20:07. It posts a video to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube.
  • The ticks at the bottom are three upkeep jobs that run every 15 minutes: 284 runs that day.

Step 2: Know how it differs from a chat AI

QuestionChat AIHarness
How do you ask?Open a window and typeWrite the task into files ahead of time
When does it work?While you sit at the windowAt the times on its timetable, with nobody there
Where is the result?On screenIn log and report files you open later
What must be running?An open chatA PC that is on, with you signed in to Windows

"Signed in" (Windows calls it logged on) means your Windows account is in use on the PC. The kit schedules jobs to run only while you are signed in, so it never stores your password. A schedule set up inside a chat session stops when you close that session; with a harness, Windows itself keeps the time.

The harness calls Claude Code as claude -p. The -p flag answers one request without opening a chat window and then exits, which is called headless mode. You try it yourself in Part 4.

Step 3: Learn the kit's four parts

The kit you download in Part 6 has four moving parts. An office comparison helps:

PartOffice comparisonIn the kitWhat it does
Task SchedulerTimetableregistered by register-job.ps1The scheduler built into Windows. It wakes the runner, for example at 09:05 every day
Job cardOne card per taskjobs folderA job card (a job definition file in the jobs folder) says which instructions, which model, which tools are allowed, and the time limit
PromptWork orderprompts folderWhat Claude should do. Report jobs use only numbers found in the files, and every job ends with a "verdict" line
RunnerThe clerk who runs itrun-job.ps1Runs one job, blocks overlapping runs, enforces the time limit, and writes the work log (logs, reports, state folders)

The kit was written in Korean. Its default prompts, the line the runner prints when a job ends, and the status table's column names are Korean. English prompts sit in prompts/en; to use one, change the job card's "prompt" to prompts/en/<job>.md. A .ps1 file is a PowerShell script: a file of saved commands. "Model" means which Claude model a job uses; the kit uses haiku for its test job and sonnet for the rest.

SugarMount's real harness has more parts that this series does not build:

Only in the real harnessWhat it does
DispatcherWakes every 15 minutes, runs the app dailies in order, and carries out approved requests
Approval inboxA Notion table where anything the AI must not do alone (money, accounts, big changes) waits for a person
Guard hookChecks each tool call just before Claude makes it and blocks dangerous commands
WatcherReads only state and log files, with no model, and reports failures and missed runs
Data collection serverGathers the previous day's ad and GA4 numbers at 09:00 every day (runs in Docker)

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Check what you need and what it costs

  • PC: one Windows 11 PC. Claude Code's documented minimum is Windows 10 1809 or later, 4 GB of RAM or more, an x64 or ARM64 processor, and an internet connection. Part 2 shows how to check your version.
  • Claude plan: Pro is $20 a month ($17 a month billed yearly), Max is $100 a month, Ultra is $200 a month (claude.com/pricing, checked Nov 11, 2026). The free plan does not include Claude Code.
  • A PC that stays on: at job time the PC must be on and you must be signed in.
  • Marketing accounts: GA4 (downloading a report needs the Viewer role on the property), Google Ads, and your TikTok, Instagram and YouTube channels.
  • Docker Desktop: optional. The kit runs without it (Part 5).

It worked if

You can answer yes four times: the PC runs Windows 10 1809 or later; you can pay for a Claude plan; the PC can stay on at the morning job time; you can sign in to GA4 or Google Ads. Then go on to Part 2.

Step 5: Look at the series map

GroupPartsWhat you have at the end
Install2 to 5PowerShell open, Git and Claude Code installed, signed in, and a first unattended question answered. Docker is optional
Automate6 to 7The kit downloaded, a first job run by hand, then scheduled for the same time every day
Marketing8 to 10A morning GA4 report, ad budget suggestions, and a plan for TikTok, Reels and Shorts videos
Operate11A start-up order and a morning check routine taken from a 17-day record of real runs

The kit never touches your ad account; it writes suggestions. It never uploads videos; it writes plans. A person makes the changes and does the posting.

When this setup doesn't fit

If this is youWhyWhat to do
Your PC is off most of the time, or nobody is signed inKit jobs run only while you are signed in. A missed run fires once after the PC is back onKeep the PC on at job time, or schedule jobs after the time you usually switch it on
You want the AI to own the ad budget or posting outrightThe kit only suggests and plans. Even the real harness sends money and account decisions to a personStart with suggestions you read and apply yourself (Part 9)
You only have the free Claude planThe free plan has no Claude CodeYou need Pro or higher
Your Windows is 32-bitClaude Code does not support 32-bit WindowsUse a 64-bit Windows PC
You can't download GA4 and ad numbers by hand each dayThe kit reads only CSV files you download and drop inAutomatic collection is outside this series; run the report on the days you do download

In the real harness

SugarMount's harness started on October 25, 2026. An older harness that ran in a Linux environment was stopped and rewritten for Windows from scratch, keeping the lessons but none of the code.

As of November 11, 14 jobs were registered in Task Scheduler; the dispatcher calls the rest in order. Each job names its model: opus for the app dailies, which involve the most judgment, sonnet for fixed screen work such as posting, and haiku for self-checks.

Windows harness series: all 11 parts

  • 1. What a harness is
  • 2. Before you start: PowerShell
  • 3. Install Git and Claude Code
  • 4. Log in and ask a first unattended question
  • 5. Install Docker Desktop
  • 6. Download the kit and run a first job
  • 7. Schedule it to run every day
  • 8. A morning GA4 report job
  • 9. Ad budget checks and approvals
  • 10. Planning TikTok, Reels and Shorts
  • 11. Two weeks of running it, and the safeguards

Next: Before you start: PowerShell

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can I run a harness on the free Claude plan?

No. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise or Console account; the free claude.ai plan does not include it (official docs, Nov 11, 2026).

What happens to a scheduled job if my PC is off?

It does not run at that time. The kit schedules a missed run to fire once after the PC is back on and you are signed in. Part 7 walks through each setting.

Do I need any programming experience?

The series is written for people who are opening a command window for the first time. Part 2 starts with how to open PowerShell and paste a command.

As of Nov 12, 2026. Claude Code official docs (code.claude.com), claude.com/pricing (checked Nov 11, 2026), Microsoft Task Scheduler docs, SugarMount harness runner logs (Nov 10, 2026) and job list (Nov 11, 2026), and the kit used in this series.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Run Claude Code every day with Task Scheduler – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Run Claude Code every day with Task Scheduler

One line with register-job.ps1 schedules hello for the same time every day. Each morning, the status table shows the last result, the next run and whether you need to log in again.

Windows harness series, part 7 of 11 · Previous Download the kit and run a first job · Next A morning GA4 report job

This part puts the hello job from part 6 into Windows Task Scheduler, the scheduling tool built into Windows. Once it is registered, hello runs by itself at the same time every day, as long as the PC is on and you are logged on.

You keep using the $HOME\harness folder from part 6. You do not need an administrator window. The kit's console lines and the status table are in Korean, and this page translates them; to get English answers from Claude, point a job card at the English prompts in prompts/en as shown in part 6, step 3.

When you finish this part

  • Result: hello runs by itself at 09:05 every day (while the PC is on and you are logged on).
  • You need: a PC that has finished part 6 (hello ran by hand).
  • Cost: none. Scheduled runs use the Claude plan you logged in with in part 4.

Step 1: Register hello for 09:05 every day

  1. Open a new PowerShell window and go to the kit folder.

    cd $HOME\harness

  2. Paste the execution policy line from part 6, step 4. register-job.ps1 is a script too, so this window has to allow it.

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Force

  3. Register hello. After -At, give the time as hours:minutes.

    .\register-job.ps1 -Name hello -At 09:05

You are done when

You see TaskName : hello and a NextRunTime line with the next run time. On our Korean-language PC it read 2026-11-12 오전 9:05:00 (오전 means AM); your date and format will differ.

register-job.ps1 registers the job with these settings. The values below were read back from Task Scheduler after registering.

SettingKit valueIn plain words
TimeDaily at 09:05Starts at the same time every day.
Missed runs (StartWhenAvailable)OnIf the PC was off or asleep at that time, the job runs once after it is back on.
BatteryStarts on battery, keeps runningBy Windows default, a task does not start on battery and stops if the PC switches to battery. The kit lets it run on a laptop battery.
Overlap (MultipleInstances)IgnoreNewIf the previous run is still going, the new one is dropped.
Run limit (ExecutionTimeLimit)Job card limit + 10 minutes, at least 1 hourThe job card (the job definition file in the jobs folder) sets a time limit; the kit adds 10 minutes. Past this, Task Scheduler stops the job. The Windows default is 72 hours. In our test a 300-second job got 1 hour and a 5,400-second job got 1 hour 40 minutes.
Logon (LogonType)InteractiveRuns only while you are logged on. No password is stored.
Rights (RunLevel)LimitedRuns with normal rights, not as administrator.

At run time, Task Scheduler starts PowerShell with a hidden window (-WindowStyle Hidden) and with the same Bypass execution policy as part 6 (-ExecutionPolicy Bypass), then runs run-job.ps1. That is why scheduled runs do not need the line from part 6. Even with the window hidden, a window may flash briefly as the run starts.

Registering the same name again replaces the earlier schedule, so to change the time, run the same command with the new time. The schedule goes into a folder named \my-harness\ inside Task Scheduler.

Step 2: Start it once now

Instead of waiting for 09:05, start the scheduled job right away.

  1. Start the job now. This command only starts it and returns at once.

    Start-ScheduledTask -TaskPath '\my-harness\' -TaskName hello

  2. Wait about 15 seconds, then look at the last-run information. In our test it started at 2:22:05 AM, and the status table's finished-at time was 02:22:13.

    Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskPath '\my-harness\' -TaskName hello

  3. Check that new start and end lines were added to the log.

    Get-Content .\logs\hello.log

You are done when

LastRunTime shows the time you just started it, and the last log line shows status=ok exit=0.

LastTaskResult is the result the last run returned. It was 0 in our test, and the state file said ok at the same time. Microsoft's docs do not list what each number means, so judge a run by the log and the state file.

Step 3: Check the status table each morning

The status table is what status.ps1 shows: one row per job with its last result, finish time, next run and a sign-in warning. There are two ways to open it.

Way 1: double-click status.cmd in File Explorer

  1. In File Explorer, open the harness folder inside your user folder. If a PowerShell window is open, this line opens it too.

    explorer $HOME\harness

  2. Double-click status.cmd. A black window shows the status table, and the last line reads Press any key to continue . . ..

  3. Read the table, then press any key to close the window.

status.cmd calls status.ps1 with the Bypass execution policy, so it needs no execution policy line. We ran it through cmd on our PC and saw the table and that last line.

Way 2: in a PowerShell window

  1. Open a window, enter cd $HOME\harness and the execution policy line, then show the table.

    .\status.ps1

The table headings are in Korean. Read them left to right:

  • 작업 (job): the job card name from the jobs folder.
  • 마지막결과 (last result): the result from the state file (ok, error or timeout). A job that has never run shows -.
  • 끝난시각 (finished at): when the last run ended.
  • 다음예약 (next run): when Task Scheduler will run it next. A job that is not scheduled shows 등록 안 됨 (not registered).
  • 로그인경고 (login warning): 다시 로그인 필요 (log in again) appears if the last run printed the login expiry warning. Log in again as in part 4, step 5.

A last result of ok only tells you the run ended without an error. Every kit prompt ends its report with a verdict line, 판정: 완료 (done) or 판정: 일부 실패(reason) (partly failed), or Verdict: done / Verdict: partial failure (reason) with the English prompts, so read that line too. Open the most recent report with this line:

notepad .\reports\latest-hello.md

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Step 4: Schedule other jobs, and remove one

You register ga4-daily, ads-check and shorts-plan one at a time in parts 8 to 10. In each part you add your data and run the job once by hand, then register it with the same register-job.ps1 command, spacing the times apart (for example 09:30, 09:40 and 10:00). On the practice data, all three jobs finished within 20 seconds.

To remove a schedule, use the line below. It prints a Korean line saying the hello schedule was removed, and the kit files stay where they are. Afterwards the next-run column in the status table reads 등록 안 됨 again. Removing a schedule that does not exist ends with an error, and that line is not printed.

.\remove-job.ps1 -Name hello

If you get stuck

If you seeWhyDo this
running scripts is disabled on this systemThe new window does not have the execution policy line.Paste the line from part 6, step 4 and run again.
파일이 없습니다. 작업 이름을 확인하세요. (the file does not exist, check the job name)The name after -Name does not match a file in jobs.Use the file name from jobs without .json.
Registered, but the next-run column says 등록 안 됨You registered into another folder with -Folder.Add the same -Folder to status.ps1.
It did not run at the scheduled timeThe PC was off, or you were not logged on.A missed run fires once after the PC is back on. Stay logged on.
remove-job.ps1 prints an error starting CIM 서버 에서 Root/Microsoft/Windows/TaskScheduler/... (on our Korean-language PC)There is no such schedule: it was already removed, or the name or -Folder differs.Check the next-run column in the status table.
The login warning column says 다시 로그인 필요The last run printed the login expiry warning.Log in again in the separate settings folder, as in part 4, step 5.

In the real harness

As of Nov 11, 2026, the SugarMount harness had 14 jobs registered in one Task Scheduler folder, and that morning every LastResult in the list was 0.

The kit is a cut-down version of this harness. The real one has extra safeguards added after something went wrong; two of them came from these events.

SafeguardWhat happenedIn the kit
Separate production copyFrom the evening of Nov 4 to the morning of Nov 6, about 38 hours, every job stopped at a pre-run check. Harness code that was being edited had not been committed (recorded as final) in the repository. Since Nov 7, production runs from a separate copy, and only changes that pass checks reach it.None
Verdict lineOn Nov 10 one app's social job posted nothing because there was no video queued, yet its status was ok, and that night's status board said zero failures or misses. Since Nov 11 every job ends with a verdict line.Yes, in all four prompts

The way the window is hidden also differs. The real harness starts PowerShell through conhost.exe --headless, but we found no official documentation for that option, and security tools sometimes treat it as a warning sign, so the kit does not use it.

FAQ

What happens to a scheduled job if the PC is off?

It does not run at that time. The kit registers missed runs to fire once after the PC is back on, and even then you need to be logged on.

Do scheduled jobs run on a laptop battery?

With the kit, they do. By Windows default a task does not start on battery, but register-job.ps1 sets it to start on battery and keep running.

item.title: Malicious file set for a document viewer – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

A malicious file set for a document viewer: ZIP bombs, CFB loops and XSS, generated and wired into tests

If your app opens received files, commit a generator and an expected-verdict table instead of hostile samples. The unit test task checks 50 rows, but XSS rendering checks live outside that loop.

SugarDoc, our Android viewer for HWP (the Korean word-processor format), HWPX and PDF, generates 50 hostile documents with nothing but the Python standard library and compares each file's expected verdict with the Kotlin guards. The set started at 36 files on October 5, 2026 and reached 50 the same day after a review. On October 23 we fixed the whole test skipping on our Windows build machine. What runs on the set's files in the unit test task is the container verdict. Whether XSS executes on screen is checked by device instrumentation with staged documents and a conditional node test.

Sources: this app's git history (origin/main 512dbef), code, ADR-0002, the implementation plan, device E2E reports and GitHub Actions history and repository settings (queried November 7, 2026; log read for one run). Compression ratios were recomputed with Python 3.12 zlib while writing this note; the tests and the generator were not run.

One row holds the file and its expected verdict

generate.py is 682 lines. It writes ZIP, CFB (Compound File Binary, the container inside HWP 5 files), HWPX and PDF by hand with the standard library and emits 50 files plus manifest.tsv. It is deterministic and its output is never committed. There are 10 families, among them ZIP bombs, parser differences, pixel bombs and CFB, plus 2 control rows.

file                   family    sniff    guard        preview
bomb_1gb_lying.hwpx    zip_bomb  HWPX     RATIO        shown
multi_bomb_noisy.hwpx  zip_bomb  HWPX     TOTAL_BYTES  shown
cfb_bomb.hwp           cfb_bomb  HWP5     LOOP         shown
xss_text.hwpx          content   HWPX     OK           shown

MaliciousSetTest reads the table row by row and compares it with DocSniffer, ZipGuard/Hwp5Guard and HwpPreview. It collects every mismatch into one failure, and it also fails if a single file takes 1,000 ms or the table has fewer than 30 rows. The Gradle task generateMaliciousSet builds the set ahead of the :core:docs unit tests, and release_gate.sh calls the same tests. On bomb rows, "shown" means the viewer refuses the engine and shows the preview instead.

The ratio rule stops some bombs; budgets stop the rest

ZIP bombs meet three layers. A 1 GiB entry with an honest size ends at ENTRY_TOO_LARGE before anything inflates. bomb_1gb_lying.hwpx declares 1000 bytes, so it reaches the ratio rule, which counts real output: past 1 MiB, more than 1000:1 is refused. In the October 5 JVM run both took 2 ms, and the file carrying the 1 GiB was 1.07 MB.

The rule only just catches the set's zero bomb. Recomputing the generator's deflate in memory gives about 1,012:1, 1.2% over the limit. The code comment's 1030:1 is closer to deflating the same zeros in one pass, about 1,029:1 when recomputed; the generator writes separate blocks, so it lands a little lower. multi_bomb_noisy.hwpx scatters random bytes between the zeros and lands near 103.8:1 per entry, far under the rule. It has 16 entries of 40 MiB, 640 MiB in all, and the fourth pushes it past the 128 MiB real-byte total for everything outside BinData/. BinData/ is the folder for images inside a document, with its own total limit (256 MiB by default); everything else counts against the 128 MiB, including images placed outside that folder.

The 64 MiB per-entry and 128 MiB total budgets are normal-document maximums plus a margin. Across 46 HWPX files in a local corpus, the largest entry outside BinData/ was 2.9 MB and the largest total 3.4 MB, which the code records as a 20x margin.

A visited set stops CFB loops, but each path needs its own row

In cfb_bomb.hwp a stream's FAT chain (the sector link table) points back to its own start. CfbReader walks chains and directories with a visited set and a length cap, so the second visit to a sector ends in LOOP.

MaliciousSetTest never calls extents(), and that gap surfaced on October 24. We split one guard-table row into forEachChunk and extents, and the new cfb.streamingLoopCopy row passed at first with the guard removed. extents() is what PreviewScrubber uses to overwrite the preview streams of a received file, and it had no loop test. CfbReaderTest covers it now (afd5b8d).

XSS rows only get a container verdict

xss_text.hwpx carries markup as body text and xss_font.hwpx carries it in a font name. MaliciousSetTest only decides that both are containers the viewer may open. Our topic list said XSS ran on every build; reading the code again showed that rendering is checked in three other places.

  • Device instrumentation, RhwpHostTest, opens each document and audits the DOM. It needs the documents staged on the device and skips without them, and neither CI nor release_gate.sh runs it. On October 5, on debug builds on a Galaxy S21 (WebView 153) and an API 33 emulator (WebView 103), xss_text, xss_font and nest had one script (viewer.js) and zero on* attributes, javascript: values, banned elements or CSS url() rules.
  • The node test test_web_engine.mjs renders the generated files with rhwp and inspects the first two sanitized pages. If the files aren't in a home cache it skips, and webTests doesn't pass the set's path.
  • The node test test_web_units.mjs runs under webTests but uses only inline strings.

In the WebView, SecurePathHandler answers every request with a bundled asset, a one-time document token or a 403. The early test build returned null, which left only blockNetworkLoads and the CSP in the way, so the product forbids null.

The CSP goes on every response, 403s included, because a module Worker obeys the CSP of its own response; a CSP on viewer.html alone would leave the Worker unrestricted. Raw SVG from the engine is parsed into an inert document and sanitized against an allow-list before it reaches the page.

The canary test tries to reach a local server. The main thread's 14 paths, the Worker's 9 and the external_link document all scored 0 hits, while an unhardened control WebView scored 1. Without the control, you can't tell a hardened page from a broken test that never reaches the server.

A review showed the 75/75 report did not cover every guard

Commit ca1ade4, which brought in the set and the guards, is co-authored by Claude. The October 5 M2 result said removing 75 guards failed all 75 and marked four completion criteria as met. Those 75 were hand-picked. A review the same day found about 15 guards in ZipArchive and CfbReader with no test, plus PIXELS_TOTAL in Hwp5Guard.

Hwp5Guard had a gap too. It counted only the compressed size of HWP 5 streams. After the review it inflates chunk by chunk and counts real bytes. ZipGuard gained the budget outside BinData/, and an image whose size can't be read is now refused. The set grew from 36 to 50 files and guard removal reached 146/146.

The generator was wrong too. A bug in how it wrote CFB sibling links surfaced on the first comparison with the Kotlin verdicts.

The repository doesn't record who did that review, and it has no record of a person editing the code. The operator's rule that a guard must fail when removed went into the M2 criteria and produced the 75/75 measurement. The 64 MiB and 128 MiB budgets still carry an owner-confirmation tag in the code.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

On Windows, the test was silently skipping

We moved the build machine to Windows on October 18, 2026. core/docs looked on PATH for a file named exactly python3, Windows has python.exe, so generateMaliciousSet was never registered, the set's directory property stayed empty and assumeTrue skipped the test.

Commit 62488f2 at 05:02 on October 23 says the tests had never run on Windows since the move, and logs a full unit run as 1,254 tests, 0 failed, 7 skipped. It doesn't name the seven. About eight hours later d573f8a fixed the lookup. We found nothing in the records we read that compared skips by name. The skip was fixed during an automated check run on a Windows-built release; the log doesn't say how it was noticed.

d573f8a's verification line reads "1 test run, 0 skipped, 51 set files", the same as 50 documents plus the manifest. How a skip disappears into a green run is covered in Silently skipped tests keep CI green. With no python, this test still skips; only release_gate.sh stops with BLOCK. The same script calls a missing node a "failure, never a skip".

The operations log says it doesn't know which machine built the 1.2.0 and 1.3.0 AABs, so we can't say whether a release between October 18 and 23 skipped the set.

0 of 99 CI runs passed: CI can't gate the set

As of November 7, 2026, GitHub Actions lists 99 CI runs and none succeeded (78 failed, 21 cancelled). The one run whose log we read, 512dbef, did not fail on python. generateMaliciousSet printed wrote 50 files, the build failed on one unit test in :core:designsystem, and the log has no task line for :core:docs:testDebugUnitTest. All 99 runs are pushes to main, and main has no branch protection, so a failing CI doesn't hold code back. What stops a release AAB when the set fails is release_gate.sh, and running that script is left to the release checklist.

A generator instead of samples, and rhwp's unmeasured limits

The generator's docstring says "no real documents, no binary blobs", so what stays in the repository is 682 lines and the expected verdicts. The test compares every row, so in the docstring's words the generator and guards "cannot drift apart". Unlike sample files, a changed verdict or file content shows up as a code diff rather than a binary, and no hostile file stays in the repository. The same files go into device E2E, where the S21 and S20 each passed the manifest 50/50.

The set only covers known patterns, so it guards against regressions; finding unknown inputs is a fuzzer's job, and we found no fuzzing record in the repository's docs or tests.

Leaving limits to rhwp was rejected. The wasm contains text about an inflate limit, but nobody measured it, so the Hwp5Guard comment says the guard "does not rely on them".

No real encrypted files, and a 29.1 s TIMEOUT on the S21

The flags family only sets flag bits; real encrypted and DRM documents aren't in the set.

The 1,000 ms cap is JVM time on a development machine. paras_50k.hwpx, 50,000 paragraphs, came to 1,220 pages and parsed in about 21 s under node 20 with rhwp 0.8.6 on a desktop on October 5, 2026, between the 10 s slow prompt and the 30 s forced fallback. On the S21 its first page took 26.1 to 27.9 s or hit TIMEOUT at 29.1 s, and the emulator hit TIMEOUT at 29.3 s.

In the October 5-6 device E2E run, the 64-level nested table in nest.hwpx reported itself drawn while showing a blank page. After the follow-up fix, release builds ended on the damaged-file screen with "open with another app" in 3 of 3 runs. MaliciousSetTest can't see this defect.

Write the verdicts first, then remove guards to check them

  1. Split threats into families and write each file's expected verdict first.
  2. Write a deterministic generator with no outside dependencies that emits the files and the manifest together and prints how many it wrote.
  3. Have a test compare the manifest row by row, and assert a per-file time cap and a minimum row count.
  4. Set budgets from a corpus of normal documents: take the maximums and multiply by a margin. This app went from 46 files, 2.9 MB and 3.4 MB to 64 MiB and 128 MiB.
  5. Attach it to the unit test task. This app still skips when python is missing, but don't leave a security set skippable. The snippet below is a proposal, not code from the repository. 
    val dir = System.getProperty("sugardoc.malicious")?.let(::File)
if (System.getenv("CI") == "true") check(dir?.isDirectory == true) { "security set missing" }
assumeTrue(dir != null && dir.isDirectory)
  6. Measure rendering on a device, and first confirm an unhardened control WebView scores a hit.
  7. Remove guards one at a time and watch tests fail. If a guard sits on two paths, give it two rows.

Still to do: a green CI, no skips, and the webTests wiring

Three things were not done as of November 7, 2026: fixing the test failure in another module so CI runs to the end, turning the skip into a failure on a CI machine with no python, and passing the generateMaliciousSet output to webTests. The log we read doesn't show whether MaliciousSetTest runs in CI without a skip, and we did not download the report files.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

How do you stop ZIP bombs in an Android app?

Ignore declared sizes and count real bytes while inflating. This app combines a per-entry cap, a 1000:1 ratio rule past 1 MiB and total budgets.

Can HWP or HWPX files be decompression bombs?

Yes. HWPX is a ZIP, and HWP 5 keeps deflate streams inside CFB. The set has rows that inflate to 1 GiB in both formats.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: GMA Next-Gen ad callbacks run off the main thread – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Incident

GMA Next-Gen called our full-screen ad callback on a background thread: how a photo app crashed after 243 passing unit tests

In our app, GMA Next-Gen called the ad-shown callback on its own background thread, GMA(BG) 4. Code that navigated from it passed every test and crashed on the emulator.

Four minutes after 243 unit tests finished with zero failures, Compress Image dropped to the launcher on the emulator when we tapped Start over after a second job. That was 16:10 on September 23, 2026, and the crash log named the thread GMA(BG) 4. We hit two traps that afternoon while adding three ad formats. One is this crash. The other is that UMP, Google's ad consent SDK, returned false from canRequestAds() at every launch, so the splash screen never waited for an app open ad. Commit 254313b fixed both.

The same app also crashed that night because R8 stripped a constructor; that story is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app. How often our block puzzle game shows interstitials is a separate note: We set interstitial frequency from device timelines. Both defects here appeared in an unminified debug build and have nothing to do with frequency rules.

Sources: the app repository's git history (254313b, 5107152, bf62e81, 8e5bd25), the CHANGELOG entry for 2026-09-23, the ad design document, code and tests, the agent session log from that day and three independent review reports. Times are Korea Standard Time; checked on November 8, 2026.

popBackStack threw on GMA(BG) 4

The crash was caught by a journey script the agent wrote that afternoon. It launches the debug build against AdMob test ad units and walks six steps (listed in step 4 of the procedure below). Step 6 finishes the second job and taps Start over, the first place an interstitial can appear. In the first journey, finished at 15:31, the interstitial showed there without trouble. In the 16:10 run the app vanished and left the launcher on screen, so the agent read the crash buffer.

FATAL EXCEPTION: GMA(BG) 4
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Method setCurrentState must be called on the main thread
  at androidx.lifecycle.LifecycleRegistry.enforceMainThreadIfNeeded(LifecycleRegistry.kt:382)
  at androidx.lifecycle.LifecycleRegistry.setCurrentState(LifecycleRegistry.kt:139)
  at androidx.navigation.NavBackStackEntry.updateState(NavBackStackEntry.kt:161)
  ...
  at androidx.navigation.NavController.popBackStack(NavController.android.kt:244)
  at ...SugarCompressNavHost...(SugarCompressNavHost.kt:135)

The result screen's Start over handler called popBackStack() to return HOME. Navigation then changed the lifecycle of the screen being popped, and LifecycleRegistry refused because it was not on the main thread. The caller was the SDK's onAdShowedFullScreenContent callback, which, in our log, GMA Next-Gen invoked on its own background thread. Nothing caught the exception, so the whole process died.

A review fix moved navigation into the callback

The interstitial code from the night before, commit 5107152, received the same callback and never crashed. All the callback did was complete a CompletableDeferred, which is safe from any thread. Commit bf62e81, at 00:26 on September 23, confirmed on the emulator that an interstitial showed after the third job and that closing it returned to HOME. Back then the app navigated after the ad closed.

On the afternoon of September 23 the operator proposed shipping all three ad formats at once, and asked for a version that had been analyzed in depth and cross-checked. That proposal and request are the operator's whole part on record; no person edited the code afterward. The agent brought in a separate reviewer agent told to report, not edit (it only ever read code). By then the working tree navigated to HOME first and showed the ad second. The second review, at 16:02, said HOME was drawn and tappable before the interstitial appeared. That is the "ad appears unexpectedly while the user is interacting" pattern AdMob warns about, and a quick tap could open the photo picker together with the ad. The reviewer's fix: stay on the result screen and navigate to HOME the moment the ad covers it.

The agent took that moment from the SDK's onAdShowedFullScreenContent and passed the navigation function into it. Both installing the callback and calling show() happen inside withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate), which fixes the thread of the code doing the installing, not the thread the SDK later calls back on.

The banner loader from commit 8e5bd25 on September 20 had posted adView.destroy() to a main-looper Handler from day one. That handling never made it to the full-screen code.

Why 243 tests and the third review missed it

A unit test covered exactly this behavior. FullScreenControllersTest has a test that checks navigation happens only once the ad covers the screen ("Start over navigates only once the ad covers the screen, or right away without one"). Its fake ad, though, calls onAppeared() directly on the test thread. A single-threaded fake cannot reproduce a threading bug, so the test passed.

The first and second reviews came before the callback navigated at all; only the third saw that code. At 16:07 it marked "Navigate under the ad: resolved", and opened its report by saying it had only read code and had built or run nothing. The crash three minutes later is the log above.

The cross-check found the eight pacing defects the CHANGELOG lists, including an interstitial after a failed job, a retried job counted twice, ad requests for a Pro user with a stale cache, and an ad shown on a stopped Activity.

We don't call an ad build done until it has run on an emulator or device up to the point where a real ad appears.

All four callbacks now go through one main-looper Handler

The 16:12 threading fix lives in one file, GmaFullScreen.kt, which interstitials and app open ads share (other third-review findings were fixed across several files at the same time). The shown, failed-to-show, dismissed and paid callbacks all hand their work to the same main-looper Handler.

private val mainHandler by lazy { Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) }
onShowed = {
    mainHandler.post {
        onAppeared()          // navigates to HOME here
        appeared.complete(true)
    }
},
onDismissed = {
    mainHandler.post {
        onDismissed()
        dismissed.complete(true)
    }
},

Posting only the shown callback would have stopped the crash. The code comment gives the reason for moving all four: queued on one looper in arrival order, "shown" is always handled before "dismissed". Going back to the pre-review order, navigating first and showing the ad second, was off the table, since the second review had flagged it as a policy risk.

The 16:17 rerun reached step 6, showed the ad screen (AdActivity), and returned to the app after it closed. The crash buffer had no FATAL entries. The ad design document gained a line saying anything new hooked to an SDK callback must assume a background thread.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

UMP starts every cold launch with canRequestAds() false

The UMP problem showed up about 40 minutes before the crash. In the first journey, finished at 15:31, the cold-start app open ad never held the splash. A 15:33 cold start with added logging printed splash not held: BlockedNoConsent. Holding the splash depended on consent state, and a code comment assumed that in Korea, where no consent form is required, consent from the previous session would already allow ads.

The agent's next suspect was UMP's debug settings. At 15:45 it cold-started a build with them and a build without them, twice each. All four runs began with canRequestAds=false and status 0 (UNKNOWN). The consent update took 2,246 to 2,413 ms, SDK initialization another 1,266 to 1,412 ms, finishing 4,767 to 5,116 ms after process start. All four timed out the 2 s wait with "consent/SDK not ready in 2000 ms". UMP did not carry "consent not required" into the next launch, so every cold start paid the round trip again.

A new AdGate.wants() decides whether to hold the splash from the Pro state and the feature flag alone. Actual ad requests still go through decide(), which checks consent and initialization first. The wait went from 2 s to 3 s. The 2 s came from our Korean spell-check app, which initializes the SDK before consent, an order this app's ad rules forbid. Google's app open sample waits 5 s. A fill that arrives after the budget is kept for the next return.

Even 3 s was not enough on the emulator. The final 16:25 journey logged "consent/SDK not ready in 3000 ms" at step 2, with the Play purchase check taking 4,139 ms. The ad design document records this limit with the emulator's 3.4 to 4.1 s for the purchase check.

Measured only on an API 35 emulator with no consent required

We have not measured the startup state or round trip in the EEA or other regions where the consent form appears, and we have not checked callback threads in the older, pre-Next-Gen GMA SDK. Google's Next-Gen interstitial page and migration guide don't say which thread callbacks arrive on (checked November 8, 2026). The only threading advice in the migration guide is to initialize the SDK on a background thread.

Code whose callbacks only do thread-safe work, like 5107152 above, doesn't need this fix. The ad design document's October 4 notes say a sideloaded Galaxy S20 got its Play answer in 3.34 s, so it showed no cold-start ad either way, while a Galaxy S21 showed cold-start ads from the second launch. The S21's Play latency wasn't measured.

Five steps before hooking an SDK callback

  1. Find every ad SDK callback body and mark calls that touch navigation, lifecycle or views. rg -n "onAd(Showed|Dismissed|FailedToShow)FullScreenContent" is a start.
  2. Post the marked calls to a main-looper Handler, and send all callbacks of one ad through the same Handler so their order holds.
  3. Add a test that fires callbacks from another thread. A controller-level fake skips everything below the Handler, so this has to be a Robolectric test that calls the SDK-side function, GmaFullScreen here, directly. The module has no Robolectric dependency yet, and the function waits for dismissal, so the thread should call onDismissed() too. An untested sketch: 
    var onMain: Boolean? = null
// fire shown and dismissed from another thread, like the SDK, and wait for it
install = { cb -> thread(name = "fake-GMA(BG)") { cb.onShowed(); cb.onDismissed() }.join() },
onAppeared = { onMain = Looper.myLooper() == Looper.getMainLooper() },
// then drain the posts queued on the main looper
shadowOf(Looper.getMainLooper()).idle()
assertEquals(true, onMain)  // false once mainHandler.post is removed
  4. Run the debug build against test ad units up to the point where an interstitial really appears. Our journey has six steps: first launch, cold start, Home key and back after 35 s, open the photo picker and cancel after 35 s, Start over after the first job, Start over after the second job. Then check that adb logcat -b crash has no FATAL entries.
  5. Log canRequestAds(), the consent status, the consent round trip and SDK init time at process start, and set the splash wait and its budget from those numbers. These are the lines our app wrote (collected from different runs): 
    GmaAdsAdapter: UMP at start: canRequestAds=false status=0 debugSettings=false
GmaAdsAdapter: UMP consent update took 2246 ms
GmaAdsAdapter: GMA initialized in 1295 ms, 4767 ms after process start
AppOpen: app open skipped (cold): consent/SDK not ready in 2000 ms
AppOpen: cold: entitlement answered in 4139 ms

Nothing in 465d85b tests the main-looper post

As of origin/main on November 7, 2026 (465d85b), what protects this fix is a comment in GmaFullScreen.kt and one sentence in the ad design document. Deleting mainHandler.post would leave every unit test green, so the test in step 3 is the next thing to add. Backlog item C-12, tuning the cold-start budget from real-device logs, is still open, and whether to shorten the wait for the Play purchase check is waiting on an operator decision.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Which thread do GMA Next-Gen full-screen ad callbacks run on?

In our crash log it was one of the SDK's background threads, GMA(BG) 4. The Next-Gen guides we checked (interstitial, app open, banner, migration) don't say, so post any UI work from those callbacks to the main looper.

Why does "setCurrentState must be called on the main thread" crash the app?

Calling Navigation's popBackStack() off the main thread made LifecycleRegistry throw when it tried to change a screen's lifecycle. In this app, the call came from the ad-shown callback returning to HOME.

Is it normal for UMP canRequestAds() to be false at app start?

In our measurements it was false, with status UNKNOWN, at the start of every cold launch, even where consent is not required. It changed only after the consent update finished, about 2.3 s on the emulator.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: CLAUDE.md rules: why the same incident came back – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Retrospective

Most CLAUDE.md rules came from an incident, and some incidents came back anyway

A reply-language rule went in five minutes after the incident and still broke on five later dates. After a project memory about pkill, that project had no more exit 144, while other projects had 7.

At 08:39 KST on October 2, 2026, the operator got a status report in English and asked for Korean. Five minutes later another session wrote a Korean-reply rule into the global CLAUDE.md (the global instructions below). Session logs show the rule breaking on October 4, 5, 8, 11 and 24, after it had been attached to those sessions' context. Over the same stretch, calls containing pkill -f kept ending in exit 144: that stopped in the project that got a memory note, and 7 more landed in projects without it.

Sources: rule text from the global instructions, project memory files, Claude Code session logs (jsonl) and the Claude Code documentation. Exit 144 counts were scripted on 2026-11-07 from the 137 logs directly under the project folders, leaving out folders we don't publish, scheduled harness sessions and subagent logs. For Korean relapses we searched the same logs for requests to reply in Korean, kept only sessions where the global file had already been attached, and stopped at October 24. Times are KST.

exit 144 happened more often than the note said

Commands that used pkill -f, or pgrep -f with kill, to stop a process also cut off the agent's own shell. The Bash tool wraps each command in bash -c '...pattern...', so the pattern also matches the calling shell's command line. The call ends in exit 144 and the rest of it never runs. The note says the target survives, but in the 4 cases we checked, the target had stopped. We could not confirm why the value is 144. A SIGTERM usually gives 143, and the shell changed on October 18, so we could not reproduce it.

The agent recorded this in memory at 16:53 on October 4, 2026 and wrote that it happened "twice". The note doesn't say which two it meant. The game project's main session logs do show 2 that day. Counting Bash calls that contain pkill -f or pgrep -f and ended in exit 144 gives 5 in the same project, including 3 from the day before, and 24 across all counted projects from September 14 up to the note. All 31 in the logs, including those after the note, contain pkill -f or pgrep -f with kill; no exit 144 happened without one of them.

From the note until October 18, none of the game project's 1,348 Bash calls ended in exit 144, and none used pkill -f. Two pgrep -f calls remained, for waiting or checking, and neither led to a kill. Our first count missed normal exits and claimed zero such calls; a fact-checking agent found these two.

Other projects had 4 failures on October 5 and 3 on October 11. The documentation scopes auto memory per repository. The note sat in the game project's memory, and a search for pkill in the global instructions finds nothing, so it did not load in sessions elsewhere. The project behind 3 of the October 5 failures wrote its own line to the same effect at 13:21 that day.

The development environment moved on October 18 and the shell changed with it, so later zeros are left out. The game project's zero is also just 14 days in one project. Other projects also had no exit 144 after 15:12 on October 11, so we don't claim the note caused the drop.

The Korean rule broke after it was attached

The operator asked for this to go into the global instructions. In a session with the file attached, the same request came back at 01:23 on October 4. The reply before it had 0 Hangul characters and 1,691 Latin letters.

While drafting this note, Claude's first guess was session age: the relapsing session began on September 30, two days before the rule, so it might never have seen it. The logs rule that out. The global instructions were attached to that session at 11:24 on October 3, right after its first compaction, and the relapse came later. A session started at 11:50 that day, with them attached from the first moment, also answered in English on October 4 and 5. The five dates are days the operator objected in 4 such sessions: 2 in the game project, one each in the spelling and utility apps. Requests at 11:38 on October 3, 21:57 on October 8 and on October 18 are left out because no attachment could be confirmed.

The memory files and logs show several paths. On October 4, replies drifted into English after a run of English messages from other sessions. On October 5 the questions and options in the AskUserQuestion tool were in English. On October 8 a session answering in Korean gave only its final report in English, right after English table output. On October 24 every reply in the turn was in English, from the first one after a Korean question. On October 11 the operator refused an English question in the spelling app project and had it asked again in Korean.

Objection dates only catch days the operator spoke up, so we counted replies too. We took the last reply before the operator's next message, after a Korean message, excluded code, kept replies of 80 or more letters with under 10% Hangul, and read all 55. Five API error and usage-limit messages and 16 internal classifier turns were false positives, so they left the denominator as well. In 16 of the 34, automatic input such as another session's message arrived in between.

PeriodEnglish replies / allRate
Sep to Sep 280 / 2180.0%
Sep 29 to the rule (Oct 2, 08:44)5 / 3713.5%
First 7 days after the rule17 / 2486.9%
Oct 9, 08:44 to Oct 173 / 2011.5%
Oct 18 to Nov 79 / 4142.2%

There were none through September 28; English replies first appeared in the three days before the rule. Of the 20 after the rule, 17 came in the first seven days, and the rate then fell to 1.5%. The first week includes sessions from before attachment and the samples are small, so we don't read the drop as the rule working. 15 of the 20 came from the game project. We don't know why English appeared in late September, and we did not check for English hiding in replies the filter skipped.

Three settings we have only read about

The documentation calls these files "context, not enforced configuration", and to block an action it points to a PreToolUse hook. A reply sentence is not a tool call, so that hook never sees it. Our reading: pkill is one command to avoid, but reply language follows the input around it, as it did on October 4 after a run of English messages. That doesn't explain days like October 24, when the message just before was in Korean.

We checked the three options below in the documentation on 2026-11-07. None is in our user settings now, and we haven't used any of them to enforce a rule.

  • The language setting passes its value to Claude as "an instruction to always respond in that language". That is one more instruction and enforces nothing.
  • A Stop hook runs when Claude finishes responding and receives last_assistant_message; exit 2 keeps Claude going. This is where reply language could be checked. We haven't measured false positives on code-heavy replies or the cost of retries.
  • Bash(pkill *) under permissions.deny in ~/.claude/settings.json applies to every project and also matches subcommands. The documentation says other invocation forms such as bash -c get through, and pgrep -f with kill, 2 of the 31, is not covered.

Six rules and the incidents behind them

"Install alone is not verification" in the October 1 memory became the same line in the global instructions. The ban on gradlew --stop came from September 23, when a build in another session kept stopping the Gradle daemons.

RuleLives inIncidentDate and number
Reply in KoreanGlobal section 1English status report on a Korean bug reportOct 2, rule 5 minutes later
Run the release build before saying doneGlobal section 3QA never ran the minified build; crash on launchSep 23, 1.0.3 (4)
Install alone is not verificationGlobal section 3Missing VIBRATE permission; crash on first tutorial tap (VIBRATE crash and the fresh-install monkey test)Oct 1, Galaxy S24
Adversarial review after big changes, other paths of the same defectGlobal section 3Chat app: defects found after 1,000 tests passedSep 7-9, 3 reviews
Re-read shared files, edit in part, no unrequested commitsGlobal section 3Another session's commit swept in files in progressSep 23, 32fca47
Do not kill processes by patternProject memoryKilled the calling shellOct 4, exit 144

Three of the six lines in section 3 of the global instructions became the four rows above; the verification line splits into the release build and install rows. The multi-agent research line is a working preference with no incident behind it, and one line is left out because its record falls outside what we publish. The secrets line comes up below. For a repository's AGENTS.md, see How to write AGENTS.md for an AI coding agent; this note covers personal global instructions and project memory.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Two rules where the answer differs by project

Going by exit 144 alone, putting every rule in the global instructions looks easy. The device and commit rules differ by project.

On October 5, 2026, 7 minigame_check checks failed on a Galaxy S21. At 12:17 the agent said it would check on the emulator whether the failures were real, and the same suite passed 58/58 there. The cause was another session launching its own app on the S21 mid-run. The agent wrote this up in project memory that day, with a diagnosis: look in the device logcat for START u0 lines from foreign packages.

The game project's October 5 note calls the emulator a good fallback, while on October 11 the operator told the family app project not to start a PC emulator and to use the S20. Commits work the same way: the global instructions say not to commit unless asked, and on October 22 the game project reversed that and commits after each unit of work.

The documentation warns that instructions given only in conversation can disappear after compaction; Claude Code auto-compaction: what 9 summaries kept covers what survives. If you run one session at a time, you don't need the shared file rule. This record comes from global instructions used by one person; we haven't tried it on instructions shared by a team.

Two rules with no incident on record

The secrets rule went in at 08:55 on October 2, 11 minutes after the Korean rule, at the operator's request, and we found no earlier leak in the source files. The October 8 instruction to ask before anything that costs money or looks odd also became a memory without a recorded incident. Write money and secrets rules before the first incident, because that one is hard to undo.

Five steps after an incident

  1. Write the rule in one line with a Why: the date, the command you ran, the result.
  2. Count the symptom in your session logs. This script counts only tool results that start with the string you pass, so mentions in messages or notes don't count. Change the argument for other symptoms. Passing our unpublished folders as skip arguments gives 31. 
    # python count_results.py "Exit code 144" [folder substrings to skip ...]
import glob, json, os, sys
needle, skip, ids = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2:], set()
for path in glob.glob(os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl")):
    if any(s in path for s in skip):
        continue
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        if needle not in line:
            continue
        try:
            content = json.loads(line).get("message", {}).get("content")
        except (ValueError, AttributeError):
            continue
        for block in content if isinstance(content, list) else []:
            if isinstance(block, dict) and block.get("type") == "tool_result":
                body = block.get("content")
                text = body if isinstance(body, str) else " ".join(
                    x.get("text", "") for x in body or [] if isinstance(x, dict))
                if text.startswith(needle):
                    ids.add(block["tool_use_id"])
print(len(ids))
    Mind the scope: it reads only logs directly under the project folders, skips subagent logs and has no date limit. A relapse that leaves no tool result needs another method. For English replies, pull candidates by the Hangul share of each turn's last reply and read them all.
  3. Pick the scope. If it shows up in two or more projects, use the global instructions; if the right answer differs by project, use project memory.
  4. If the rule bans a specific command, mark it as a deny rule or PreToolUse hook candidate, for example {"permissions": {"deny": ["Bash(pkill *)"]}}.
  5. When it relapses, add the date and the new path to How to apply.

If an incident happens twice, recount it from the logs before you edit the sentence.

The pkill line and relapses after October 24

The pkill line is still not in the global instructions, only in two project memories. By step 3 it belongs there, but exit 144 has not appeared since the shell changed on October 18, so we haven't decided. The five dates are a lower bound: they count days the operator objected, up to October 24. The logs run to November 7, and the table above includes English replies from October 30, October 31 and November 1. The next recount will include scheduled harness sessions.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does Claude break rules written in CLAUDE.md?

CLAUDE.md is read as context and is not enforced. In our logs, 4 sessions with the global instructions attached still answered in English.

Should a rule go in the global CLAUDE.md or in project memory?

Project memory doesn't load in sessions for other repositories. Use the global instructions when the same incident shows up across projects, and keep only rules whose answer differs by project, such as emulator use, in project memory.

Why does pkill -f give exit 144 in Claude Code?

The pattern matches the calling shell, so the shell gets cut off too. We could not confirm why the value is 144. We find the exact PID instead, using a bracket trick such as grep "[b]lock_full_e2e.py".

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.
