item.title: Quiz reach 2.6% to 17.7%: a morning notification – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

Quiz reach rose from 2.6% to 17.7%, and 63% of quiz opens came from one morning notification

The share of active users who opened the quiz went from 2.6% to 17.7%, and 63% of quiz opens came from a local notification sent at 8 a.m.

The plan we wrote with the coding agent called a chat bubble the biggest lever. On October 10, 2026, GA4 showed that bubble behind 13.5% of quiz opens in SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling app, while a morning notification left on the "later" list accounted for 63%. Reach rose from 21 of 818 active users on version 1.6.020 to 388 of 2,190 on 1.6.024 and 1.6.025. The other three paths together reach 5.4% to 8.9% of active users, below the 10% target.

Sources: commits 0da3593, 87a0cce, 129d5f8, 5193152, 19dbee4 and 7b997f8 in the app repository, the quiz plan document, and the monitoring table where GA4 values were recorded. Checked on November 7, 2026.

Measured on one event, reach went from 2.6% to 17.7%

The metric is users who logged quiz_open divided by active users of that version. The baseline filters appVersion=1.6.020 over September 22 to October 5 and was fixed on October 6. The comparison combines 1.6.024 and 1.6.025 over September 26 to October 9 and was read on October 10. The versions differ, and the two windows share only ten days.

There is a third number, 3.4%, and it measures something else. It comes from a September 21 query: 339 of 9,859 active users in the previous 90 days viewed the quiz screen (ActivityMistake). quiz_open didn't exist yet, so that figure counts screen views, and it can't sit next to 2.6% or 17.7%. The plan borrowed it as a provisional baseline until the real one arrived on October 6.

Metric (GA4)1.6.020 baseline1.6.024+025
Active users8182,190
quiz_open users (reach)21 (2.6%)388 (17.7%)
quiz_open events461,063
quiz_done users (completion)5 (24%)227 (58.5%)
quiz_answer per open2.87.9
Correct-answer rate55% (72/130)60% (5,018/8,359)
Active users who finished a set0.6%10.4%

Five main commits and three complaints in five days

Until September 21 the quiz was the eighth of 13 items in the navigation drawer, and nothing in the spell-check flow led to it. People who found it stayed 35 seconds per view, so we read the problem as discovery and reward. Free users who answered correctly saw a subscription prompt in place of the explanation, and 47 of the 124 explanations were still placeholders.

  • 0da3593 (Sep 21): added quiz_open and related events, opened explanations to everyone, added a daily set of five questions and moved the item to second place in the drawer. It shipped in 1.6.020 on September 22.
  • 87a0cce (Sep 22): redesigned the screen and added a "Next question" button.
  • 129d5f8 (Sep 23): added a question bubble after spell-check results in Chat mode and a banner in Classic mode, whose result is a single text field.
  • 5193152 (Sep 24): fixed seven bugs and five UX problems.
  • 19dbee4 (Sep 25): added numbered progress circles, permanent records of solved questions and an 8 a.m. local notification.

The operator pushed back three times: on September 21 that the screen looked dated, on the 24th that it still looked off and seemed buggy, and on the 25th that not much seemed to have changed and that a morning notification ought to exist. Unit tests and the release build had passed through 87a0cce. After the second complaint, a fresh pass over code and screenshots found that "More questions" handed over all 119 remaining questions as one set, which collapsed the progress bar into 119 zero-width segments.

A September 21 query, before 1.6.020 shipped, put screen-view reach for September 2026 at 2.8%. With the item moved up and explanations open to everyone, the quiz_open baseline on 1.6.020 was 2.6%.

Bubble and notification reached crowds of the same size; their conversion differed 2.8-fold

The two paths were shown to nearly identical numbers of people on 1.6.024 and 1.6.025: 1,187 users saw the bubble (quiz_bubble_show) and 1,189 saw the notification (quiz_reminder_show), each about 54% the size of the 2,190 active users. Notification views can include people who didn't open the app, so they aren't necessarily a subset of active users. From the bubble, 96 users (8.1%) continued to the quiz screen. From the notification, 270 (22.7%) did. The verdict table has no bubble view count, so there's no event-based rate to compare. The 2.8 times compares only users who entered at least once in 14 days. Over that window the notification went out about 6.4 times per user who saw it.

Users of the three other paths sum to 194, duplicates included. Taking the 270 notification users from the 388 who opened the quiz leaves 118, so 118 to 194 distinct users came by other paths, or 5.4% to 8.9% of active users. Taking that upper bound of 194 from 388 means at least 194 users came only through the notification, half of reach or more. The 5.4% to 8.9% is not what reach would have been with no notification, because someone reminded by it may have come back through the drawer or the bubble. entry=drawer opens rose from 5.6 to 9.4 per 100 active users. The verdict table has no per-path figure for 1.6.020, but every entry in that version's code sends drawer, so we used all 46. The value combines the drawer item and the quiz icon on the Classic main screen. The icon exists in all three versions, and the drawer layout is the same in 1.6.020, 1.6.024 and 1.6.025.

The explanation that follows comes from the app's structure; we did not measure it. The drawer works only if someone opens it. The bubble appears once per session, after a spell check, for people already in the app, and they can answer right there, which reduces the reason to change screens. The notification arrives at 8 a.m. whether or not the app was opened, and its body carries the day's first question with both choices.

This does not make the bubble useless. The two rates also differ in depth: the 8.1% answered a question and then tapped More questions, while the 22.7% tapped once. An answer given in the bubble logs quiz_answer with mode=chat and no quiz_open, so reach never counts it. The rule we wrote before release says to read that pattern as people answering in the bubble and stopping there, but the verdict row has no count for them.

The plan left the notification for later

The September 21 plan, written with the agent, opened its bubble section with "the biggest lever" and the fact that 78% of users pass through Chat. The 78.0% was correct. The mistake was choosing the lever from in-app traffic alone. Notifications appeared as one line in the list of candidates to consider after the verdict, limited to users who had already solved a question.

The operator pulled the notification forward and also reversed its default. In 19dbee4 the agent built it off by default, with a switch on the result card, which you only see at the end of a set. The same day, 7b997f8 turned it on by default. No production build had the default off, so we have no reach number for that setting. Android 13 and later get one permission prompt, and declining leaves the result card switch off.

We don't leave notification defaults or frequency to the agent. They land in a user's notification tray, and the retention data that would judge the choice doesn't exist yet, so a person decides and records why.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

A local alarm instead of server push

The code says entry=push, but nothing is pushed from a server. QuizReminder schedules a local notification with AlarmManager. The daily set is chosen on the device from a date seed, so the notification can include the question itself. We rejected an FCM console campaign for three reasons: it couldn't carry the question, sending daily would need a recurring console campaign or a scheduler, and without segments it would reach everyone and likely raise opt-outs, a design judgment we never measured. Waking the device with an FCM data message and building the body there never came up in the plan. We didn't measure on-time delivery, and the local notification uses setInexactRepeating, which can deliver minutes late.

Two other ideas went too. A time picker was left out because we expected fewer people to turn the feature on. The bubble was set to once per session from the start, because showing it after every check would look like an ad.

The 58.5% completion rate includes bubble answers

The screen hypothesis was that the missing "Next question" button held completion down, since moving on required knowing you could swipe. The table recorded completion rising from 24% to 58.5% and answers per open from 2.8 to 7.9, and marked the hypothesis as supported.

Those two numbers overstate the screen's effect. quiz_done and quiz_answer include answers from the Chat bubble, the 7.9 in the table isn't filtered by mode, and since 5193152 a final answer in the bubble also sends quiz_done, so the numerator can grow while quiz_open users stay flat. The redesign, the bubble, the notification and a review of the question bank (47 explanations written, 68 corrected, 26 questions changed) all fall inside the 1.6.024 window, so GA4 can't separate them. The plan said as much for the bubble and the screen, and assigned reach to one and completion to the other.

The path breakdown above speaks to reach only. Active users who finished a set went from 0.6% to 10.4% because reach and completion rose together, and we didn't measure how much the redesign contributed.

21 baseline users and 1,442 who couldn't get the notification

The baseline has 21 users and five completions, so a handful of people would swing the 24%. This is also a before-and-after comparison across versions, not a randomized experiment. A provisional analysis on October 4 (September 28 to October 4, 1.6.025) pointed the same way, with 22.0% reach and 8.2% excluding the notification, but it covers a different window and sample.

Apps where many users block notifications may not get this result. On October 22, more users with the alarm set could not receive it (quiz_reminder_blocked, 1,442) than could (1,261). How those background events inflated GA4 totalUsers is covered in Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%, so once an app has background alarms, use activeUsers as the denominator.

It also won't fit a feature with nothing new to say each day. Our notification body is that day's question.

We still don't know what the notification costs. Version 1.6.030 tested four notifications a day on October 17 (qr_extra), and the test ended with no verdict. A 50:50 split showed up as 2,188 to 1,061 active users because the property recorded who was actually receiving extras, so people caught by the fatigue guard (four unopened in a row means mornings only for seven days) and dormant users who never opened the app were tagged as control. Raw uninstall rates of 7.8% for control and 18.9% for the extra arm can't be read as cause and effect.

How to measure this in your own app

If a feature's reach is in single digits, add an entry parameter before you redesign it again, and put the paths that start outside the app in the same verdict.

  1. Add entry to the open event and register the GA4 custom definition before release. Registration doesn't apply to past data.
  2. Put a parameter on the completion event for the screen where the set ended. Our quiz_done has none, so completion can't be split by screen.
  3. Take a baseline on the last version before new entry points, filtered by appVersion. If the screen and the entry points ship together, assign each its own metric first.
  4. Write the target and what a miss would mean before release.
  5. Put paths outside the app in the same verdict row as paths inside it. Ours lists entry=push beside the drawer, the bubble and the banner.
  6. Pull exposed users, entering users and event counts for each path, using the five formulas below.
  7. Label the sum of per-path users as an upper bound, because one person can use two paths. Our three paths other than the notification summed to 194, and adding the 270 notification users overshoots actual reach of 388 by 76.
  8. In a notification A/B test, store the assigned arm as a user property from the first day. We only added qr_arm in 1.6.033.
reach             = quiz_open users / activeUsers of the same version
notification rate = quiz_open(entry=push) users / quiz_reminder_show users
bubble rate       = quiz_open(entry=chat) users / quiz_bubble_show users
completion        = quiz_done users / quiz_open users
answers per open  = quiz_answer(mode!=chat) events / quiz_open events

Completion's numerator can include users who finished in the bubble without a quiz_open, so it isn't guaranteed to be a subset of the denominator.

Still open: the November 15 verdict and bubble-only answers

A new reading with qr_arm, on three notifications a day with the afternoon slot removed, is due on November 15, 2026. In the earlier test, opens by slot were 10.4% in the morning, 18.9% at lunch, 7.7% in the afternoon and 12.2% in the evening. If uninstalls in the extra arm are significantly more than 2 percentage points worse than control, the proposal will be to turn extras off.

The monitoring table has no reach verdict after October 10, so we don't know whether 17.7% held. Counting quiz_answer users with mode=chat would show what the bubble really contributes. We also haven't measured whether people who arrive by notification finish a set, and the verdict table has no figure for how many users keep it on. The table lists the next improvement: reviewing the questions with correct-answer rates of 13% to 32%.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

Should you fix the screen or the entry points first?

Measure first. We then fixed the screen and added entry points after it, reasoning that the destination had to work before we sent people there. Both shipped in one release, and we never tested the opposite order.

Should notification conversion be counted by users or by events?

Look at both, and judge reach by users. This notification converted 22.7% of users and 8.8% of events, because the same person receives it on many days.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • 203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names
  • We pressed BACK at seven moments before shipping one 'Save as PDF' button

item.title: Agent reported zero GA4 users; the table said 43 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

An AI agent reported "GA4: zero in 28 days"; the table report had 43 users

The zero came from reading the Firebase overview page as text, once. A table report for the last 28 days showed 43 active users and 10,522 events, and the app code had nothing to fix.

An AI agent told the operator that GA4 had recorded nothing for 28 days and that measurement was broken; 10 minutes and 26 seconds later the same agent took it back. It was 23:57 Korea time on Saturday, October 17, 2026, one week after our HWP document viewer SugarDoc went public on Google Play, in a Claude Code session that was collecting the app's numbers through Chrome. The subagent sent to investigate read 43 active users and 10,522 events for the last 28 days from a GA4 table report, 34 users and 7,728 events of them on the Play release build.

Sources: the Claude Code session logs (the main session and the investigating subagent, both jsonl), docs and commits in the sugar-utils and game repositories, and the GA4 page text captured in those logs. The logs store UTC; times here are converted to Korea time (UTC+9). GA4 property numbers and other account or app identifiers are left out. Checked again on 2026-11-03.

One read of the overview page after a 4-second wait

At 23:50 the operator tried, in the same session, to re-authenticate gcloud Application Default Credentials (ADC) with an analytics scope. The command failed because the shell it ran in had no gcloud. The operator then told the agent to go through Chrome if the login didn't work, and at 23:52:56 the main agent opened the Firebase overview dashboard in GA4. The screenshot taken right after failed with "Can't interact with browser-internal or unparseable URLs", so it waited 4 seconds and pulled the page text once, at 23:53:06. That was its only look at GA4. Its next calls went to Play Console statistics and Android vitals.

The text it got was 1,736 characters long. It contained exactly one number that was a value, "active users in the last 30 minutes: 0"; the other digits were chart axis ticks. Ten places said "no data available", including the cards for event count by event name, users by country and users by device model. The first card, user activity over time, had no value in its text, only the date tick "17 Oct". In the 23:57 report this became a table row: "last 28 days: users 0, events 0, no records even from QA devices."

The agent went wrong when it turned wording into a number. It combined "no data available" with a 30-minute zero into a 28-day total of zero, then set that next to Play Console's 2 to 3 daily active users. Side by side, "the app is not sending analytics at all" looked like a reasonable story.

The zero went into the subagent brief as a fact

At 23:56:38 the main agent handed the root-cause hunt to a subagent. The brief opened by stating that the GA4 property showed zero users and zero events for the last 28 days, not even from QA devices. The five required checks (whether the google-services plugin was applied, the Firebase resources in the built bundle, FirebaseApp initialization, the consent default, the event call sites) were all code or build; a logcat check on a connected phone was listed as optional. Nothing asked it to confirm the zero in a GA4 report, and it was told to fix any bug it found in a separate git worktree.

Eighteen seconds later the main agent ran the production promotion for version 1.1.0 (versionCode 4), which the operator had approved earlier. Claude Code's auto-mode permission classifier blocked it as "[Production Deploy]". The 23:57 report, four minutes after the page-text read, passed the command to the operator with a caveat: if the analytics bug was also in 1.1.0, it would be better to ship a fixed 1.1.1 straight away. A worktree and branch for the fix were listed as work in progress.

No person corrected anything in those ten minutes. The permission classifier blocked the production promotion for its own reasons, unrelated to the zero; the hotfix and the hold that came from the zero were withdrawn after the investigating subagent's report. Do not change a release decision on the strength of a zero read off a dashboard. This zero reached the report and the brief without the name of the page or the date range it came from. More rules for writing subagent briefs are in Six hard rules in one subagent brief, and five agents cut off by usage limits.

The investigator checked code, then a phone, then the report

The subagent followed the brief's order and started with code and build. For about three minutes from 23:56 it checked the condition that applies the google-services plugin, the Firebase resources in the 1.1.0 release APK (key names only), the initialization provider, and the path that switches the consent default on. It found no defect. The static check of the 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 app bundles came later, at 00:04, after the phone test. At 23:59 the Firebase Management API showed both apps, release and debug, linked to two GA4 data streams.

Around midnight it moved to a Galaxy S21 with the 1.1.0 release build already installed. With Firebase debug mode switched on for the package, logcat showed initialization succeeding, collection enabled and analytics_storage=granted, and at 00:00:52 this line:

V/FA-SVC: Network upload successful with code, uploadAttempted: 204, true

At 00:01 it tried to pull the numbers through the GA4 Data API. Both tokens it had, the ADC token and the gcloud user token, lacked an analytics scope, so both calls returned 403. That left the GA4 pages in Chrome. The data streams page said "no data received in the past 48 hours" for both streams. The realtime overview showed 0 at 00:02:44 and, six seconds later on the same page, one app_entry and one session_start event. At 00:05:38 the subagent opened the "Pages and screens" table report; the text it read 11 seconds later had a total row with 43 active users and 10,522 events for the last 28 days.

34 of the 43 users were on the Play release

At 00:06 it split the tech details table by app version: 1.0.0 (the Play release) 34 users and 7,728 events, 1.0.0-debug 6 users and 2,712 events, 1.1.0 (internal test track) 5 users and 82 events. The debug build alone accounted for 25.77% of events. The user counts per version add up to 45, while the total row said 43.

According to the subagent's report, GA4 had 5 users after the public launch on October 10 (3 on 1.0.0, 2 on 1.1.0): about 4 on the 10th and 0 or 1 a day after that. So 3 of the 34 users on 1.0.0 came after launch; who the rest, seen before launch, were was not broken down in that session. Midnight also passed between the two reads: the overview's "last 28 days" was September 19 to October 16, and the table's "last 28 days" was September 20 to October 17.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The loading guess was never checked; the streams guess contradicts the log

In its 00:07:49 correction the main agent wrote that the zero came from reading the overview text before the cards had finished loading. That may be true, but nobody checked it. There is no record of the same overview page being opened again to see whether the cards filled in.

The subagent offered a different guess: the main agent had probably looked at the data streams page with its "no data in 48 hours" line, at the realtime zero, or at the wrong property or a filter. The session log rules that out. The only GA4 page the main agent opened was the Firebase overview. The streams message itself was accurate: the app really had zero users on October 16 and 17.

The main agent never opened a report with a total row and never checked the number by a second route. The Data API was blocked, so the browser was the only route, but in that same browser the subagent went from opening a table report to reading its total in 11 seconds.

Data API, code review, a screenshot, a hotfix

The Data API's runReport call returns activeUsers and eventCount as JSON, so it does not depend on whether a card has rendered. That night both tokens lacked the analytics scope and got 403, and the operator's re-login attempt at 23:50 had failed. The growth plan committed the next day (8475f45) still said Claude could not see GA4 numbers directly and left every cost-per-install and conversion figure as an estimate. The GA4 report tool in the game repository read GA4 with a service-account token; commit 7a61407 on October 22 made it mint that token from ADC alone, with no gcloud user login. Why gcloud's default login could not get analytics access, and the impersonation command that gets the token instead, are in gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate. Ten days after the incident the daily ops check (68215b5, covering October 27) was reading per-app GA4 Data API numbers through that tool's filter.

The brief sent the investigator to the code first, and that review only showed there was no defect; the 28-day total appeared once a table report was opened. The growth plan named an operator's GA4 screenshot as a fallback, which puts the decision on hold until a person opens the page. The 1.1.1 hotfix and the held promotion were dropped once the table report was on screen. Version 1.1.0 (4) never went to production; the next day 1.2.0 (5), which added direct PDF saving, did (6687cd0, c676b49).

Some zeros are real, and raw counts run high

For an app with almost no traffic, many pages are right to show zero. According to the subagent's report, SugarDoc had zero GA4 users on October 11 to 14 and October 16 to 17. The steps below only tell you which page and which date range a zero belongs to.

Raw counts can also run high: in the October 27 daily check, SugarDoc's raw active users were 13; with test devices and Play pre-launch robots removed, there were 4. That was the day the robots tested the newly uploaded 1.3.3 (versionCode 9). How we filter raw counts is in GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real.

The on-device check used only the sideloaded 1.1.0 build. Neither connected phone had 1.0.0 installed from Play, so the evidence that 1.0.0 collected data is a static check of its app bundle and the 1.0.0 rows in GA4.

Overview card, total row, logcat 204, metric definitions

We looked at four pages this time, and a zero or "no data" meant something different on each.

PageRangeWhat we sawHow to read it
Firebase overview cardsPage range (last 28 days)one value (0 active users in the last 30 minutes) and "no data available" in 10 placesNot a value
Realtime overviewLast 30 minutes0, then app_entry 1 and session_start 1 six seconds laterOnly whether data is arriving now
Data stream statusLast 48 hours"No data received"Can be true for a low-traffic app
Table report total rowLast 28 days (to yesterday)43 users, 10,522 eventsThe number to decide on
  1. Find the page your zero came from in the table above and write down its range.
  2. Read the total row of a report with a table. This time the subagent opened the "Pages and screens" report and the Tech details report (r=user-technology-detail in the URL), and in Tech details switched the primary dimension to "App version" to get the version rows. With the range set to 28daysAgo through yesterday, runReport returns the same range.
  3. Watch an upload from a device. Turn on debug mode for the package, launch the app, find the upload response code in logcat, then look for the events in DebugView or the realtime report. This time the realtime report was used instead of DebugView; one app_entry appeared about two minutes after the upload.
  4. Line up metric definitions. Play Console's active users and GA4's active users are counted differently. Inside GA4, the version rows summed to 45 against a total of 43, and debug builds, test devices and pre-launch robots sit in the raw numbers.
  5. Only then open the code. When handing this to a subagent, do not state the zero as a fact; make steps 1 and 2 its first tasks.

The runReport call for step 2 is the request that stopped at 403 that night, with identifiers removed; only endDate was changed to yesterday so the range matches the reports. The scopes are the ones in the re-login command the subagent left in its report.

gcloud auth application-default login \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" \
  -H "x-goog-user-project: <cloud-project-id>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  https://analyticsdata.googleapis.com/v1beta/properties/<property-id>:runReport \
  -d '{"dateRanges":[{"startDate":"28daysAgo","endDate":"yesterday"}],
       "metrics":[{"name":"activeUsers"},{"name":"eventCount"}]}'

The device check for step 3 runs as below. According to the subagent's report, the two log.tag properties could not be set back to empty and stayed at VERBOSE; it noted they clear on reboot.

adb shell setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app <package-name>
adb shell setprop log.tag.FA VERBOSE
adb shell setprop log.tag.FA-SVC VERBOSE
adb logcat -s FA FA-SVC          # look for "Network upload successful with code"
adb shell setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app .none.
adb reboot                       # clears the two log.tag values (an empty setprop did not work in this session)

Play's 2 to 3 daily users against GA4's 0 to 1

The gap between Play Console's 2 to 3 daily active users and GA4's 0 or 1 a day after launch was not settled by these steps; the session stopped once it found the two metrics are defined differently, without deciding whether it was a bug. The subagent's suggested next step was to split app_entry since October 10 by entry path (launcher or file open) and compare first_open with Play installs. That was not done in the session, and on November 3 we found no table in the sugar-utils docs that lines the two up by date.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

GA4 shows zero for my app. Should I start with the code?

Read the total row of a table report first. Here, a 28-day value read as zero on the overview page was 43 users and 10,522 events in a table report, and three minutes of code and build review found no defect.

A data stream says "no data received in the past 48 hours". Is collection broken?

It can simply mean no events arrived in those 48 hours. SugarDoc had zero real users on October 16 and 17, which is why the message appeared; after the phone uploaded its events, app_entry showed up in the realtime report about two minutes later.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Google Ads for a puzzle game: CPI 30x break-even – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Four Google Ads app campaigns, $36.4, 105 installs, about 3% ROAS: CPI ran 30 times break-even

Block Turn KR, the best of four first-round campaigns, paid $0.59 per install, about 30 times its break-even CPI, the ad revenue one installer brings in before leaving.

Four Google Ads app campaigns for two puzzle games spent $36.4 between launch and the morning of October 17, 2026, and GA4 attributed 105 installs to paid traffic (medium cpc). ROAS (ad revenue over ad spend) ran from 0.1% to about 3% per campaign. The go/no-go criteria set on October 15 had a CPI ceiling, D1 and same-day uninstalls, and no break-even line. A break-even CPI had been sitting in a September 30 document all along; we took it out again only after doubling the budget.

Sources: the game repository's ad analysis and verdict documents and its git history, the promotion results and ad restart planning documents, and daily snapshots from a personal dashboard (Oct 24 to Nov 2), the operating harness's budget rule, and the daily analyses run on Nov 4 and Nov 6 (reporting Nov 3 and Nov 5). Dollar figures are Google Ads cost; won figures use the analysis documents' assumed rate of 1,400 won per dollar. Checked on 2026-11-06. Ad account and campaign identifiers are left out, and so are the amounts of break-even CPI and per-player ad revenue.

First round: four campaigns, $36.4, 105 installs

The first round ran one Korean (KR) and one English campaign for each of Arrow Knots and Block Turn; the English ones targeted Southeast Asia (SEA) or the whole world. On the morning of October 17 the agent joined GA4 paid installs to Google Ads cost per campaign. For Block Turn, GA4 logged about 35% less ad revenue than AdMob, so that revenue was corrected to AdMob's figures; the two Arrow Knots rows were not corrected.

CampaignSpendGA4 installsCPIROAS
Arrow Knots SEA EN (stopped Oct 15)$10.5654$0.200.1%
Arrow Knots KR$7.496$1.250.7%
Block Turn EN / worldwide (stopped Oct 15)$7.0726$0.270.4%
Block Turn KR$11.2419$0.59about 3%
Total$36.4105

By CPI the cheapest campaign was Arrow Knots SEA EN at $0.20; Block Turn KR cost three times as much. By ROAS the order flipped: Block Turn KR led at about 3% and Arrow Knots SEA EN came last at 0.1%.

Actual CPI about 30 times break-even

Break-even CPI is the ad revenue one installer brings in before uninstalling: average revenue per daily active user (ARPDAU) times expected active days. The October 17 analysis computed it from the retention of a 22-player Block Turn KR cohort and Korean ARPDAU, and the actual CPI of $0.59 came out about 30 times higher.

The same document also tried D1 doubled and ARPDAU tripled, and still found a 7x loss. Its conclusion: at any budget, this funnel could not pay back its ad spend. Nor was there evidence that ads bought store ranking (the analysis counted one organic Block Turn install).

Expected active days were short because of the first session. When the analysis rebuilt the event sequences of 17 Block Turn KR paid players (16 device models), 7 of them (41%) finished the three tutorial boards and then left on board R004 without solving it once. It notes that they left before seeing a banner. How the stuck boards were found is in Puzzle game day-one churn: per-device event timelines, exact board math and four walls in chapter one.

Against the industry benchmarks gathered in the same analysis, our CPI was cheap and D1 sat near the median. Day-0 uninstalls (58%) ran about twice the benchmark, and ARPDAU was at the bottom of the range.

Ads counted 94 installs; GA4 saw 24 first opens

The cost per install shown in the Google Ads console was far lower than the CPI above. In the October 17 promotion results document, Ads put it at 101 won for Block Turn EN and 371 won for Block Turn KR. Divided by GA4 installs, the same campaigns cost $0.27 (about 380 won) and $0.59 (about 830 won).

The gap is in the denominator. Against 94 install conversions Ads counted for Block Turn EN, GA4 logged 24 first opens in Indonesia (26%); for Block Turn KR it was 19 against 38 (50%). (Ads counted Sep 17 to Oct 16, GA4 from launch to Oct 17.) Three out of four Southeast Asian ad installs never showed up as a GA4 first open. In the October 17 to 23 retest the console had 55 conversions against 25 GA4 paid installs (45%), and for October 26 to November 1 it had 102 conversions against 50 GA4 installs on the dashboard.

We did not find out why Ads conversions exceed GA4 first opens. This record only gives the ratio, so the payback math uses GA4 first opens as the denominator. The device filter arrived midway: test phones were removed from October 18 and Play pre-launch devices from October 25, so the first-round table predates both. The filter is described in GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real.

The October 15 criteria had no break-even line

The agent's October 15 analysis blamed the quality of Southeast Asian traffic. Indonesian players all had their phones set to Indonesian, the app only shipped Korean and English, and they played 84 to 92 seconds each. That diagnosis held up. The same document called Block Turn's Korean paid traffic "the only paid traffic that earns anything", and the operator stopped the SEA campaigns and raised Block Turn KR from 2,000 to 4,000 won a day.

The document's "decision (user)" section set the criteria for the October 22 verdict: keep or raise the budget if CPI was at most 1,500 won, D1 at least 25% and same-day uninstalls under 40%. A unit-economics document written on September 30 in the same repository had already computed a break-even CPI from assumed values, and the 1,500 won ceiling sat far above it. The retest's 1,107 won per install (27,681 won over 25 GA4 installs) clears that table's CPI line easily. Its D1 of 20% missed 25%, so the table would not have said keep or raise; it would have said extend a week.

The October 17 analysis redid that calculation with measured retention and measured ARPDAU instead of assumptions, and break-even came out lower still. Compute break-even CPI before switching a campaign on, and put it in the first row of the go/no-go table. Don't raise a budget on a table that only has a CPI ceiling.

A 7-day learning budget instead of a stop

The October 17 analysis recommended stopping Arrow Knots KR and pausing Block Turn KR until a fixed build shipped, on the grounds that more money into a leaking funnel would only confirm what we knew. That day the operator paused every campaign for both games, said the money should now go to learning who the players are, and turned Block Turn KR alone back on at 4,000 won a day with an end date of October 23.

The verdict used the three first-experience criteria the October 17 analysis had set (at least 80% solving the fourth board, at least 30% D1, under 40% same-day uninstalls), and that table had no CPI or break-even row either. On October 24 two of the three missed, and version 1.1.6, which moved the stuck fourth board R294 to position 41, shipped the same day. The board-level numbers are in that note's October 24 addendum.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Second round: Block Turn KR alone, 7-day ROAS 8 to 10%

On October 24 the operator switched Block Turn KR back on at 4,000 won a day until November 1, with an early-stop check on October 27 and a final verdict on November 2. The personal dashboard's daily snapshots use a rolling 7-day window, so values up to October 30 still include retest days. The October 31 and November 1 snapshots, which cover only second-round days, show 7-day ROAS of 8% and 10%.

Snapshot10-2410-2710-2910-3111-01
7-day ROAS6%8%9%8%10%
7-day CPI (GA4 installs)$0.74$0.55$0.45$0.47$0.41

On version 1.1.8 (October 25 to 30), 39 of 46 players solved the first board R001 (85%), which the daily analysis judged level with 6 of 8 on 1.1.6, one player apart. The next wall was the fifth board, R085, solved by 12 of 23 on 1.1.8. The October 26 to 27 new-player cohort had a D1 of 0 out of 16. The October 30 daily analysis noted 7-day ROAS of 8% and kept the budget until the November 2 verdict, and that day version 1.1.9, which moves R085 to position 35, was submitted.

November 2 verdict: under the cut line, back on at 3,000 won

The November 2 verdict used the cut line in the budget rule, which shrinks the budget when 7-day ROAS is under 30%; the first-experience criteria were not used. 7-day ROAS was 10%, and the campaign had already stopped at its end date. The Ads screen showed 27,705 won and 102 conversions for October 26 to November 1. The agent recommended not resuming; with the operator's approval it went back on at 14:25 the same day, at 3,000 won a day with no end date.

The first 1.1.9 cohort (October 30 to November 1) had fewer than 20 players, so it was read as fractions: R001 12 of 13, the fifth board R005 6 of 7, R364 8 of 10, judged the same as 1.1.8. By then the budget rule had a cut line and a raise condition (7-day ROAS of at least 100% with at least 20 installs in 7 days), but the verdict table had no break-even row at 100%. Both entered the budget rule on October 30.

Why SEA, event bidding and a bigger budget were dropped

Keeping the SEA English campaigns looked reasonable on one number. In the October 18 document, a player who finished the tutorial cost about 225 won from SEA and about 404 won from Korea. The same document put D1 at 4% for SEA against 22% for Korea; the October 17 comparison had already shown three in four SEA ad installs missing from GA4 first opens, and there was no Indonesian translation, so the option was dropped.

Switching the campaign goal from installs to tutorial completions was also considered. The bar written in that document was at least 10 conversions a day, and Block Turn KR produced about 3 tutorial completions a day. The goal stayed on installs, with tutorial completion and reaching level 10 added only as secondary conversions. Raising the budget was ruled out by the October 17 calculation: even with D1 doubled and ARPDAU tripled, the loss was 7x.

The first-round 3% and the second-round 8% are different formulas

First-round ROAS divides the ad revenue of everyone installed since launch by spend over the same period, with only Block Turn's revenue corrected to AdMob. The dashboard's 7-day ROAS uses GA4 ad revenue: the last 7 days of revenue from all players the campaign ever brought in, over the last 7 days of spend. GA4 logged about 35% less ad revenue than AdMob, so reading the two as "up from 3% to 8%" would be wrong.

The samples are small. Sixteen players started the fourth board in the October 24 verdict, so one player moved the rate by 6 points. The exchange rate is an assumption. Break-even here counts ad revenue only; an app that earns mostly from in-app purchases, or a genre that keeps players for weeks, puts different numbers into the same formula.

Five things to compute and compare before the next campaign

  1. Compute break-even CPI from your own measurements. Expected ad revenue per installer = expected active days x ARPDAU, and that value is the break-even CPI. The September 30 document defines expected active days as the sum of the retention curve. Here, count install day as 1 and add 1 + D1 + D2 + D3 + … A made-up example, unrelated to this game: ARPDAU of 10 won with D1 40%, D2 20%, D3 10% and nothing after gives 1.7 days and a break-even CPI of 17 won.
  2. Put break-even CPI or 100% ROAS in the first row of the go/no-go table, then the funnel criteria (first-board solve rate, D1, same-day uninstalls), the verdict date and where the verdict will be written.
  3. Per campaign, set the conversions (installs) column on the Ads campaign screen next to GA4 first_open split by firstUserMedium=cpc and country, and take the ratio.
  4. Remove test phones and Play pre-launch devices before counting. The first figure in the October 25 midpoint check, 6 of 12 solving R001, included four pre-launch robots; without them it was 6 of 8.
  5. Run a fixed budget for 7 days and change one thing between runs. Between the retest and the second round only the fourth board changed (R294 to R364), but during the second round 1.1.8 went live and 1.1.9 was submitted, so this rule was broken.

Cut on November 6: 7-day ROAS 6%, down to 2,000 won a day

Block Turn KR, back on at 3,000 won a day, was first set for a verdict on November 4. The November 4 daily analysis corrected that: the date had counted the start day as day one, and with the last budget change on November 2 the rule that a campaign's budget changes only once every three days lands on November 5. That analysis put 7-day ROAS at 9%, under the cut line.

Scheduled game jobs then started failing on the evening of November 4, the November 5 daily analysis never ran, and the November 5 verdict was applied in the November 6 rerun. 7-day ROAS was 6%, 7-day CPI $0.47, 7-day installs 38, and the budget dropped to 2,000 won a day. On 1.1.9, 15 of 18 players solved R005 between October 30 and November 5. This verdict also used the cut line. In the budget rule, 7-day ROAS of 100% appears only as a condition for raising the budget, and the daily analyses' verdicts have no break-even row. The next verdict is due November 9, and its table should have that row.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Is a low CPI on game ads a reason to spend more?

Only if it is below break-even CPI. The cheapest CPI here was $0.20 with 0.1% ROAS, and the best campaign, Block Turn KR, still paid about 30 times its break-even.

Why do Google Ads install conversions and GA4 first_open differ?

We did not find the cause; we measured the ratio. Block Turn EN had 94 Ads conversions to 24 GA4 first opens (26%), KR had 38 to 19 (50%), and the October 17 to 23 KR retest had 55 to 25 (45%).

How do you compute break-even CPI for an ad-funded game?

Break-even CPI is the expected ad revenue per installer: expected active days x ARPDAU. Expected active days are 1 for install day plus the daily return rates (D1, D2, D3 and on).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Silently skipped Flutter tests and a green CI – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Silently skipped tests keep CI green: three crypto cross-checks and an integration test that went stale for six days

Make a required test fail in CI instead of skipping. Our three crypto cross-check tests skipped when a Python module was missing, and the CI job had no step to install it.

The skip count from flutter test was 13 on September 11, 13 and 15, 2026. One of those 13 was a relay integration test that had been broken for six days. Outside the 13 sat three crypto cross-check tests that would join them if one Python module was missing. On the night of September 15 we added an install-and-check step to CI, so in CI those three can no longer drop out unnoticed for lack of the module.

Sources: git history of our Flutter peer-to-peer chat app (commits b559ba0, 32ce058, cab4bed, 7048e46), its CI workflow, the test files and the September 15 E2E report. Skip counts were recounted from the tree at commit 7048e46; the tests were not rerun. Checked November 3, 2026.

Three crypto tests outside the 13 skips

Recounting the skip: declarations at commit 7048e46 gives 13 tests that drop out when an environment variable or server is missing: 9 soak tests (BOS_SOAK), 2 signaling server integration tests, 1 DB benchmark and 1 live two-process E2E. The September 13 record of 3,160 passed / 13 skipped is covered in What "100% E2E pass" really meant; the September 15 release cross-check read 3,186 passed / 13 skipped.

The three crypto tests run when they find the Python cryptography package and skip when they don't. On September 15 the development machine had it (version 50.0.1) and all three ran; the skip count of 13 recorded since September 11 matches the 13 environment-gated tests, so nothing suggests these three were among the skips.

The CI Flutter job installed only SQLite before testing

The cross-check recomputes the app's X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM and frame layout with Python cryptography and compares the results. According to the file's header comment, it is the only test that can catch both sides being wrong in the same way, and the same comment settles what happens without the module:

// External-process dependency: this test SKIPS (it does not fail) when
// `python3 -c "import cryptography"` does not succeed, so it is safe on
// machines and CI images without the module.

Until September 15 the CI Flutter job installed nothing but SQLite before running flutter test. From there to a green check:

  1. The CI job looks only at the exit code of flutter test.
  2. That exit code ignores skips; the count appears only as ~N on the result line.
  3. The test skipped without the module, and CI had no step that installed or checked it.
  4. Nothing compared the skip count against a baseline, so 13 turning into 16 had nowhere to raise an alarm.

"Safe" in a comment, and a browser guard the same day

That comment and the test arrived in commit b559ba0 at 10:45 on September 11, co-authored by Claude. At 14:32, commit 8f5a0a5, also co-authored by Claude, fixed message eviction guards that sat behind an environment variable CI never set, so switching eviction off left 659 tests green (that commit's story is in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database). 8f5a0a5 also gave the CI web step a guard that fails loudly when no browser exists. The same rule never reached the crypto test written four hours earlier.

On September 15 the operator asked whether the E2E tests were done. Checking showed that since the UI redesign of September 13 and 14, only the in-process E2E tests had been running; everything else was skipping behind environment gates. That night the gates were opened one at a time, and at 22:12 commit 7048e46 added this step to CI:

- name: Ensure python cryptography exists (the crypto cross-check must never silently skip)
  run: |
    python3 -m pip install --quiet --upgrade cryptography || true
    python3 -c 'import cryptography; print("cryptography", cryptography.__version__)' || {
      echo "::error::(message: cryptography is missing, so the cross-check would skip and CI would pass)"
      exit 1
    }

While skipped, the relay test fell behind two rules

The relay integration test, one of the 13, had not been touched since September 6. On September 9 two rules landed in production: a fingerprint gate that refuses to send when no approval hook is wired (df1dddc, 684ff8c), and a room binding that drops frames whose roomId is not the session's room (684ff8c, 6c99027). When the test finally ran against a live signaling server on September 15, it hit both. sendMessage without the hook was refused with "Peer identity is not verified yet", and a message sent to the literal 'room-relay' was dropped with no error.

Commit 32ce058 at 21:13 put it as "the product is right and the test is stale" (translated from Korean). The fix wired an approval hook into the test and read the room the handshake had bound through debugSessionRoomId, rather than copying the naming rule into the test where the next rule change would break it again. With the server running, all 13 tests in test/integration passed.

The device smoke test (emulator, API 35) stalled on the settings screen the same night. tester.pageBack() looks for a back button by the English tooltip "Back", and since the app was pinned to Korean that tooltip reads "뒤로" (Korean for "back"). Finding the widget with find.byType(BackButton) made it pass 2 of 2 (cab4bed).

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Why a skip-count check or "always fail" falls short

The judgment below is our own analysis while writing this note; the repository has no record of it. Failing the build when the skip count differs from 13 would catch 13 becoming 16, but not a test that is always skipped going stale, which is what the relay test did (the count was 13 on all three recorded dates). Making the test fail whenever the module is missing would turn the whole suite red on any development machine without it, the case the original comment chose skipping to avoid. What the repository added was a CI step guard, and the commit says it follows the same pattern as the browser guard on the web job.

Starting the signaling server inside CI to run the integration tests was also possible. It wasn't done, and no reason is recorded. Instead, the commands for the three kinds CI does not run (live two-process, signaling integration, device smoke) went into section 4.1.1 of the deployment doc, to be run by a person before each release.

GitHub Actions sets CI=true on every run. If the test stops skipping when it sees that value, a missing prerequisite turns the run red on the spot, and development machines behave as before. We have not run this in the repository; it is a proposal.

final onCi = Platform.environment['CI'] == 'true';
test('bidirectional cross-check against python cryptography', () async {
  // ...
}, skip: onCi ? false : skipReason);

The branch uses dart:io, so it cannot go into a test that runs in a browser. This repository's web step runs only test/web/ in the browser, which does not include the crypto file.

One skip path the guard misses, and no CI run on record

The guard in 7048e46 checks only that python3 runs and the package imports. The test has three skip paths, and one of them, failing to find tool/crypto_vectors/cross_check.py within the working directory or the four folders above it, sits outside the guard. CI runs from the repository root, so the script is found today, but nothing pins that down.

The repository keeps no results from the CI Flutter job, and the deployment doc says the CI web step could not be run locally, so a green CI run has not been demonstrated yet. So we could not confirm that these three tests were ever actually skipped in CI. Since 7048e46, if the module still cannot be imported after the install attempt, the CI job stops with exit 1.

Four steps to find required skips and make them fail

  1. Find them with grep -rn "skip:" test/ and grep -rn "markTestSkipped" test/ (why the skip count belongs in every report is covered in What "100% E2E pass" really meant). Line counts are not skip counts: this app's 17 skip: lines become 13 only after dropping the 3 conditional crypto lines, 1 line that skips only on the web and runs on the VM and 1 helper parameter, and counting 1 relay group line as 2 tests. The 6 markTestSkipped calls are decided at run time.
  2. Mark each one required or optional. Required means no other test would catch what it catches, such as a cross-check against an independent implementation or a real server path.
  3. For required tests, add a CI step that installs and verifies the prerequisite, or stop skipping when CI=true as in the snippet above. With this app's guard, if the install fails and the module is absent, the check command turns CI red.
  4. Put tests CI cannot run on a pre-release checklist with the command and the date of the last run. When a long-skipped test fails on its first run back, check whether the test went stale before blaming the product; all 3 failures in this app were stale tests.

Still open: the test's own skip condition and two-device E2E

The crypto cross-check file has not changed since September 11, so it still skips without the module. Once a CI=true branch is added, a GitHub Actions run should show the same skip count as the development machine. There is also no automated E2E across two devices yet.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does a skipped test make flutter test fail in CI?

A skip never fails the run: the exit code stays 0 and the count shows up only as ~N on the result line. This app's own records list a run with 13 skipped as 0 failed.

How do I fail a GitHub Actions step when a Python module is missing?

Install it, then run python3 -c 'import module'; if that fails, print an ::error:: line and exit 1. The install command can carry || true, but the check must not.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Our release gates were checking something other than the release: a plaintext AAB and one missing dart-define
  • A malicious file set for a document viewer: ZIP bombs, CFB loops and XSS, generated and wired into tests
  • The 95.2% realism score never came out of the runner, and the 3D view was a fixed drawing
  • Seven edited HWP files in Hancom's Android apps: 7 of 7 opened, and the re-save waited for a human sign-in
  • App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings

item.title: Game feel fix: a heart that fell 109 ms early – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Method

Mobile game feel: frame timing showed our heart penalty landing 109 ms before the collision

Don't stop at asking an agent to fix the animation. Give it the code and the recording's frames, and have it list each event's cause and effect in order. Use timing measurements to prove the fix.

Tap a blocked arrow in our puzzle game and the heart starts to change first; the arrow hits its blocker 109 ms later. That order is on a Galaxy S21 recording of Arrow Knots, then unreleased, made on the night of October 1, 2026. When the operator called the animation sloppy, the agent committed 719 new lines 10 minutes 47 seconds later and the order stayed wrong. It changed only after a separate code and frame review that asked about timing per event. In the recording after the fix, the heart moves 16 ms after contact.

Sources: commits da0e624, 3eb21df and 65dcf41 in the game repository, the review document, and that night's agent session logs. The 109 ms and 16 ms figures were measured from the original recordings on November 4, 2026. Clock times are Korea time.

Measured again, the heart led by 109 ms

The recordings from before and after the fix each hold one blocked tap. We decoded both frame by frame, counted pixels whose brightness changed by more than 25 between frames, split the count into the header and the board, then checked the result against contact sheets by eye. The median frame gap was about 8 ms, which set the resolution. A 60 Hz screen would limit it to about 17 ms.

EventBefore (level 151)After (level 52)
Arrow starts moving3,807 ms3,851 ms
Heart starts changing3,815 ms3,984 ms
Contact (board shake before, contact ring after)3,924 ms3,968 ms
Heart relative to contact109 ms early16 ms late

Before the fix, the heart began to swell 8 ms after the arrow set off and had faded about halfway by the time anything touched. The review document describes this scene as the effect coming before the cause. That night the reviewer printed time-stamped 60 fps frame differences, and the output showed the heart changing at 3.817 s and the board at 3.933 s, but the review document recorded no measured value. The 109 ms was measured from the original frames a month after the fix.

In the fixed code, the contact callback runs before the ring is drawn. The 16 ms in the video is about two frames, so read it as the delay until each change reaches the screen. Nobody tuned it to that value.

A 719-line rewrite left the order alone

At 22:05 the operator's verdict, roughly, was that the animation was too sloppy for anyone to bother playing. The agent assumed the game lacked effects. It added snake-like exits, five synthesized sound effects, vibration, confetti and a star card, and committed da0e624 at 22:16.

It had looked at frames too: 89 at 5 fps, then 162 and 149 at 10 fps, recorded on the S21. Its notes from that pass say the blocked bump and the heart animation checked out. Nothing in the log times their order. What it changed afterward was the result backdrop, the confetti and the coloring of touching arrows. The report said the work was checked frame by frame. In the rewritten code the heart still dropped at the moment of the tap.

About fifteen minutes later the operator told it to analyze more deeply. The agent split the work into three tracks, and the game-feel reviewer came back in 4 minutes 51 seconds with 6 problems seen on video and 14 recommendations.

The heart code sat one line after the animation call

bump launches its animation in a coroutine and returns immediately, so the next two lines run in the same frame that handles the tap.

is TapResult.Blocked -> {
    fx.bump(id, distance, r.blockers)  // starts the animation, returns at once
    lives = state.lives                // heart drops at the tap
    feedback.blocked(view)             // sound and vibration at the tap
}

One level down, state.tap() settled the outcome on the spot and the UI code sat right there, so nothing separated rule time from display time.

The poke that sends a blocked arrow to its blocker took longer with distance: (90 + 45 * distance).toInt().coerceAtMost(260). The review document put contact 90 to 260 ms after the tap; those are the two ends of this formula. Distance is k + 0.55, so a real blocked tap takes at least about 114 ms. The recording showed 117 ms. This tap sits near the formula's shortest case; by the formula, a far-blocked arrow would have widened the reversal to nearly 260 ms.

The reviewer was asked a different question

The blocked-tap behavior the first pass approved came back as a problem in the review. The reviewer also cut the same video into 149 frames at 10 fps. Its brief asked for motion timing and easing per event, feedback layering per event (visual, audio, haptic), and any abrupt cuts visible frame by frame.

At 10 fps, frames are 100 ms apart, so a 109 ms gap is a single step. The reviewer read the code first, skimmed the 149 frames, then recut only the blocked-tap section at 30 and 60 fps.

The review document pinned the reversed order on code lines and cited no frame numbers for it. An arrow flying over the hearts and status bar (frames 58, 62 and 89), the opening pop-in hidden by the splash fade (frame 21), and a red warning tint that barely showed on the vermilion arrow all came from frames. Take call order and the timing of sound and vibration from the code; take what shows on screen and the actual timestamps from the frames.

The rule stayed instant; only the display moved

Delaying the rule result until contact was an option, but the review said to keep it immediate and the build followed. The document doesn't give a reason. bump gained an onContact callback, and heart, sound and vibration moved inside it (3eb21df).

fx.bump(id, dist, r.blockers) {        // called when the poke lands
    feedback.contact(view, costsLife = !tutorial)
    if (!tutorial) lives = state.lives
}

The poke became a fixed 110 ms instead of scaling with distance, so contact no longer shifts with distance. The poke in these two taps took 117 ms both before and after; what moved was the heart. Board shake dropped from 0.12 of a cell to 4 dp, and red now appears only in the contact ring. The blocked arrow darkens and its blocker gets a white outline.

Under rapid taps, lives = state.lives in the callback jumped straight to the final count, and 6133e9e fixed that the next morning by dropping one heart per contact. That incident has its own note: Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Eight colors became six

The review measured color as well, using the Machado 2009 simulation matrices with the CIEDE2000 color-difference formula, and treated a difference under 10 as hard to tell apart. We implemented the formula separately on November 4, 2026, and every value matched.

VisionOld 8 colors, smallest differenceNew 6 colors, smallest difference
Typical12.822.5
Protan5.517.0
Deutan7.416.7
Tritan2.718.5

Against the paper background, amber reached 2.43:1 and green 2.9:1, both under the 3:1 in WCAG 1.4.11. The warning red and the vermilion arrow differed by 11.1 for typical vision but only 2.0 under tritan simulation, so blocked state ended up carried by shape and motion. The review judged that making all eight colors safe for color vision deficiency was close to impossible, and noted that six colors are enough because the neighbor graph is planar.

To fix contrast the review recommended darkening amber to B87A00, which made things worse: it cuts the deutan difference from vermilion from 7.4 to 2.4. The reviewer saw that number in its own 22:35 run and left the advice in. The agent doing the implementation searched six-color combinations and replaced the whole palette. That search missed the review's target of 20, and 16.7 became the accepted minimum.

Following the review crashed the first tap

Recommendation 14 said to replace weak vibration on Samsung devices with VibrationEffect.Composition. It didn't mention permissions, and 3eb21df shipped the change without declaring VIBRATE, so the first arrow to leave the board threw SecurityException.

At 22:46 the agent had a tutorial script finish without a crash, and on the S24 it had only confirmed install and launch. Asked whether testing was done, it said no. About four minutes later the operator found the tutorial error by hand on that S24. A monkey run on an S21 from fresh state died at event 15 of 800. At 22:47 a level-check script had removed 16 arrows on the same code without dying. The logs don't settle why either script missed it.

65dcf41 declared the permission and made vibration failures fall back to standard haptics. Three seeds of 800 events each on the S21 gave zero fatal errors. Right after that, f7beb3d turned the fresh-state monkey run into a script.

Record a blocked tap, fill the table, fix, fill it again

  1. Record a level on a real device, with every event in it at least once: blocked, removed, cleared.
  2. Cut the whole clip at 10 fps, number the frames on a contact sheet, and show the agent.
  3. Have the agent read the code too, and tell it: "For each event, give me a table of cause frame, effect frame, and where sound and vibration are called. Find where an effect comes before its cause. Mark each number as a code formula or a video measurement." Leave "make it better" out of the brief.
  4. Recut only the suspect section at 60 fps to look at it, and read times from the original frames' timestamps.
  5. After the fix, record the same scene, fill in the same table, and run monkey from fresh state, as in the fresh-install monkey test note.
adb shell screenrecord --time-limit 25 --bit-rate 8000000 /sdcard/run.mp4
adb pull /sdcard/run.mp4
ffmpeg -i run.mp4 -vf fps=10,scale=360:-1 f_%04d.png
ffmpeg -ss 3.6 -t 0.9 -i run.mp4 -vf fps=60,scale=360:-1 g_%03d.png

Replace -ss 3.6 -t 0.9 with the time of the blocked tap in your own video. The code below prints each frame's time and, for the header and board regions, how many pixels changed in brightness by more than 25. Region ratios differ per game.

import cv2
c = cv2.VideoCapture("run.mp4")
H = int(c.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_FRAME_HEIGHT)); prev = None
while True:
    ok, f = c.read()
    if not ok: break
    t = c.get(cv2.CAP_PROP_POS_MSEC)
    g = cv2.cvtColor(f, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    if prev is not None:
        d = cv2.absdiff(g, prev) > 25
        print(round(t), d[int(H*.04):int(H*.1)].sum(), d[int(H*.12):int(H*.8)].sum())
    prev = g

The table above came from decoding every original frame with OpenCV: 1,276 before the fix and 1,840 after. No frames arrive while the screen is still. Gaps in these recordings had a median of 8 ms and a maximum of 3 seconds, so never convert frame numbers to time.

Sound, haptics, fingers and long sessions stay off camera

Sound didn't make it into the screen recording, and video can't show vibration strength. Automated taps hit the exact center of a cell, so they say nothing about real finger accuracy. Long-session defects are missed as well: this game's spring-back crash appeared 28 times in a 300-level stress run the next day.

The boards being too easy was already flagged in the rewrite report, and separate level analysis measured and fixed it the same night. The generator side is covered in A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels.

Far-blocked taps and retention weren't measured

An arrow blocked from far away wasn't timed. We have no player metric, such as retention, comparing game feel before and after.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

How many milliseconds should game feedback animation take?

This game fixes the poke at 110 ms and puts heart, sound and vibration in the contact callback. We haven't validated those values for any other game.

What frame rate should I use to review a recording?

Use 10 fps to skim and 60 fps to look at a section, and read times from the original frames. This recording averaged 85.58 fps.

Is a debug build good enough for this?

It was enough to find the order; both recordings here are debug builds. We didn't repeat the measurement on a release build, so use one if you also want to compare frame delays.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • We slowed a mini game down twice before checking why it was hard: players couldn't recall the answers
  • Rapid taps and an unlocked Retry button: a 600 ms result-card lock, and the 28 crashes a stress run found next
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Testers said the time was "too long, so it's easy": checking that with a simulation before cutting puzzle par times by 30%
  • App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings
  • gcloud 'This app is blocked' for GA4: impersonate
