item.title: Why we replaced an app privacy policy template – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Retrospective

App privacy policy templates: we threw ours out and rewrote it from a code audit

Four apps shared one generated privacy policy. We replaced it with 8 pages written from source, each checked by a second agent looking for counter-evidence.

Four of our Android apps pointed at one English template that said user information "is not collected by me in any way", while one of them, the Korean spell checker SugarSpeller 1.6.025, was sending AI explanation requests and an anonymous ID to our own server. On October 4, 2026, 8 agents read the four codebases for 11 min 46 s and wrote 8 Korean and English policy pages, published at 11:30 in commit d75409b. We treat a privacy policy as a code audit report first and a legal document second, so the site's rules now say that a fact you cannot verify gets left out.

Sources: git history of this site and the app repositories, work session records from September 29 to October 4 and October 17, 2026, and SugarSpeller's release runbook and monitoring log. Commit counts and versions were re-measured on November 4, 2026. This note is not legal review, and it does not judge whether our policies meet any statute.

Where the template and the 1.6.025 code disagreed

The template still ended with "created at privacypolicytemplate.net and modified/generated by App Privacy Policy Generator". It opened with a line ending "built the This app as a Free app." The word This sat where the app name belonged.

TemplateSugarSpeller 1.6.025 code
"retained on your device and is not collected by me in any way"AI explanation requests (corrected words up to 60 characters each, error type, checker, subscription status, app version) and a Firebase anonymous ID reach our server.
Two third parties: Google Play Services, AdMobNaver and Daum (Korean portals whose spell checkers do the checking), Firebase, Vertex AI (Gemini) and the ad partner Liftoff also receive data.
"Free app", "at no cost"Sells Google Play subscriptions.

1.6.025 was the first version to send data to our own server, but text to be checked had gone to Naver and Daum for longer than that, so the third-party list was already short. The design of the AI feature is in the first LLM in our spell checker.

We wrote down that it was wrong, and it stayed until October 4

At 21:49 on September 29, commit 0b64ea6 in the SugarSpeller repository added draft policy text and a Play Data safety answer table. The draft states that the published policy "is the template as is" and does not match reality. Step 3 of the release runbook says to fix the policy and the Data safety form before submitting the app.

When an agent fetched the Google Sites page at 11:05 on October 4, the paragraph was not there. 1.6.025 was rolling out by the night of October 1, so that version ran under the wrong policy for about two and a half days. The monitoring log counted 254 users on 1.6.025 between September 22 and October 3, with no note that test devices were excluded.

The agent's release notes on the night of September 29 said the policy had to change before submission, and on September 30 it handed the item back as the owner's third remaining task. Nothing records why the item stayed open, but the structure that allowed it is visible.

  1. The policy's sentences had no source in the code. A generator wrote them, so nothing could flag a mismatch when the code moved.
  2. The policy lived on Google Sites, outside any repository. Fixing it was one manual line in a runbook, and the four app repositories have no .github/workflows (checked November 4).
  3. Four apps shared one URL, as their Play listings showed. There was no page on which to state a fact about one app.

The one-paragraph plan rested on a sentence that did not exist

The September 29 plan kept the template and added a paragraph under "Information Collection and Use". The agent-written draft says the analytics and ads section could keep its "existing text (Google Analytics for Firebase, AdMob)". Searching the template for Analytics returns zero hits.

The paragraph would not have been enough anyway. On a shared page, a sentence about sending text to Naver would also have landed in the policy of SugarAlbum, a video maker, and "Free app" would have stayed.

The owner's request on October 4 was to move policies and app information to one site. Moving alone would have carried the same sentence to a new address. The audit was the agent's addition, and so was its size: 8 agents and about 1 million tokens excluding cache reads, which the agent reported as not requested.

One writer per app, one reviewer hunting counter-evidence

Four writer agents were told to "only claim what the code does" and, when unsure, to "disclose rather than deny". Four other agents then took the files, looked for evidence against every "we don't collect or send X" sentence, and fixed what was wrong. All four apps needed fixes.

AppWriter's draftAfter review
SugarSpellerSends words, error type and checker name to Vertex AIWords and error type only. The server passes original, corrected and type.
SugarCardNo ads while subscribedThe basic plan keeps the banner, and the exit-screen ad shows on every plan.
SugarAlbumThree groups of permissions missingAdded storage write, ad API and Firebase permissions after reading the merged release manifest.
SugarClipAndroid erases it beyond recoveryRemoved with app data or the app; backup copies are deleted in the Google account.

The first row claimed too much and the second flattered the app. These agents had the source open and the "only claim what the code does" instruction in front of them, and they still wrote those sentences. The workflow script had split writers from reviewers before any draft existed.

Reviewers also settled values that live outside the code. The SugarSpeller writer flagged that "deleted after 30 days" depended on a Firestore TTL policy it could not confirm. The reviewer read it from the API (ttlConfig.state: ACTIVE) and read retentionDays: 30 from the log bucket. That TTL was step 1 of the same runbook, also manual: a query at 16:00 on October 3 found it unset, and one at 01:00 on October 4 found it ACTIVE.

The numbers we deleted and the claim the owner dropped

On October 5, bdbbe97 put "Policies describe the actual code. Don't add claims the code doesn't back." into the site's agent instructions file, AGENTS.md. On October 18, b82faac added "If a fact cannot be verified there, leave it out."

Commit 13d00b8 in our family calendar app AXFamily (October 10) changed the invite link default from 72 hours to the 24 in the code, replaced "an internal ID instead of a name" with the fact that display names are sent, and deleted two numbers found nowhere in code or repository: "integrity tokens 12 hours" and "Play grace period 7 days". The same commit's move to the Seoul region turned out wrong, a story told in the AI processing notice we changed twice in a day.

On November 1 a person made the call. The Block Turn page promised no banner or interstitial in the first three games, but a classic game over counts as two runs, so an interstitial could appear from the second game over. The owner kept the code and removed the sentence, and commit 6ab2edb records it as an owner decision.

Policy work kept coming. After d75409b, through November 4, 22 of 104 commits have privacy, policy or the Korean word for it in the subject line, mostly policies for new apps. Across the whole repository it is 29 of 117. That is a subject-line grep, so one AX notes commit is in there by accident.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The same defect in a Play Data safety form on October 17

One more place states the same facts. At 14:41 on October 17, the owner asked whether Block Turn and Arrow Knots needed a Data safety fix. That day both public store pages listed four shared data types, but the collected section said no data was collected, while our site policies already listed Firebase Analytics and Crashlytics (861c5a3 on October 8, e13de33 on October 11).

The agent lacked console permission, so the owner entered the answers from a table, and at 14:58 the agent expanded the console preview and compared it line by line. On October 4, Play policy URLs couldn't be changed through the API either, so the owner changed four by hand. No app had the URL hard-coded, so that finished the move.

Nowhere to run a check between the four apps' code and a table

AXFamily goes further. Its processors live in processors.json, the policy tables are generated, and the CI job legal-consistency compares the output with the JSON and the in-app notice with the function constants. Its policy wasn't public on October 4, so we never compared the two side by side. We would still run the per-app audit on the four old apps.

Generating the tables alone could sit in the pre-commit check of the site repository, where the policies live. The hard part is comparing the JSON with app code: the four app repositories have no CI to run that, and SugarAlbum has had no commit since January 3. A per-app audit must be redone when the code changes; generation fails a check on a mismatch but needs somewhere in the app repository to run it. So far only AXFamily uses generation. Start any new app with it.

What reading the source cannot tell you, and legal review

  • Code can't confirm legal requirements. The section list came from a list of Korean privacy law items the agent wrote into its own prompt (purpose, items, retention, third parties and overseas transfers, destruction, user rights, privacy officer) plus earlier policies, and we have no record of a person or professional reviewing that list. The photo app policy the writers took their structure from on October 4 had no section on processors and overseas transfers; they added one, and the original got its own 18 days later in 45c6b76.
  • Source is not the shipped build. The SugarCard reviewer noted it could not tell which build was on Play, and SugarAlbum's merged manifest came from a January 3 build.
  • What an SDK collects isn't in the app's code. Commit ba0fe57 (September 23) added IP address, ad interactions and diagnostics to our first policy after the fact.

We haven't tried this on a service with many servers and processors, or on an outsourced app without source. We've only run it on Android apps with one operator.

Start by marking the negative claims in your published policy

If a sentence can't be tied to a line of code or a console value, delete it. Doubt "we don't collect" first.

  1. Fetch the published policy, split it into sentences and mark every negative claim.
  2. Note the app version and build a data flow table: data, destination, code location.
  3. Count permissions from the merged release manifest, not the source manifest. Permissions added by libraries appear only there.
  4. Read each SDK vendor's data disclosure and copy the items over.
  5. Read retention and deletion settings from the API instead of assuming them.
  6. Give the table and policy to a different agent or person and ask only for counter-evidence.
  7. Compare your Play Data safety answers with the same table.
  8. Record the audited commit next to the policy and run the diff below at each release. We have not done this step for the four apps.
# Permissions and dependencies changed since the audit
git diff $AUDITED HEAD -- '*AndroidManifest.xml' '*build.gradle*' '*libs.versions.toml'
# Permissions in the merged release manifest (path varies with AGP version)
grep -rh 'uses-permission' app/build/intermediates/merged_manifest/release/
# Firestore TTL and log retention
TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "x-goog-user-project: $PROJECT" \
  "https://firestore.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT/databases/(default)/collectionGroups/$GROUP/fields/$FIELD" \
  | grep -A3 ttlConfig
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "x-goog-user-project: $PROJECT" \
  "https://logging.googleapis.com/v2/projects/$PROJECT/locations/global/buckets/_Default" \
  | grep retentionDays

This diff does not see server code or request fields. SugarSpeller's repeated AI requests live under functions/, so these paths miss them. Add your server and network code paths.

Step 6 used a review prompt along these lines, shortened and with file paths removed.

Adversarially review the privacy policy pages against the real app source.
Read-only on the source repo. Check: every claim matches code (especially any
"we don't collect/send X" claims: look for counter-evidence: ad SDK, Firebase,
network calls, other paths), ko/en say the same thing.
FIX problems directly in those two files only.
Report: what you fixed, what remains uncertain.

The gate in our release gate and R8 crash note confirms the policy URL returns 200, which proves a page exists and says nothing about its sentences. The Firestore and logging calls copy the form the reviewer used on October 4; we did not rerun them for this note.

Four policies still dated October 4

All four policies still carry an effective date of October 4. In the repositories, SugarSpeller has reached 1.6.033, SugarCard 1.0.003 and SugarClip 1.2.002. A diff of SugarSpeller shows no new dependency in build.gradle, a manifest with queries for 3 sibling apps and one new game screen, and a server that can now send the same AI request up to 3 times. We haven't done the re-audit that decides whether any of this changes the policy.

The Play Data safety forms of those four apps have not finished being compared with these policies.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Is a privacy policy template risky for an app?

It is when its sentences differ from the code. Ours said "not collected by me" while the app sent data to our server. Use a template as a table of contents and rewrite the sentences from code.

Can an AI agent write my privacy policy?

It can draft one, but don't publish that draft unreviewed. All four of our source-based drafts needed fixes from a second agent. Keep writer and reviewer separate, and decide on professional review separately.

What do I write when I can't verify something?

Delete the claim or state it broadly on the side of disclosure. We deleted unsupported numbers such as "integrity tokens 12 hours", and kept a permission we could not tie to a build as "may be declared". Don't write a denial like "we don't store this" until you've checked.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: R8 renamed Gson fields: empty release results – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names

A Gson field without @SerializedName stays at its default, with no exception, once R8 renames it, so the defect only shows up when you open the release artifacts.

On a release build, the second spell-check path (the one Chat mode falls back to when the first path fails) in our Korean spelling app SugarSpeller would have returned blank corrected text and zero errors, with no exception thrown. All 203 unit tests were passing when we found this on September 14, 2026. R8 had renamed the Gson fields output and etype to a and b; commit 3791c2c added @SerializedName and an invariant test.

Sources: git history and CHANGELOG of the SugarMount app repository (sugarspeller), session logs from that week, the 1.6.026 release APK and mapping.txt built on 2026-10-09, and a reproduction run on 2026-11-04 with R8 9.4.14. The spell-check servers are not named here.

Gson does not complain about a field it can't match

Without @SerializedName, Gson uses the Java field name as the JSON key. In the release build, R8 had done this to the Result response model:

# release mapping.txt just before 3791c2c, 2026-09-14
output -> a
etype  -> b

The server still sends "output" and "etype". The object now has only a and b, so Gson skips both keys and the fields keep their initial "". Parsing succeeds, and the screen shows whitespace and zero errors.

Unit tests run against classes R8 never touched, so none of them ever saw a renamed field. The 203 is our recount of @Test annotations at the commit before 3791c2c (the CHANGELOG says "200 or so"), and it includes tests that parse recorded server responses. The two fields had carried no annotation since the path was added on 2024-06-14. That path then stopped receiving responses at all, until commit 0b74357 revived it on 2026-09-13. Both commits shipped together in 1.6.017. We could not tell from the records whether users saw blank results while the path was alive earlier.

mapping.txt flagged 14 fields; two were defects

Finding it took 28 minutes. At 20:50 KST on September 14 the operator asked for a cross-check. The agent replayed the app's exact requests against the live servers (13 of 13 passed), then read the proguard rules and grew suspicious of model fields with no annotation. A script over the mapping.txt of a clean release build checked 19 model fields and listed 14 as renamed.

Renamed fieldCountVerdict
Already has @SerializedName5Safe, maps by annotation value
Filled by code, not JSON7Gson never touches it
output, etype2Defect

The same table explains half of why the first spell-check path kept working in release: the keys holding its values were annotated. Why its unannotated message and result survived comes later. The fix at 21:18 annotated seven fields across both paths. No usable device was available that night, so "blank screen" was a verdict from mapping.txt and the dex files. We only saw the empty values at runtime later, in the reproduction below.

The agent's claim about debug builds lasted two days

Later that night the agent added an instrumented test (4d29ca4) and wrote in the commit message that because minify is on for debug too, the test runs in the same obfuscated state as the shipping build.

It was wrong, and that came out at 08:31 on September 16. The operator had opened KVM access so an Android 14 emulator could boot, and just before rerunning the test the agent checked whether the models were really obfuscated. Release said output -> a; debug kept the original name. The mapping.txt from October 9 shows the same. We did not establish why: the debug configuration.txt has no -dontobfuscate, though running the reproduction below with R8 --debug kept the names.

The agent then signed the release APK with the debug key, installed it, and blocked the first path's host in the emulator's hosts file to force the fallback. At 08:45 the second path's corrections appeared on the obfuscated build, and commit 5c4e3d7 fixed the docs at 08:47. The v16017 tag had already gone on at 07:47.

"lateinit got lucky" was really a keep rule

3791c2c has a wrong explanation of its own. Five unannotated lateinit fields kept their names, and the commit and the agent's memory file say R8 was keeping the names "by accident." While drafting this note in November we ran javap: Kotlin's lateinit var compiles to a public field, while var output = "" is a private field with a getter. The build at the time still had a rule meant for a Kakao SDK the app never used, -keepclassmembers class * { public static <fields>; public *; }, and that rule pinned every public field name. Commit e05f8e3 removed it on September 25, as told in Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The 1.6.026 mapping.txt has message -> a.

This is a reproduction, not the real app: a Java model of the same field visibility, shrunk with R8 9.4.14, Gson 2.14.0 and the proguard files from 3791c2c, then parsed on the JVM.

AnnotatedConfigurationResult
NoneNo R8 (what unit tests see)Correct
NoneKakao rule + -dontobfuscate (stand-in for debug)Correct
NoneKakao rule (the September 14 release)output=[] etype=[], no exception
output, etype onlyKakao ruleCorrect
output, etype onlyKakao rule removedJsonIOException
All 5 fieldsKakao rule removedCorrect, message -> a

Row three reproduces the incident. Rows four and five show that annotating only output and etype would have passed on September 14, then broken eleven days later when the Kakao rule went away and message was renamed. Here the model is never constructed in code, so it ended in JsonIOException. When the code called the constructors and let the objects escape, both the September 14 configuration and the optimized one in use from September 20 ended in a NullPointerException. We did not build the real app, so we can't say which exception it would have thrown. 3791c2c annotated the lateinit fields for the wrong reason and still got it right. Annotate every field that takes a value from JSON, lateinit or not.

Finding etype in the dex proves little

Before the fix, grep -a etype already hit classes2.dex and classes3.dex. classes4.dex, which held the model, did not have it, and that file gained it after the fix. The before-and-after in 3791c2c was valid because it looked at that one file. But the AAB check that night and the pre-release check on September 16 looped over every dex and passed if etype appeared anywhere, and the report cited that as evidence. That loop would have passed the broken APK too.

Narrowing to one file no longer works either, since the 1.6.026 APK has a single classes.dex. We read all 43,818 strings in 1.6.026: 3 contain etype (a sentence with mimetype, closetype, and etype itself), 43 contain output, 97 contain message, 104 contain result.

dexdump -a from build-tools prints annotations with their values:

unzip -o app-release.apk 'classes*.dex' -d dex
dexdump -a dex/classes.dex | grep -c 'value="etype"'   # 1

The line reads VISIBILITY_RUNTIME Lkt1; value="etype". R8 renamed the annotation class to kt1 as well, so searching by class name finds nothing. Counted this way the release holds 11 spell-check keys in 13 annotations.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

An invariant test that fails when one annotation goes

ResponseModelSerializedNameTest uses reflection to require an annotation on every field of the 8 response-model classes. This is the core, shortened:

private val models = listOf(Response::class.java, Response.Result::class.java)
private val codePopulated = setOf("com.example.Response#requestId")
@Test fun `every JSON field has SerializedName`() {
    val missing = models.flatMap { type ->
        type.declaredFields
            .filterNot { Modifier.isStatic(it.modifiers) || it.isSynthetic }
            .map { it to type.name + "#" + it.name }
            .filter { (_, key) -> key !in codePopulated }
            .filter { (f, _) -> f.getAnnotation(SerializedName::class.java) == null }
            .map { it.second }
    }
    assertTrue(missing.joinToString("\n"), missing.isEmpty())
}

The real file has three tests, adding a check of annotation values against JSON keys and a check that the exemption list codePopulated (10 entries today) holds no dead names. Before committing, the agent deleted the annotation on etype, watched this test and the key test end in FAILED, and restored it.

No package keep, and a debug device test can't see this

The broadest alternative is -keep on the whole model package. 3791c2c did not add one, and the session has no record of weighing it. Judged now, the empty values would go away but safety would hang on one rule, and losing that rule would bring the incident back.

The instrumented test stayed, but on a debug build it can't see this defect. We have not tried setting testBuildType to release. A launch check doesn't help either: the R8 incident in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app was a crash at startup, and this one crashes nothing, so a cold start passes. The method behind our reproduction, shrinking the model with R8 --classfile under the app's proguard files and parsing on the JVM, showed the empty values with no device, but it is not in the repository.

Running the release APK through the whole path is the strongest evidence. On September 16 that session ran from 08:23 to 08:46, including other checks, and needed KVM access and a hosts-file block. So the invariant test runs with every test pass, and running the release APK stays a manual step in the docs for when a regression is suspected.

Auditing your own Gson models, from fromJson to the release APK

  1. rg 'fromJson|TypeToken|GsonConverterFactory' app/src/main lists what Gson fills. With Retrofit, follow the interface return types too.
  2. In the release mapping.txt, put each renamed field in one of the three rows above.
  3. Add the invariant test, delete one annotation and confirm the failure.
  4. For each key, count value="key" in dexdump -a across all dex files and compare with the number of annotations in source. In 1.6.026 message appears twice, once per model, so accepting "at least one" would miss a lost annotation.
  5. Sign the release APK with the debug key, install it, and reach a screen that goes through that parser. A path behind a fallback only runs if you block the path in front of it.

What the test misses: new models and removed keep rules

models is a handwritten list, so a new response class is unchecked until someone adds it. The test only sees annotations on the source model; it passes if the keep rule protecting the annotation disappears or a class turns abstract. Step 5, running the release APK, is where those two show up. The two existing models stayed on Gson, while the explanation feature from The first LLM feature in a spell-check app takes its response as a Map and avoids this problem. We have not used a code-generating serializer.

Stale test comments and a dex check still done by hand

  • The test's header comment and the agent's memory still say that minified debug builds rename fields, and the memory also says lateinit survives by accident. Both need correcting.
  • The dex check in the docs is still a manual grep. It should become a dexdump -a value count in the release build script, with its key list taken from the test's expected values.
  • The only device on record that ran this path on an obfuscated build is the emulator. The next release should go through the fallback on real hardware.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do I still need keep rules if I use @SerializedName?

It depends on your Gson version. Gson 2.14.0, which this app uses, ships META-INF/proguard/gson.pro with rules that protect annotated fields, and our proguard-common.pro has a similar rule. In our local cache the 2.11.0 jar contains that file and the 2.10.1 jar does not, so open your own jar first.

Is "Abstract classes can't be instantiated" the same bug?

It comes from R8 too, but the symptom is different. In our reproduction, a top-level model with no annotated fields came out of R8 as an abstract class, and Gson threw JsonIOException. gson.pro protects <init>() on classes with @SerializedName fields, and annotating that class's fields made the error go away.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Measuring 4.5:1 colour contrast in the site build – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

4.5:1 contrast in the site build: the dark hover pair that failed for 7 of 11 apps

One accent colour per app turns into 11 text-on-background pairs. Our site build computes every one of them, and its --check fails if any pair drops below 4.5:1.

In dark mode, putting the dark accent text colour on the pale accent background of a hovered outline button leaves 7 of our 11 apps below 4.5:1, the lowest at 4.17:1 (Arrow Knots). Commit b82faac (18 October 2026, the design-system rework) gave that spot its own text token, tuned against that background, and made the build compute 11 contrast pairs per app. With 13 apps today, the lowest of the 143 pairs is 4.60:1 (SugarCard).

Sources: the site repository's git history and tools/sds_apps.py, and the design docs in our utilities app repository. All ratios were recomputed on 3 and 4 November 2026 in a copy of the site, using the contrast functions in sds_apps.py.

Dark hover contrast at b82faac: 4.17 to 4.66

Each app on this site has a single accent hex in data/apps.json. sds_apps.py computes nine colour tokens from it as CSS text, and build.py writes that to a file. In dark mode the pale background bg-accent-weak is 24% accent mixed into the default dark surface #172131. The dark text colour fg-accent is the accent with its HSL lightness raised 1% at a time until it reaches 4.6:1 on #1D2940, the lightest of the three dark neutral surfaces.

Put fg-accent text on bg-accent-weak, as a hovered outline button would, and the 11 apps at b82faac score: Arrow Knots 4.17, SugarSpeller 4.20, Compress Image 4.27, Flip & Rotate Image 4.31, SugarCard 4.40, SugarAlbum 4.41, AXFamily 4.41, Block Turn 4.58, SugarClip 4.59, Convert Image 4.64, SugarDoc 4.66. Seven are under 4.5 and nine under 4.6.

Our working notes say a review agent checking the design spec flagged this pair: "7 of 11 apps, lowest 4.17". We could not find the review itself, so we recomputed it from the app list at b82faac and got the same numbers. The implementation commit already shipped the fixed pairing: in site.css, .button--outline:hover uses fg-accent-contrast for its text and border.

For 13 days the rule was one line of prose

The commit that first added the site pages, 00b093f on 20 September 2026, set the default accent in site.css to #00897B ("default accent: SugarCompress"). The same day, the first commit of the utilities app repository (7885e3e) listed "compress (temp) #00897B" in its design tokens. Both commits carry an AI co-author trailer. White text on that colour is 4.32:1, and the colour as text on the light background #F6F8FB is 4.06:1.

The next day, the "Design v2" commit 33e6cc0 in the utilities repository (also AI co-authored) caught it. Line 46 of its design spec reads "temporary #00897B (4.3:1, fails AA) is replaced by #0F766E.", and line 20 makes 4.5:1 text contrast in both themes a principle. The site picked up #0F766E (white text 5.47:1) on 5 October, when commit bdbbe97 introduced data/apps.json.

The contrast rule that commit added to AGENTS.md was a field description: accent "(hex, white text on it must reach 4.5:1)". Searching that commit's tools/build.py for lumin, contrast or 4.5 finds nothing.

The first assumption matched the line: if white text clears 4.5:1 on the accent, the accent is safe. But one accent becomes nine tokens per theme, and those tokens meet as text and background in 11 pairs. Today every white-on-accent pair across the 13 apps is 5.45:1 or higher, while the dark hover pair from the same accents goes down to 4.17.

The dark accent was tuned against a different background

The dark hover used fg-accent for text and bg-accent-weak for the background. fg-accent only guarantees 4.6:1 on #1D2940 (relative luminance 0.0222), and for the blue and teal apps the pale background is lighter than that. Arrow Knots' bg-accent-weak, #14344E, has a luminance of 0.0315, and the same text colour #0A99EE falls from 4.71 to 4.17. The purple and magenta apps passed because their pale backgrounds sit close to #1D2940: Convert Image (#2C2359, 0.0246) at 4.64 and SugarDoc (#32223C, 0.0215) at 4.66.

A second assumption, made while writing this note, was that raising the target to 4.6 would cover the hover too, but the 4.6 target is measured on #1D2940, so with today's formula the pair on the pale background is still 4.17.

The fix is a token per pair. fg-accent-contrast takes the dark accent and lightens it again, 1% at a time, until it reaches 4.6:1 on the pale background. For Arrow Knots that moves #0A99EE to #17A2F5 and 4.17 to 4.61. The header of sds_apps.py states the rule as T2: "text on bg-accent-weak is fg-accent-contrast".

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The gate computes 11 pairs per app, 143 today

Inside python tools/build.py --check, which AGENTS.md says to run before every commit, sds_gates() checks three things. The rest of that check is described in A static site that several AI agent sessions edit: one --check gate before every commit.

  • for each app, 11 pairs; any pair under 4.5:1 is an error, SDS contrast <app>: <pair names>. Pairs have names like white on accent, accent on basement and d-contrast on d-weak; the full list of 11 is in audit();
  • the tokens read back from the generated assets/sds-apps.css must equal what accent_tokens() computes (rule T1: a literal hex per app);
  • the header mark colours in site.css must match the social-image generator og.py.

The docstring explains the 4.6 target: "targets are 4.6:1 so rounding and browser blending never drop below 4.5:1". Every mix and lightness step rounds RGB to integers. Because of that margin, Block Turn (4.58) and SugarClip (4.59) also got their own token, and in the dark block of the generated CSS at b82faac, 9 of 11 apps declare a separate fg-accent-contrast.

We also ran a revert test. Setting Compress Image back to #00897B in the copy's apps.json made the gate print this (run with --check on 3 November, confirmed through audit() on 4 November):

error: SDS contrast sugarcompress: white on accent, accent on basement
1 gate error(s)

Two apps arrived later, CarDrawer (b79f2d1, 19 October) and TrimBox (7bb4744, 31 October). Each added one hex to apps.json, and sds_apps.py has not changed since b82faac. The gate now computes 13 apps x 11 pairs = 143 pairs. Had the hover kept fg-accent, 9 of the 13 would be under 4.5, with TrimBox at 4.22 and CarDrawer at 4.39.

Swap the CSS pairing and the gate still passes

On 3 November the agent that first drafted this note changed line 236 of the copy's site.css so the hover text was var(--sds-fg-accent) again, rebuilt, and ran --check, which printed up to date; gates passed with the 4.17:1 pair back in the stylesheet. The only thing sds_gates() reads from site.css is the header mark regex; contrast comes entirely from the token pairs listed in audit().

site.css uses bg-accent-weak as the background in six rules.

LineSelectorText tokenIn the gate's pairs?
210.app-tile:hoverfg-accent-contrastYes
236.button--outline:hoverfg-accent-contrastYes
242.badgefg-accent-contrastYes
250.trust lifg-accent-contrastYes
356[data-app] .notebody text fg-neutralNo
449.ax-ctanot setNo

On app pages, .note keeps fg-neutral body text (its border, links and the eyebrow use fg-accent-contrast: border on line 356, links and the eyebrow on line 358), and .ax-cta sets no text colour at all. Neither pair is among the 11, so neither is measured. We left both unfixed; that call belongs to whoever owns the build.

Both the mistakes and the catches in this history are recorded in AI co-authored commits or agent work. The spec rule that a new accent should be at least dE00 12 (a colour-distance measure) from existing ones was left out of the gate because "the new-key dE00 >= 12 rule needs a human to know which key is new"; the CLI only warns about pairs under dE00 8, currently 7 (smallest 2.2, Flip & Rotate Image and Arrow Knots).

color-mix() is banned by T3, and dark colours are not hand-picked

Letting the browser blend hover colours with CSS color-mix() is banned by rule T3. The gate compares literal hex values in the generated CSS with computed ones, and a browser-blended colour gives it nothing to compare. Hand-picking dark colours per app was dropped too: the site went from 11 apps to 13, and that approach means a person picking nine tokens for every new app.

We measured rendered pixels in another app; that write-up is Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text. sds_apps.py uses only the Python standard library and never starts a browser.

Without design tokens, with colours written per component, there is no pair list to compute in the first place. Gradients, text over photos and translucent layers don't reduce to two tokens, and this site doesn't measure them either.

From one accent hex to a 143-pair gate in six steps

  1. Keep one accent hex per brand or app in your source data and derive every other token with a function.
  2. Write down every text-on-background pair. Then search the CSS for rules that use each background token (grep -n "accent-weak" assets/site.css) and check each rule's text token against your list, as in the table above.
  3. Aim a little above 4.5 (we use 4.6), and give any pair that falls short its own token.
  4. Fail the build check when any pair is under 4.5:1, and compare the generated CSS values with the computed ones.
  5. Put an old failing colour into apps.json and run python tools/build.py --check: expect a line containing 1 gate error(s), and a line containing up to date; gates passed again once you revert. Then deliberately mismatch a CSS pairing, rebuild with build.py and run --check. Here it still says gates passed.
  6. Run python tools/sds_apps.py to print the colour-distance warnings and have a person look; today it lists 7 pairs under dE00 8.

Don't leave a contrast rule as a sentence in a doc. Make the build compute it from a list of colour pairs, and check that the list matches the pairs your CSS actually uses. We have only done the first half. The next step is a --check stage that extracts the text token of every rule with a bg-accent-weak background and compares it with the 11 pairs, and before that, measuring the .note body text and the .ax-cta text for the first time.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Which text does the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast minimum apply to?

Normal-size text. WCAG 2 success criterion 1.4.3 sets 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Our gate ignores text size and applies 4.5:1 to all 11 pairs.

How is a contrast ratio calculated?

Take the relative luminance of both colours, L1 for the lighter and L2 for the darker, and compute (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). Relative luminance linearises the sRGB channels and sums 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. The contrast() function in sds_apps.py is this formula.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Removing a feature after it moved to a sibling app – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Retrospective

10,001 lines of greeting cards: built with an AI agent, removed with one

In 1.6.020, which shipped the greeting card removal together with R8 optimization, the APK went from 25.66 MB to 13.15 MB; about 11 MB of that drop was greeting card assets.

A single commit, f6ef50e, deleted 143 files and 10,001 lines and ended the greeting card feature in SugarSpeller, our Korean spell-check app. It landed on the night of September 20, 2026, 35 minutes after the operator said the feature had been forced into the app in the first place. The feature itself had arrived in 41 commits between August 31 and December 10, 2025, and 38 of those commits credit Claude. In January 2026 the code was taken into a sibling app, SugarCard, yet it stayed in the original app for eight more months.

Sources: git history of the spell-check app and of SugarCard, the spell-check app's CHANGELOG entry for 1.6.020, a post-release monitoring document (GA4 counts), and the work session log of September 20 to 22, 2026. Numbers were recounted from git on November 4, 2026.

13.70 MB of deleted files, 0.22 MB of app Kotlin

f6ef50e deleted 124 files, modified 18 and added one. The deletions covered three greeting screens (ActivityMainGreeting, a card editor and a card fragment), a Room database for cards, an MP4 encoder and audio muxer for a falling-snow video, the card images, seven carols, a handwriting font called Gamja Flower, 13 unit tests and one instrumented test. Of the 10,001 deleted lines, 7,857 were Kotlin and 2,124 were XML.

Summing the original blob sizes of the deleted files gives 13.70 MB, and the 15 app Kotlin sources account for 0.22 MB of it. The 69 files in the card image folder came to 6.68 MB, one background image, retro.png, to 3.91 MB, the font to 1.07 MB, the seven carols to 1.02 MB and the Lottie snow animation to 0.34 MB. (The commit message rounds the first three to 6.5, 3.8 and 1.1 MB.)

The sizes below come from the CHANGELOG. The baseline is the pre-change HEAD (1.6.019) rebuilt in the same environment.

1.6.019 baseline1.6.020
APK (unsigned)25.66 MB13.15 MB (−48.7%)
AAB29.95 MB18.33 MB (−38.8%)
DEX (uncompressed)16.31 MB14.84 MB (−9.0%)

Crediting that whole drop to the greeting cards would be wrong. The same release carried a597223, which deleted the single -dontoptimize line that had kept R8 from optimizing. The CHANGELOG splits the result: about 11 MB was greeting card assets, and the optimization's share sits inside the 1.5 MB DEX reduction. The optimization side has its own note, Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized.

Commits claimed 95% coverage; the repo had no coverage tool

The first commit, 0a0f404 on August 31, 2025, added 2,495 lines across 21 files, built the card list and a Room module, and claimed "95% coverage (30+ test cases)". Two more commits that day fixed a clash between Material 3 and the app's existing theme. On September 3, be41ccb, titled as a complete Y2K glitch-neon card editor, touched 60 files and reported "zero memory leaks and crashes". On September 10 greeting cards became a third screen mode, UIMode.GREETING, next to the chat and classic layouts. Holiday categories followed in late November, and on December 7 and 8 a ten-second falling-snow MP4 share and seven carols.

24 of the 41 commits landed in September 2025. Together they added 18,087 lines and deleted 9,188 (docs included, over 102 days).

Five of those commits (six, counting the docs commit db2ee27 from the same week) claim 95% or 99% test coverage. Neither git log --all -S jacoco nor -S kover returns a single line anywhere in the repository's history, so no coverage tool was ever installed. The habit of writing "complete" into commit subjects is counted in A year of AI coding in 701 commits. The Room database that the first commit called "a complete greeting module" had zero callers in the app code (main) outside its own four files when it was deleted. And on September 11, c05d669 made the greeting screen the default for users with no saved mode and forced that mode in debug builds. About 24 hours later 0c5ceab put the default back to chat. The next release tag was November 28, so no shipped version had the greeting default.

A third main screen, and a copy kept for eight months

Greeting cards came in as one of three parallel main screens, not as a separate module. Card artwork and carols therefore shipped in the APK of every user who only wanted spell checks, and any fix to the main screen had to be made three times.

The structure stayed after the sibling app existed. SugarCard's first commit, c623dd8 on January 15, 2026, started with 297 files and 17,030 lines, and its message says "Greeting card functionality migrated from sugarspeller". Nobody removed the feature from the original app at that point. Between then and September 13, five commits in the spell-check app edited ActivityMainGreeting, and all five were shared fixes for ads or the back button made alongside the chat screen. The September 13 fix for "press back again to exit" (289ed55) changed 26, 23 and 22 lines in the three screens. We found no record of why the removal waited.

When a feature moves to another app, delete it from the original app in the same release. During those eight months this app got five shared fixes that also had to patch a screen that already lived in SugarCard.

Two menu entries became links; saved values fall back to chat

On September 20 the operator asked to take greeting cards out of this app entirely, keep the two buttons in the side drawer and the top mode menu but send them to SugarCard, and focus the app on Korean spelling. The operator also expected the app to get much smaller. Six minutes later the operator added Play's code optimization requirement (deadline February 2027) to the same job, which became a597223.

The kept buttons now call a new SugarCardLauncher. If SugarCard is installed it opens the app; otherwise it tries market://, and if that fails, the https store page. Since Android 11 (API 30) an app has to declare another package under <queries> in its manifest to see whether it is installed, so the manifest gained one entry. Each tap logs sugarcard_open(installed) to GA4.

Users who had picked greeting mode before updating still have the string "greeting" in their settings. The code that reads the mode already sent unknown values to chat:

fun fromString(value: String?): UIMode {
    return values().find { it.value == value } ?: CHAT
}

So there is no migration code. UIModeTest gained one test asserting that "greeting" resolves to CHAT, with a comment saying these users must not get stuck behind the splash screen.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The agent guessed 10 MB and 9 tests; a person checked the device

The agent's plan named the screens and modules to remove, but its numbers were low. It added card images (6.5 MB), retro.png (3.8 MB) and the snow animation (0.3 MB) to get "roughly 10 MB", and counted 9 unit tests to delete. The real commit also removed the font and the seven carols, and deleted 13 unit tests.

The agent had no device attached, said so, and left a release APK signed with the debug key. It asked the operator to try checks against Naver and Daum (two Korean portals whose spell-check results the app parses), history, subscriptions, KakaoTalk sharing and the greeting card menu. The operator replied the next day that everything worked, and 1.6.020 shipped on September 22.

One wrong assumption stayed in the launcher. If opening market:// threw, it fell back to the browser, and the comment on that branch read "device without the Play Store app". On October 9 the same pattern was added for a games menu (efc0acf). On a Galaxy S21 the link showed a chooser instead of an exception, because three store apps accepted it. 8bbe179, 59 minutes after the games commit, made both the game and SugarCard links target the Play package first. The full account is in A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones.

The menus stayed, opened the app first, and shipped in one release

Deleting the menus too was ruled out by the operator's first request. The Korean label lost its "switch to" wording, since tapping it no longer switches modes.

Sending every tap straight to the store was an option the agent raised in its plan. The operator kept the app-first order, which is why the manifest needs <queries>. As the launcher comment says, without that declaration the installed check always fails and every tap goes to the store.

Shipping the removal and the R8 change in separate releases would have made the size change easy to attribute. The operator chose to ship them together, which is why the size section uses a separately built baseline.

Stored user data would change the order

This removal needed no data migration only because no screen called the Room database by the time of removal (none had since September 3, 2025, and no release shipped while one did). If users had saved cards in it, an export path or a handoff to the sibling app would have to come first.

If the mode parser had thrown on unknown values, one test would not have been enough. Updated users could get stuck at launch, and a migration that rewrites the saved value would have to ship first.

We found no record of how often the greeting screens were used; the only numbers are menu taps after the removal. For a feature many people use, check screen usage before deleting it.

Steps for handing a feature to a sibling app

  1. Count the files and bytes to be deleted with git. Get the deleted blobs from git diff --raw and sum them with git cat-file -s, so you know whether lines or bytes dominate.
  2. Count the callers of the module with git grep -l. Zero callers outside the module means no data migration.
  3. Read where a saved setting goes when its value no longer exists, and pin that path with one unit test.
  4. If the menu stays, add a sibling-app launcher. Declare the package under <queries>, and open the store in this order: market:// targeted at the Play package, plain market://, then the https page.
  5. Compare sizes against the pre-change HEAD built in the same environment. If the release has other changes, split the shares.
  6. Install the release APK on a real device and tap the kept menu with the sibling app installed and not installed.
  7. Log menu taps with the installed state to see demand.

We don't yet know whether the 54 taps became installs

In the two weeks after release (September 22 to October 5), sugarcard_open fired 54 times from about 39 users, and SugarCard was installed at the moment of the tap in none of them, so every tap went to the store (GA4, per the monitoring document). Another 61 SugarCard taps came in from October 9 to 22; installed only records the state at tap time. Starting with 1.6.027 the event is called sibling_app_open (target=sugarcard); the next step is to line it up against SugarCard's install sources.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

What happens to users who saved a mode that the update removes?

It depends on where the parser sends unknown values. This app's fromString already mapped unknown values to chat, so a leftover "greeting" opens the chat screen, and a unit test pins that path.

I removed a feature and the APK barely shrank. What should I check?

Check the bytes of the deleted files first. Here 10,001 lines went away but the app's Kotlin sources were 0.22 MB; the size came from images, a font and audio.

Why does my check for another installed app always say "not installed"?

Since Android 11 (API 30), getLaunchIntentForPackage only finds the other app if its package is declared under <queries> in the manifest. f6ef50e declared just SugarCard's package; more were added later for the games menu.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: SAF PDF save: cancelling without empty files – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

We pressed BACK at seven moments before shipping one 'Save as PDF' button

BACK pressed at seven delays after the Save tap split cancel from done at 0.9 to 1.0 s on a Galaxy S20 and 0.75 to 0.9 s on a Galaxy S21, and left no empty file.

This is the release check of 'Save as PDF' in HWP Viewer SugarDoc 1.2.0 on October 18, 2026, run on a minified release build. BACK went in between 0.3 and 1.8 s after the Save tap, and neither side of either boundary left a partial file. Only after that did 'PDF Save' go into the store title.

Sources: the app repository's 1.2.0 release record, commits 6687cd0 and c4f1dd3 (Oct 18, 2026), the app store optimization (ASO) plan, and the Claude Code session logs from Oct 17-18 (reports from the implementing, reviewing and release-checking agents). Numbers rechecked against the repository on Nov 4, 2026. Device serials are left out.

The BACK boundary: 0.9 to 1.0 s on the S20, 0.75 to 0.9 s on the S21

The test document was a 47-page HWP file (HWP is the Korean word processor format the app opens). SugarDoc saves at most the first 15 pages of a long document, so the save shows a notice that only the first 15 of 47 pages will be saved and then writes a 15-page PDF. After tapping Save in the system file picker, the script sent BACK at 0.3, 0.45, 0.6, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0 and 1.8 s, then checked the Download folder: was a file left, and if so, did it start with %PDF-, end with %%EOF and hold all 15 pages?

On the Galaxy S20 (Android 13), BACK up to 0.9 s cancelled the save and the file was deleted; from 1.0 s the save had already finished and the full 15-page PDF stayed. On the Galaxy S21 (Android 15), BACK cancelled up to 0.75 s and met a finished save from 0.9 s. Neither phone produced a zero-byte file, a header-only file or a crash.

Three conditions before 'PDF Save' could go in the title

SugarDoc had a 'Print / Save as PDF' menu item since 1.0.0: it opened the system print screen, where the user picks 'Save as PDF' instead of a printer. On October 17 we started work on the app's Play search ranking, and the lead agent assumed PDF saving had never shipped. A research agent that read the code corrected it. What was missing was a direct save that skips the print screen, and a store title that says the app can do it.

The ASO plan written that day put three conditions on the new title, 'SugarDoc HWP Viewer & PDF Save' in English: the direct save ships; a minified release build saves and reopens a PDF on recorded devices; the saved PDF opens in another PDF app. A user who arrives from that title and meets a print dialog is likely to leave a one-star "PDF save doesn't work" review, and with zero reviews at the time, that one review would be the whole rating.

Two ways of building it were dropped. Drawing pages into a PdfDocument inside the app had already failed an earlier spike: a 50-page manual peaked at 1.95 GB of memory and writeTo took 10.9 s, and bundling fonts would push the APK past its 26 MB size gate. Saving past the 15-page cap by writing 15-page chunks and merging them was out too: the WebView renderer holds about 7 to 8 MB per page until the document closes, and a PDF merge library would need its own license check. So the save keeps the WebView PrintDocumentAdapter the print path already used and only swaps the destination for a document SAF creates. The cap stays the same as printing: 15 pages, 6 on low-end phones.

One save passes five stages, and the empty file comes first

'Save as PDF' starts the system picker with ActivityResultContracts.CreateDocument("application/pdf"), which is SAF's ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT. When the user names the file and taps Save, the document provider creates an empty document right there and returns its URI. The app records that URI as a just-picked target and refuses to write or delete any URI that is not on that list, because the app has a rule never to write to a user's original files.

Next the app lays out the pages through the same path as printing, opens the file on an IO thread with openFileDescriptor(uri, "wt") (falling back to "w" for providers that refuse truncation), and calls onStart, onLayout, onWrite and onFinish on the WebView print adapter itself, with no print dialog. The result callbacks have constructors that are package-private in the SDK, so only that piece lives in the android.print package, as a 99-line file; there is no reflection. When the write ends the app checks for a zero-byte file and closes it. A failed or cancelled save deletes the created document with DocumentsContract.deleteDocument.

The document exists before any byte is written, so a stop at any later stage leaves a named, empty PDF in the user's folder unless the app deletes it. Close and delete is the default on any stop, but while the WebView is writing to the fd, closing it was the dangerous part.

Defect 1: the fd was closed while the WebView was still writing

The implementing agent's first version closed the fd and deleted the file as soon as a save stopped, whether from BACK, a timeout or the reader closing, without waiting for the WebView's write result. Its report listed this as a risk and assumed that a late write would simply fail. The debug build passed 17/17 on both phones and all 504 unit tests were green.

A review agent started in a fresh context rated that assumption a High defect. According to the review and the code comment that now sits on the writer, the WebView (Chromium's AwPrintManager) writes to the raw fd number from a background thread without duplicating it. Once the app closes the number, another file the app opens next, a database or a document copy, can get the same number, and the late PDF bytes land in that file instead of failing. onFinish was also being called before the write ended. We did not open the Chromium source ourselves this time.

The fixed writer reports a settled flag with the result. A stop before the write starts is settled, so the app closes and deletes at once. A stop during the write is not settled: the app leaves the fd open, never counts it as saved and deletes the document, and the writer calls onFinish and closes the fd after the adapter's own write result arrives. If the WebView never answers, one fd stays open until the process ends; the review judged that a smaller harm than a corrupted file. Three Robolectric tests pin this rule.

No person edited this code. The review happened because of the operator's standing rules: get a review from a separate context after a large change, and do not call anything done before the minified release build has run on real phones.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Defects 2 and 3 sat in the short gap while the file opened

Defect 2 lost BACK presses. The cancel handle was registered when the write started, and while the file was opening on the IO thread after page layout, the handle was still empty, so a BACK in that gap was ignored and the save went on. The implementing agent had listed this gap among its risks. The review added a pending-cancel flag that stops the write the moment the handle is registered, plus one controller test.

Defect 3 was the Activity going away while the file opened. If the coroutine was cancelled there, the opened result could be dropped: the fd would leak, an empty PDF could stay in the user's folder and the progress cover could stay up. Now the cancellation handler closes the fd, deletes the document, ends the save as cancelled and rethrows. This is Activity code, so there is no JVM test; it was checked on the phones by recreating the screen and killing the process.

After the three fixes, unit tests stood at 508 debug (504 + 3 + 1) and 469 release, all passing. The guard-removal table, which deletes each guard in turn and expects a test to fail, grew from 29 to 32 rows. The review also noted that some existing rows only pinned source strings, so breaking the behaviour while keeping the string would still pass; the Robolectric tests cover that. The guard-removal method has its own note, 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database: checking tests by deleting the guard.

Four of the first five delays hit a finished save

The release-checking agent first chose BACK delays of 0.3, 1.0, 1.8, 2.6 and 3.5 s. In the first S21 run, on an earlier build with the flag on, only 0.3 s cancelled. The other four all left a complete 15-page PDF of 851,990 bytes: BACK arrived after the save had finished and just closed the reader, leaving the launcher on top.

Seeing that, the agent packed six delays between 0.3 and 1.0 s and kept 1.8 s, which produced the boundaries at the top of this note. The same first run had two failures, both from the test method. The developer option always_finish_activities did not take effect when changed at run time, so Activity recreation moved to a font_scale change and process death to am kill. Chrome 155 on the phones would not open a content:// PDF, so the Chrome check stopped counting as pass or fail.

On the 1.2.0 (5) build the 37 items passed 37/37 on the S21 and 36/37 on the S20. The S20 failure came from uiautomator dump dying with an NPE. The base script's crash filter did not match on the package name, so it counted the test tool's crash; that log had zero lines from the app's package. A rerun on the earlier flag-on build scored 37/37 on both phones.

The SAF save checklist we ran on the release build

These are the items from the 37 that carry over to other apps, in order. Run all of them on a minified release build with the feature flag on; a debug build never exercises code that R8 removed or rewrote.

  1. Cancel in the picker and confirm no file appears.
  2. Save a small document and check the %PDF- header, %%EOF and the page count. We used a 3-page HWPX.
  3. Save a document over the cap and check the notice and the capped page count (15).
  4. Reopen the saved PDF in the app twice. We got 15 drawn pages and 0 failed pages.
  5. Find when the save finishes with a coarse grid of BACK delays, then press again every 0.15 s in front of that point. Each time, check for leftover files, zero bytes, header and end marker, and crashes.
  6. Cancel with BACK after 0.15 s, then save again and confirm it works.
  7. Recreate the Activity while the picker is up, and 0, 0.3 and 0.6 s after the save. Changing font_scale does it.
  8. Kill the process with am kill while the picker is up and confirm no empty file is left when the result comes back.
  9. Count Accessing hidden lines for the app process, StrictMode and R8 errors (ClassNotFound, NoSuchMethod) in logcat, and filter the crash buffer by the app's package. All were 0 on this build.
  10. Open the saved PDF in another PDF app. The phone's Chrome refused it, so we checked all 15 pages in desktop Chrome.

If you ship a SAF save, do not stop after pressing BACK at one moment. Here cancel and done were 0.1 to 0.15 s apart. On Oct 18, the day of this run, commit 6687cd0 went in at 10:53 KST, the operator ran the production promotion command by hand at 12:08, and commit c4f1dd3 applied the new title at 12:11 (the desktop Chrome check is recorded in that commit).

Whether BACK hit the write stage could not be seen from outside

From outside the phone there was no way to tell whether BACK landed during page layout or while the bytes were being written to the file. What we know is that on both sides of the cancel-to-done boundary (0.75 to 1.0 s) there were no leftover files, no zero-byte files and no crashes. We did not watch the defect 1 fix act mid-write on a device.

The boundaries come from two phones and one 47-page document. Another phone or another document will have its own boundary, so the grid has to be found again. The write-timeout path cannot be forced on a device and was checked only by unit tests. If a document provider hands over a pipe instead of a regular file, the size reads as -1, the zero-byte check does nothing, and the app trusts the adapter's result callback alone.

The WebView print path and the 222-document measurements are in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents.

A 6-page-cap phone and saving to Drive are still untested

We had no phone in the low-end tier (6-page cap), so that path has only unit tests. Saves went only to the default Download folder; Google Drive, SD cards and other document providers were not tried. There are no records yet for an S23, tablets or foldables, landscape, or saving with TalkBack on. For Drive, the first question is whether it actually takes the pipe path above.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does cancelling ACTION_CREATE_DOCUMENT leave an empty file?

Cancelling in the picker returns a null URI and creates no file. After the user taps Save, the provider creates an empty document first, so if your write fails or is cancelled after that, you must delete it yourself with DocumentsContract.deleteDocument.

Can I close the ParcelFileDescriptor right away when the user cancels?

Only if the write has not started. If a WebView print adapter is already writing, keep the fd open until the adapter's write result arrives. Another file of your app can reuse a number you closed early, and late PDF bytes can land in it.

Can a WebView be saved as a PDF without the print dialog?

It can: call onStart, onLayout, onWrite and onFinish on the adapter from createPrintDocumentAdapter yourself. The result callback constructors are package-private in the SDK, so the file that creates them must sit in the android.print package, and you should check a release build for hidden-API warnings and R8 errors.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Quiz reach rose from 2.6% to 17.7%, and 63% of quiz opens came from one morning notification
  • 203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names

item.title: Gemini in an Android app: cost, eval, daily caps – SugarMount
item.description:
AX Notes · Measurement

The first LLM feature in a spell-check app: cost, model evaluation and daily caps for "Why is this wrong?"

A 59-case eval picked the model at $0.93 per 1,000 calls (about $1.1 after the v3 prompt the next day). Spend is capped by the function itself, which refuses LLM calls past 3,000 a day.

The first eval run on the night of September 27, 2026 failed on all 59 calls with HTTP 402. It used an AI Studio key that the coding agent had said around noon that day would be billed against our Firebase credit, and we were in the middle of giving our Korean spelling app SugarSpeller its first server function and LLM. After the key was replaced with Vertex AI, gemini-3.8-flash gave a correct reason for all 59 corrections (the right rule for 54), with a p95 latency of 4.3 seconds and a cost of $0.93 per 1,000 calls. In the two weeks after the October 1 release, 3.7% of users who ran a check tapped the button; among users who had opened the correction sheet, it was 41%.

Sources: the design doc in the app repository (approved 2026-09-27), commits de79cfd, 350a6c6, df8f740 and 4c99287, the WATCH.md decision log (rows for Oct 17 and Oct 28), and the agent session log. Usage comes from GA4; cost comes from the usage documents the function writes to Firestore. Rechecked against the repository on 2026-11-02. Times are Korea Standard Time (UTC+9). Cloud project and account identifiers are left out.

The 59-case eval: flash-lite at 78%, 3.8-flash at 100%

The feature explains one correction at a time: the user taps a corrected word and gets a one-line reason plus the name of the Korean orthography rule behind it. We picked the model with 59 corrections taken from real checker responses stored as test fixtures in the app: 38 from Naver's spell checker and 21 from Daum's (Naver and Daum are the two big Korean portals, and the app uses their checkers). The pass mark was written into the design doc before the run: at least 90% correct and a p95 of 2.5 seconds or less. Every call went to the Vertex AI global endpoint.

Model (prompt)Reason correctRule also correctp50 / p95Per 1,000
gemini-3.5-flash-lite (v1)43/59 (73%)30/591.06 s / 1.26 s$0.27
gemini-3.5-flash-lite (v2)46/59 (78%)38/591.08 s / 4.6 s$0.42
gemini-3.8-flash (v2)59/59 (100%)54/59 (92%)2.0 s / 4.3 s$0.93

Prompt v2 added an order of checks for spacing errors and a table of reasons for the most common corrections. It moved flash-lite from 73% to 78% and no further. Its wrong answers included explaining a noun fused with hada ("to do") as an ending or particle, garbled syllables, and calling an archaic spelling of a polite ending a past tense. 3.8-flash made no typos; its five misses were all wrong rule citations. It costs more than twice as much as flash-lite v2 per 1,000 calls, and it was the only model over the 90% bar, so it became the default.

The first 3.8-flash run returned 59 empty answers. The model's thinking tokens used up the 160-token output limit before any JSON came out; setting thinkingBudget: 0 fixed it. The 2.5-second target was missed. This model is served only from the global endpoint (the Seoul and Tokyo regions returned 404), and each call took 2.1 to 2.8 seconds. Because that was still inside the app's 8-second timeout and the button shows a progress indicator, the design doc moved the target to a p95 of 5 seconds.

The AI Studio key never touched the $300 credit

The 402 came from billing. The error read Your prepayment credits are depleted, and authentication had succeeded. In this project, AI Studio billing was prepaid only, so it had no link to the 90-day $300 free-trial credit (held in Cloud Billing) that came with moving the Firebase project to the pay-as-you-go Blaze plan.

At 12:01 the agent wrote that with the $300 credit, paid-tier Gemini API usage would be billed to the same project, and ten minutes later it produced a table showing the credit applied to both. The spec switched to keyless Vertex AI at 12:18 (220b267), then at 12:21 went back to an AI Studio key the operator had already created, on the grounds that it shared the billing account (740b9d5).

The function, the quota code and the cache were all tested against a fake provider during the day, so the first real Gemini call was the eval run around 10 p.m. When the agent reported the 402 at 22:04, its first recommendation was to buy AI Studio prepaid credit (minimum $5). At 22:06 the operator asked why, if the $300 was supposed to cover it. The agent then said its earlier explanation was wrong: AI Studio keys used to bill a project's Cloud billing account after the fact, and this project didn't work that way.

Commit de79cfd at 22:10 moved Gemini authentication to Vertex AI with ADC (Application Default Credentials, the service account the code already runs as). Vertex bills through Cloud Billing, which per the design doc is where the credit applies, and there is no API key to store or rotate. The deploy 49 minutes later hit one more snag: declaring an unused secret on the function was enough to make the deploy query Secret Manager and fail with 403, so the secret is now declared only in key mode (e67a4f7).

Before building an LLM feature, make one real call and check which bill it lands on. A 200 response does not say which balance paid for it. After the move to Vertex, this app computed its cost from token counts the function records times the list price, and the repository has no record of the credit deduction being checked against a billing report.

The function refuses LLM calls past 3,000 a day

explainCorrection is a single callable function on Cloud Functions for Firebase (2nd gen). The app signs in anonymously when its process opens the first screen, and the Firebase SDK attaches the auth token to each call. The function validates input, checks the cache, takes from the quota, calls the LLM, then stores the result. The cache comes before the quota, so an explanation that already exists costs the user nothing.

ControlDefaultHow to change it
Free quota5 a day per anonymous uidFirestore doc config/limits (cached 60 s)
Subscriber ceiling100 a day per uidSame doc
Global cap3,000 LLM attempts a daySame doc; 0 closes it
App Check enforcementOff (measured only); current setting unconfirmedrequireAppCheck in the same doc
Button in the appOnRemote Config explain_enabled = false

The day rolls over at midnight Korea time. The day key is computed by adding nine hours to UTC milliseconds rather than trusting the server's time zone. The global cap counts LLM attempts, not requests: retries and hedged duplicates each count, and only attempts that failed before billing (network errors and the like) are given back. Timeouts stay counted, because the provider may already have charged for them.

A budget alert sends an email and does not stop charges, which is why the design doc calls the 3,000-call cap the real safeguard. At the eval price ($0.93), a full day at the cap is about $2.8; with the longer v3 prompt from September 28 (about $1.1 per 1,000) it is about $3.3 by our calculation. A call cap works as a money cap only because each call is bounded: the original and corrected words are limited to 60 code points each, and the output to 160 tokens. The agent's morning estimate (under 0.1 won per call, under 1,000 won a month) used flash-lite prices; the chosen model costs 3.4 times flash-lite v1 per 1,000 calls.

In the first release stage the function trusts the app's claim that the user subscribes. A forged claim buys 95 extra explanations a day at under 10 won (well under a cent), so receipt checks were deferred. Putting the daily total document in the same transaction as the user's quota made concurrent requests die on lock timeouts, and on September 28 the total moved outside the transaction (73085eb). As a result, the global cap can overshoot by the number of requests in flight.

Remote Config refreshed only on the launcher screen, and people who used only the mini window (opened from text selection in another app) never pass through it, so switching off explain_enabled would have left their button in place. The September 29 release review caught it, and the mini window now fetches config before it opens the sheet (4c99287).

A 7.9-second cold start pushed the app timeout to 15 seconds

The smoke test after the production deploy on the night of September 27 measured 7.9 seconds for the first call and 1.6 to 3.0 seconds after that. The function runs with zero minimum instances, and the app's timeout was 8 seconds, so a cold call came within 0.1 seconds of it. Commit df8f740 raised the app timeout to 15 seconds. Keeping one instance warm (about $3 to $4 a month) stayed in the function docs as a fallback if cold starts became a problem. LLM calls on October 26 and 27 cost $0.020 in total, so the warm instance would cost far more than the feature itself.

The next day, one repeated eval call that stretched to 44.5 seconds set the server-side deadlines: 6 seconds per attempt and 12 for the whole request. From October 25 the function hedges: if an attempt is silent for 4 seconds, it sends the same request again and takes whichever answers first. Failures went from 16 of 25 in the October 24 function log to 0 of 16 on October 26 and 27.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

3.7% of checking users, 41% of sheet openers

The decision rule went into WATCH.md before release. Fourteen days in, if 8% or more of users who ran a check tapped the button, keep it; under 3%, test a new position and wording. The October 17 review (October 2 to 16, app 1.6.025 or later) counted 56 of 1,527 checking users, 3.7%, with 77 requests. That sits between the two thresholds.

Over the same period, 138 users (9.0%) tapped a corrected word to open the sheet, and 56 of them pressed the button. 41% of people who reached the sheet wanted the reason, so the bottleneck was finding the sheet rather than the button. Version 1.6.031, rolled out in stages from October 18, added a one-time hint that the highlighted words can be tapped.

With about 8 requests a day, the 14-day cache hit rate was 11% against a 40% target. How the shared cache key was built is covered in the blind A/B that let us stop sending context to the LLM.

Mass-created anonymous accounts hit only the global cap

A uid's quota starts over when the app is reinstalled. A script that keeps creating anonymous accounts makes the per-user limit of 5 meaningless; what remains is the global 3,000 and App Check, which defaults to measuring only. If one explanation were expensive, verify the subscription on the server from day one.

The 59 cases came only from the checkers' red, green and blue groups (Naver red 25, green 13; Daum red 14, green 5, blue 2); there was not one purple or violet case, and the September 27 scoring was done by the same agent that wrote the code. No human scored it. A model that lives only on the global endpoint also changes what a privacy policy can say about where data is processed; another of our apps ran into that with the same model, written up in the privacy-policy note on AI processing location.

Adding the same feature to your app

  1. Make one real model call through a path that bills to Cloud Billing (Vertex AI here). On 402 or 403, stop and settle the billing path first. On 200, check the billing report for the credit deduction.
  2. Pull about 50 cases from your app's test data and put accuracy, p95 and cost per 1,000 calls for each candidate in one table. Write the pass mark first, and set the thinking budget of thinking models to 0.
  3. Expose one callable function that requires anonymous auth, with three limits (free per user, subscriber ceiling, global) keyed by day in your users' time zone. Keep the limits in a document you can change without a deploy, with 0 meaning closed.
  4. Cap input length and output tokens.
  5. Give the app a remote switch that hides the button, and check that every entry screen refreshes it.
  6. After the production deploy, time the first call to a cold instance and set the app timeout above it. Before release, write the decision rule: two usage thresholds, cache hit rate, failure rate and daily cost.

The default limits and the thinking switch (MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS is 160):

// functions/src/limits.ts
export const DEFAULT_LIMITS: Limits = { freePerDay: 5, entitledPerDay: 100, globalPerDay: 3000, requireAppCheck: false };
// functions/src/llm/gemini.ts, part of the generateContent config
maxOutputTokens: MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS,
thinkingConfig: { thinkingBudget: 0 },

Still open: usage after the tap hint, and a price doubling

The tap hint in 1.6.031 is judged by whether 6% or more of users who saw it request an explanation. The review was due November 1, and as of November 2 the log has no row for it yet. 3.8-flash is scheduled to double in price on January 1, 2027, to $1.50 input and $7.50 output per million tokens; on that day the prices and the worst-day figure need recalculating. We also haven't seen a real bill yet, since the 90-day credit is still running.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can Firebase Blaze credit pay for the Gemini API?

Per the design doc, only Vertex AI is on the credit path in this project; we haven't confirmed it on an invoice yet. The AI Studio key was on prepaid-only billing, so all 59 eval calls on September 27, 2026 were rejected with 402.

How do you cap the cost of an LLM feature?

Count LLM calls inside the function and refuse them past a daily limit. A budget alert only sends an email. This app closes at 3,000 calls a day, and one Firestore document can change that number or set it to 0 without a deploy.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • No XML file said white, yet the dialog buttons vanished: three places a theme colour leaked
  • Quiz reach rose from 2.6% to 17.7%, and 63% of quiz opens came from one morning notification
  • 203 unit tests missed a release-only blank result: R8 and Gson field names
  • We pressed BACK at seven moments before shipping one 'Save as PDF' button
  • App campaign ad assets from gameplay recordings
